label: II-2
title: Construction — Fire protection, fire detection and fire extinction
text: Construction — Fire protection, fire detection and fire extinction Sets the structural and system-based fire-safety requirements for the ship as a whole, organised into parts covering general provisions, structural fire protection, and fire suppression/detection systems. Regulation 10 within this chapter is Part C's core requirement for active fire-fighting capability. Sets the structural and system-based fire-safety requirements for the ship as a whole, organised into parts covering general provisions, structural fire protection, and fire suppression/detection systems. Regulation 10 within this chapter is Part C's core requirement for active fire-fighting capability.

title: Application
text: Application Applies structural and operational fire safety requirements to ships constructed (keel laid) on or after 1 July 2002; defines core functional objectives including division of ship into main vertical zones, restricted use of combustible materials, detection and containment of fire, and preservation of escape routes. Applies structural and operational fire safety requirements to ships constructed (keel laid) on or after 1 July 2002; defines core functional objectives including division of ship into main vertical zones, restricted use of combustible materials, detection and containment of fire, and preservation of escape routes.

title: Application dates and keel-laying thresholds
text: Application dates and keel-laying thresholds Unless expressly provided otherwise, Chapter II-2 applies to ships constructed on or after 1 July 2002; ships constructed before 1 July 2002 shall comply with requirements applicable before that date. Unless expressly provided otherwise, Chapter II-2 applies to ships constructed on or after 1 July 2002; ships constructed before 1 July 2002 shall comply with requirements applicable before that date.

title: Fire safety objectives and functional requirements
text: Fire safety objectives and functional requirements Sets fundamental safety objectives to prevent fire and explosion, reduce risk to life, reduce risk of damage to ship and cargo, and contain/extinguish fire in space of origin. Sets fundamental safety objectives to prevent fire and explosion, reduce risk to life, reduce risk of damage to ship and cargo, and contain/extinguish fire in space of origin.

title: Probability of ignition
text: Probability of ignition Requires arrangements to prevent ignition of flammable materials, including insulation of hot surfaces exceeding 220°C, jacketing of high-pressure fuel oil lines, protection of flammable liquid storage, and cargo tank inerting for oil tankers. Requires arrangements to prevent ignition of flammable materials, including insulation of hot surfaces exceeding 220°C, jacketing of high-pressure fuel oil lines, protection of flammable liquid storage, and cargo tank inerting for oil tankers.

title: Arrangements for fuel oil, lube oil and other flammable oils
text: Arrangements for fuel oil, lube oil and other flammable oils Uninsulated surfaces exceeding 220°C capable of igniting fuel spray must be insulated; high-pressure fuel delivery lines between high-pressure pumps and fuel injectors must be shielded with a jacketed piping system to contain fuel spray. Uninsulated surfaces exceeding 220°C capable of igniting fuel spray must be insulated; high-pressure fuel delivery lines between high-pressure pumps and fuel injectors must be shielded with a jacketed piping system to contain fuel spray.

title: Gaseous fuel arrangements for domestic purposes
text: Gaseous fuel arrangements for domestic purposes Gaseous fuel systems used for domestic purposes shall be approved by the Administration and stored in dedicated, well-ventilated spaces on open decks. Gaseous fuel systems used for domestic purposes shall be approved by the Administration and stored in dedicated, well-ventilated spaces on open decks.

title: Cargo tank inerting requirements for oil tankers
text: Cargo tank inerting requirements for oil tankers Oil tankers of 20,000 DWT and above (and new oil tankers of 8,000 DWT and above constructed on or after 1 January 2016) carrying crude oil or petroleum products with flashpoint under 60°C must be fitted with a fixed inert gas system complying with FSS Code Chapter 15. Oil tankers of 20,000 DWT and above (and new oil tankers of 8,000 DWT and above constructed on or after 1 January 2016) carrying crude oil or petroleum products with flashpoint under 60°C must be fitted with a fixed inert gas system complying with FSS Code Chapter 15.

title: Containment of fire
text: Containment of fire Requires fire integrity of bulkheads and decks to preserve structural divisions ('A-60', 'A-30', 'A-15', 'A-0', 'B-15', 'C' ratings) and sets construction and damper rules for ventilation duct penetrations. Requires fire integrity of bulkheads and decks to preserve structural divisions ('A-60', 'A-30', 'A-15', 'A-0', 'B-15', 'C' ratings) and sets construction and damper rules for ventilation duct penetrations.

title: Fire integrity of bulkheads and decks
text: Fire integrity of bulkheads and decks Bulkheads and decks separating adjacent spaces must maintain fire integrity according to fire division tables ('A' class divisions constructed of steel with insulation preventing temperature rise exceeding 140°C above ambient for 60, 30, 15, or 0 minutes). Bulkheads and decks separating adjacent spaces must maintain fire integrity according to fire division tables ('A' class divisions constructed of steel with insulation preventing temperature rise exceeding 140°C above ambient for 60, 30, 15, or 0 minutes).

title: Fire dampers & ventilation duct penetrations
text: Fire dampers & ventilation duct penetrations Ventilation ducts passing through 'A' class bulkheads or decks must be fitted with automatic fire dampers constructed of steel at least 3 mm thick with a spigot joint length of at least 80 mm. Ventilation ducts passing through 'A' class bulkheads or decks must be fitted with automatic fire dampers constructed of steel at least 3 mm thick with a spigot joint length of at least 80 mm.

title: Ventilation systems in machinery spaces, galleys, and ro-ro spaces
text: Ventilation systems in machinery spaces, galleys, and ro-ro spaces Dedicated exhaust ducts from galley ranges must be fitted with grease traps, automatic fire dampers at the lower end, and remote shutdown controls for exhaust fans. Dedicated exhaust ducts from galley ranges must be fitted with grease traps, automatic fire dampers at the lower end, and remote shutdown controls for exhaust fans.

title: Fire fighting
text: Fire fighting Requires every ship to carry fixed water-based fire-fighting capability (fire mains, pumps, hydrants, hoses), portable fire extinguishers, and, for certain spaces and cargo arrangements, additional fixed suppression measures — sized and arranged according to ship type and tonnage rather than a single fixed specification. Requires every ship to carry fixed water-based fire-fighting capability (fire mains, pumps, hydrants, hoses), portable fire extinguishers, and, for certain spaces and cargo arrangements, additional fixed suppression measures — sized and arranged according to ship type and tonnage rather than a single fixed specification.

title: Containment and structural fire arrangements
text: Containment and structural fire arrangements Covers fire-containment arrangements for specific spaces and cargo stowage areas (e.g. open-top container holds and on-deck container stowage on ships built on or after 1 January 2016), requiring means to contain a fire at its space/area of origin and cool adjacent areas to limit spread and structural damage. Covers fire-containment arrangements for specific spaces and cargo stowage areas (e.g. open-top container holds and on-deck container stowage on ships built on or after 1 January 2016), requiring means to contain a fire at its space/area of origin and cool adjacent areas to limit spread and structural damage.

title: Water supply systems
text: Water supply systems Requires every ship to be fitted with fire pumps, fire mains, hydrants and hoses meeting this regulation's standards, with the detailed sub-paragraphs setting pipe/valve arrangement, minimum hydrant pressure, pump numbers, and hose/nozzle specifications. Requires every ship to be fitted with fire pumps, fire mains, hydrants and hoses meeting this regulation's standards, with the detailed sub-paragraphs setting pipe/valve arrangement, minimum hydrant pressure, pump numbers, and hose/nozzle specifications.

title: Fire mains and hydrants
text: Fire mains and hydrants Sets material, placement, drainage and freeze-protection requirements for fire main piping and hydrants; requires isolating valves separating the machinery-space section of the fire main so the rest of the ship can still be supplied if that section is shut down; requires minimum hydrant pressures scaled by ship type and tonnage; and requires ships of 500 GT and above to carry an international shore connection built to the FSS Code. Sets material, placement, drainage and freeze-protection requirements for fire main piping and hydrants; requires isolating valves separating the machinery-space section of the fire main so the rest of the ship can still be supplied if that section is shut down; requires minimum hydrant pressures scaled by ship type and tonnage; and requires ships of 500 GT and above to carry an international shore connection built to the FSS Code.

title: Fire pumps
text: Fire pumps Sets which shipboard pumps may be accepted as fire pumps (with change-over arrangements if normally used for oil transfer), the minimum number of independently-driven fire pumps by ship type/tonnage, and location/access/ventilation requirements for the space housing the emergency fire pump so it stays usable even if the main machinery space is on fire. Sets which shipboard pumps may be accepted as fire pumps (with change-over arrangements if normally used for oil transfer), the minimum number of independently-driven fire pumps by ship type/tonnage, and location/access/ventilation requirements for the space housing the emergency fire pump so it stays usable even if the main machinery space is on fire.

title: Fire hoses and nozzles
text: Fire hoses and nozzles Requires non-perishable fire hoses of a minimum 10 m length (capped at 15/20/25 m depending on the space), kept ready with nozzle and couplings near the hydrants, with interchangeable couplings across the ship's hose complement. Requires non-perishable fire hoses of a minimum 10 m length (capped at 15/20/25 m depending on the space), kept ready with nozzle and couplings near the hydrants, with interchangeable couplings across the ship's hose complement.

title: Portable fire extinguishers
text: Portable fire extinguishers Requires portable fire extinguishers of appropriate type and number to be distributed through accommodation, service and machinery spaces, supplementing the fixed water-based systems required earlier in the regulation. Requires portable fire extinguishers of appropriate type and number to be distributed through accommodation, service and machinery spaces, supplementing the fixed water-based systems required earlier in the regulation.

title: Fixed gas fire-extinguishing systems
text: Fixed gas fire-extinguishing systems Category A machinery spaces and cargo holds must be protected by an approved fixed gas fire-extinguishing system complying with FSS Code Chapter 5. Category A machinery spaces and cargo holds must be protected by an approved fixed gas fire-extinguishing system complying with FSS Code Chapter 5.

title: Fixed water-spraying & water-mist systems in machinery spaces
text: Fixed water-spraying & water-mist systems in machinery spaces Category A machinery spaces exceeding 500 m³ in volume must be fitted with an approved fixed local-application water-based or water-mist fire-fighting system complying with FSS Code Chapter 7. Category A machinery spaces exceeding 500 m³ in volume must be fitted with an approved fixed local-application water-based or water-mist fire-fighting system complying with FSS Code Chapter 7.

title: Automatic sprinkler, fire detection and fire alarm systems
text: Automatic sprinkler, fire detection and fire alarm systems Passenger ships and cargo ships must be fitted with automatic sprinkler, fire detection, and fire alarm systems complying with FSS Code Chapter 8. Passenger ships and cargo ships must be fitted with automatic sprinkler, fire detection, and fire alarm systems complying with FSS Code Chapter 8.

title: Fixed deck foam fire-extinguishing systems on tankers
text: Fixed deck foam fire-extinguishing systems on tankers Tankers of 20,000 DWT and above carrying crude oil or petroleum products must be fitted with a fixed deck foam system complying with FSS Code Chapters 6 and 14. Tankers of 20,000 DWT and above carrying crude oil or petroleum products must be fitted with a fixed deck foam system complying with FSS Code Chapters 6 and 14.

label: I
title: General provisions
text: General provisions The administrative backbone of SOLAS: Part A fixes who the Convention applies to and defines its core terms; Part B establishes the entire survey-and-certification machinery (initial/renewal/periodical surveys, the family of safety certificates, their duration and endorsement); Part C covers casualty investigation obligations. Every statutory certificate a ship carries traces its legal authority back to this chapter. The administrative backbone of SOLAS: Part A fixes who the Convention applies to and defines its core terms; Part B establishes the entire survey-and-certification machinery (initial/renewal/periodical surveys, the family of safety certificates, their duration and endorsement); Part C covers casualty investigation obligations. Every statutory certificate a ship carries traces its legal authority back to this chapter.

title: Application
text: Application Applies the regulations to ships engaged on international voyages unless a chapter expressly provides otherwise; each chapter then defines its own precise classes of ships and extent of application. Applies the regulations to ships engaged on international voyages unless a chapter expressly provides otherwise; each chapter then defines its own precise classes of ships and extent of application.

title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines the Convention's core vocabulary: Administration (the flag State's government), international voyage, passenger (anyone other than crew/ship's-business persons and infants under one year), passenger ship (more than twelve passengers), cargo ship, tanker, fishing vessel, nuclear ship, and new/existing ship by keel-laying date. Defines the Convention's core vocabulary: Administration (the flag State's government), international voyage, passenger (anyone other than crew/ship's-business persons and infants under one year), passenger ship (more than twelve passengers), cargo ship, tanker, fishing vessel, nuclear ship, and new/existing ship by keel-laying date.

title: Exceptions
text: Exceptions Excludes warships and troopships, cargo ships under 500 GT, ships without mechanical propulsion, primitive wooden ships, non-trading pleasure yachts, and fishing vessels from the regulations (except where expressly provided, e.g. parts of Chapter V). Excludes warships and troopships, cargo ships under 500 GT, ships without mechanical propulsion, primitive wooden ships, non-trading pleasure yachts, and fishing vessels from the regulations (except where expressly provided, e.g. parts of Chapter V).

title: Exemptions
text: Exemptions Lets the Administration exempt a ship making a single exceptional international voyage from requirements (subject to adequate safety), and exempt ships embodying features of a novel kind from Chapters II-1, II-2, III and IV where applying them would seriously impede research into those features. Lets the Administration exempt a ship making a single exceptional international voyage from requirements (subject to adequate safety), and exempt ships embodying features of a novel kind from Chapters II-1, II-2, III and IV where applying them would seriously impede research into those features.

title: Surveys of passenger ships
text: Surveys of passenger ships Requires an initial survey before service, a renewal survey every 12 months, and additional surveys as occasion arises; the initial survey is a complete inspection of structure (including the outside of the bottom and inside/outside of boilers), machinery, electrical and radio installations, fire safety, life-saving appliances and navigational equipment. Requires an initial survey before service, a renewal survey every 12 months, and additional surveys as occasion arises; the initial survey is a complete inspection of structure (including the outside of the bottom and inside/outside of boilers), machinery, electrical and radio installations, fire safety, life-saving appliances and navigational equipment.

title: Surveys of radio installations of cargo ships
text: Surveys of radio installations of cargo ships Subjects cargo-ship radio installations (including those in life-saving appliances) to initial, renewal (max five-year), periodical (within three months either side of each Safety Radio Certificate anniversary) and additional surveys, with periodical surveys endorsed on the certificate. Subjects cargo-ship radio installations (including those in life-saving appliances) to initial, renewal (max five-year), periodical (within three months either side of each Safety Radio Certificate anniversary) and additional surveys, with periodical surveys endorsed on the certificate.

title: Surveys of structure, machinery and equipment of cargo ships
text: Surveys of structure, machinery and equipment of cargo ships Establishes the survey regime for a cargo ship's structure, machinery and equipment backing the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate — the chief-engineer-relevant counterpart to the equipment and radio survey regulations. Establishes the survey regime for a cargo ship's structure, machinery and equipment backing the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate — the chief-engineer-relevant counterpart to the equipment and radio survey regulations.

title: Issue or endorsement of certificates
text: Issue or endorsement of certificates Names the statutory certificates and what each attests: Passenger Ship Safety Certificate (Ch. II-1, II-2, III, IV, V compliance), Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate (II-1/II-2 structure side), Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate (II-1, II-2, III, V equipment side), Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate (Ch. IV), and the combined Cargo Ship Safety Certificate alternative. Names the statutory certificates and what each attests: Passenger Ship Safety Certificate (Ch. II-1, II-2, III, IV, V compliance), Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate (II-1/II-2 structure side), Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate (II-1, II-2, III, V equipment side), Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate (Ch. IV), and the combined Cargo Ship Safety Certificate alternative.

title: Control (port State control)
text: Control (port State control) The port State control regulation: officers of a port State may verify a visiting ship holds valid certificates and take steps (up to preventing sailing) where the ship or its equipment does not substantially correspond to them, while making all possible efforts to avoid undue detention — with compensation payable if a ship is unduly detained or delayed. The port State control regulation: officers of a port State may verify a visiting ship holds valid certificates and take steps (up to preventing sailing) where the ship or its equipment does not substantially correspond to them, while making all possible efforts to avoid undue detention — with compensation payable if a ship is unduly detained or delayed.

label: II-1
title: Construction — Structure, subdivision and stability, machinery and electrical installations
text: Construction — Structure, subdivision and stability, machinery and electrical installations The chapter a marine engineer lives in: Parts A/B cover structure, subdivision, damage stability and watertight integrity; Part C covers machinery installations (steering gear, boilers, going astern, bridge control, automation); Part D covers electrical installations including main and emergency power; Part E covers periodically unattended machinery spaces; Parts F/G cover alternative designs and ships using low-flashpoint fuels (the hook that makes the IGF Code mandatory). The chapter a marine engineer lives in: Parts A/B cover structure, subdivision, damage stability and watertight integrity; Part C covers machinery installations (steering gear, boilers, going astern, bridge control, automation); Part D covers electrical installations including main and emergency power; Part E covers periodically unattended machinery spaces; Parts F/G cover alternative designs and ships using low-flashpoint fuels (the hook that makes the IGF Code mandatory).

title: General machinery requirements
text: General machinery requirements Requires main propulsion, control systems and auxiliaries to be designed and constructed so that the safety of the ship and persons on board is preserved under all operating conditions, with dead-ship restoration capability within 30 minutes. Requires main propulsion, control systems and auxiliaries to be designed and constructed so that the safety of the ship and persons on board is preserved under all operating conditions, with dead-ship restoration capability within 30 minutes.

title: Propulsion & auxiliary machinery reliability
text: Propulsion & auxiliary machinery reliability Main propulsion and essential auxiliary machinery arrangements must ensure operation under all normal and maneuvering conditions without reliance on external supply. Main propulsion and essential auxiliary machinery arrangements must ensure operation under all normal and maneuvering conditions without reliance on external supply.

title: Dead-ship restoration capability
text: Dead-ship restoration capability Arrangements must be provided to ensure that main propulsion and auxiliary power can be restored from a dead-ship condition within 30 minutes without external power. Arrangements must be provided to ensure that main propulsion and auxiliary power can be restored from a dead-ship condition within 30 minutes without external power.

title: Machinery (safeguards)
text: Machinery (safeguards) Requires safeguards on machinery including the classic exam figure: internal combustion engines of 200 mm cylinder bore or 0.6 m3 crankcase volume and above must have crankcase explosion relief valves of suitable type and relief area, discharged so as to minimise injury risk; main propulsion and auxiliaries must shut down automatically on failures (e.g. lube-oil supply loss) that could lead rapidly to breakdown or explosion, with Administration-permitted overrides. Requires safeguards on machinery including the classic exam figure: internal combustion engines of 200 mm cylinder bore or 0.6 m3 crankcase volume and above must have crankcase explosion relief valves of suitable type and relief area, discharged so as to minimise injury risk; main propulsion and auxiliaries must shut down automatically on failures (e.g. lube-oil supply loss) that could lead rapidly to breakdown or explosion, with Administration-permitted overrides.

title: Crankcase explosion relief valves
text: Crankcase explosion relief valves Internal combustion engines with cylinder bore of 200 mm or above, or crankcase volume of 0.6 m3 and above, must be fitted with approved crankcase explosion relief valves of suitable type and relief area. Internal combustion engines with cylinder bore of 200 mm or above, or crankcase volume of 0.6 m3 and above, must be fitted with approved crankcase explosion relief valves of suitable type and relief area.

title: Automatic safety shutdown arrangements
text: Automatic safety shutdown arrangements Main propulsion and auxiliary machinery must shut down automatically upon critical failures (such as lube-oil supply loss) that could lead rapidly to breakdown or explosion, with bridge/control alarms. Main propulsion and auxiliary machinery must shut down automatically upon critical failures (such as lube-oil supply loss) that could lead rapidly to breakdown or explosion, with bridge/control alarms.

title: Means of going astern
text: Means of going astern Requires sufficient astern power to control the ship in all normal circumstances, a demonstrated and recorded ability to reverse propeller thrust and bring the ship to rest within reasonable distance from maximum ahead service speed, and stopping-trial data (times, headings, distances) kept on board for the master's use. Requires sufficient astern power to control the ship in all normal circumstances, a demonstrated and recorded ability to reverse propeller thrust and bring the ship to rest within reasonable distance from maximum ahead service speed, and stopping-trial data (times, headings, distances) kept on board for the master's use.

title: Astern power requirement
text: Astern power requirement Ships must have sufficient astern power to maintain control during maneuvering and bring the vessel to rest from maximum ahead service speed within a reasonable distance. Ships must have sufficient astern power to maintain control during maneuvering and bring the vessel to rest from maximum ahead service speed within a reasonable distance.

title: Stopping trial records on board
text: Stopping trial records on board Recorded stopping times, headings, and distances from sea trials must be documented and maintained on board for the guidance of the master and navigation officers. Recorded stopping times, headings, and distances from sea trials must be documented and maintained on board for the guidance of the master and navigation officers.

title: Steering gear
text: Steering gear Sets main and auxiliary steering gear requirements, including the sea-trial compliance methods (even keel, rudder fully submerged, half max-revolutions speed or 7 knots, whichever is greater) and the requirement for power operation where needed — mandatory where the rudder stock exceeds 230 mm diameter in way of the tiller. Sets main and auxiliary steering gear requirements, including the sea-trial compliance methods (even keel, rudder fully submerged, half max-revolutions speed or 7 knots, whichever is greater) and the requirement for power operation where needed — mandatory where the rudder stock exceeds 230 mm diameter in way of the tiller.

title: Main steering gear performance (28-second stroke)
text: Main steering gear performance (28-second stroke) The main steering gear must be capable of steering the ship at maximum service speed and moving the rudder from 35 degrees on one side to 35 degrees on the other side, and 35 degrees to 30 degrees on the opposite side within 28 seconds. The main steering gear must be capable of steering the ship at maximum service speed and moving the rudder from 35 degrees on one side to 35 degrees on the other side, and 35 degrees to 30 degrees on the opposite side within 28 seconds.

title: Auxiliary steering gear performance (60-second stroke)
text: Auxiliary steering gear performance (60-second stroke) The auxiliary steering gear must be capable of moving the rudder from 15 degrees on one side to 15 degrees on the other side within 60 seconds at half maximum service speed or 7 knots, whichever is greater. The auxiliary steering gear must be capable of moving the rudder from 15 degrees on one side to 15 degrees on the other side within 60 seconds at half maximum service speed or 7 knots, whichever is greater.

title: Power operation threshold (230 mm stock)
text: Power operation threshold (230 mm stock) Power operation must be provided for the main steering gear where the rudder stock diameter in way of the tiller exceeds 230 mm (excluding ice strengthening requirements). Power operation must be provided for the main steering gear where the rudder stock diameter in way of the tiller exceeds 230 mm (excluding ice strengthening requirements).

title: Hydraulic single-failure isolation criteria
text: Hydraulic single-failure isolation criteria Hydraulic power steering gear on tankers of 10,000 GT and above must be provided with isolation valves to maintain steering capability following any single hydraulic loop failure. Hydraulic power steering gear on tankers of 10,000 GT and above must be provided with isolation valves to maintain steering capability following any single hydraulic loop failure.

title: Machinery controls
text: Machinery controls Requires main propulsion controls to be operable from the navigation bridge with independent emergency stop, and engine order telegraph communication between bridge and engine room. Requires main propulsion controls to be operable from the navigation bridge with independent emergency stop, and engine order telegraph communication between bridge and engine room.

title: Bridge propulsion control & emergency stop
text: Bridge propulsion control & emergency stop Propulsion speed and thrust direction must be controllable directly from the navigation bridge; an independent emergency stop device must be fitted on the bridge independent of the bridge control system. Propulsion speed and thrust direction must be controllable directly from the navigation bridge; an independent emergency stop device must be fitted on the bridge independent of the bridge control system.

title: Engine order telegraph communication
text: Engine order telegraph communication An engine order telegraph must be fitted to provide visual and audible indication of orders and responses between the navigation bridge and the machinery control room. An engine order telegraph must be fitted to provide visual and audible indication of orders and responses between the navigation bridge and the machinery control room.

title: Boilers and boiler feed systems
text: Boilers and boiler feed systems Every steam generating system essential to safety needs at least two separate feedwater systems from and including the feed pumps, overpressure protection, feedwater quality supervision to keep oil and contaminants out, at least two water-level indicators (one a direct-reading gauge glass), and a high-water-level alarm on water tube boilers serving turbine propulsion. Every steam generating system essential to safety needs at least two separate feedwater systems from and including the feed pumps, overpressure protection, feedwater quality supervision to keep oil and contaminants out, at least two water-level indicators (one a direct-reading gauge glass), and a high-water-level alarm on water tube boilers serving turbine propulsion.

title: Steam pipe systems
text: Steam pipe systems Steam pipes and fittings must be designed for the maximum working stresses they can see, with drainage arrangements wherever dangerous water hammer could otherwise occur, and protection where a pipe may receive steam from a higher-pressure source. Steam pipes and fittings must be designed for the maximum working stresses they can see, with drainage arrangements wherever dangerous water hammer could otherwise occur, and protection where a pipe may receive steam from a higher-pressure source.

title: Main source of electrical power and lighting systems
text: Main source of electrical power and lighting systems Requires a main electrical power source sufficient for dead-ship starting capability (alone or combined), transformer continuity where transformers are essential, and mutual independence between main and emergency lighting so a fire or casualty in the space containing either source cannot disable the other system. Requires a main electrical power source sufficient for dead-ship starting capability (alone or combined), transformer continuity where transformers are essential, and mutual independence between main and emergency lighting so a fire or casualty in the space containing either source cannot disable the other system.

title: Main electrical power source redundancy
text: Main electrical power source redundancy The main electrical power source must consist of at least two generating sets capable of supplying all essential safety and operational services even with any one generator out of service. The main electrical power source must consist of at least two generating sets capable of supplying all essential safety and operational services even with any one generator out of service.

title: Dead-ship generator starting arrangements
text: Dead-ship generator starting arrangements Dead-ship starting arrangements must enable main generating sets to be started from a dead-ship condition without external electrical energy. Dead-ship starting arrangements must enable main generating sets to be started from a dead-ship condition without external electrical energy.

title: Emergency source of electrical power in passenger ships
text: Emergency source of electrical power in passenger ships Specifies the 36-hour emergency load schedule for passenger ships — navigation lights, GMDSS radio installations, internal emergency communications, navigational equipment, fire detection/alarm, one fire pump, sprinkler pump and emergency bilge pump — and requires the emergency generator, prime mover and battery to deliver full rated power upright and at up to 22.5 degrees of list or 10 degrees of trim, with periodic testing of the complete system including automatic starting. Specifies the 36-hour emergency load schedule for passenger ships — navigation lights, GMDSS radio installations, internal emergency communications, navigational equipment, fire detection/alarm, one fire pump, sprinkler pump and emergency bilge pump — and requires the emergency generator, prime mover and battery to deliver full rated power upright and at up to 22.5 degrees of list or 10 degrees of trim, with periodic testing of the complete system including automatic starting.

title: Emergency generator load schedule (36h / 18h)
text: Emergency generator load schedule (36h / 18h) The emergency generator must supply emergency lighting, navigation lights, GMDSS radio, internal communications, fire pumps, and steering gear for 36 hours on passenger ships and 18 hours on cargo ships. The emergency generator must supply emergency lighting, navigation lights, GMDSS radio, internal communications, fire pumps, and steering gear for 36 hours on passenger ships and 18 hours on cargo ships.

title: 45-second automatic starting and connection
text: 45-second automatic starting and connection The emergency generator must start automatically and connect to the emergency switchboard within 45 seconds of main electrical power failure. The emergency generator must start automatically and connect to the emergency switchboard within 45 seconds of main electrical power failure.

title: Emergency power heel and trim operational limits
text: Emergency power heel and trim operational limits The emergency source of power, prime mover, and emergency switchboard must remain fully operational upright and at list angles up to 22.5 degrees and trim up to 10 degrees. The emergency source of power, prime mover, and emergency switchboard must remain fully operational upright and at list angles up to 22.5 degrees and trim up to 10 degrees.

title: Supplementary emergency lighting for ro-ro passenger ships
text: Supplementary emergency lighting for ro-ro passenger ships On passenger ships with ro-ro or special category spaces, all public spaces and alleyways need supplementary electric lighting able to run at least 3 hours after all other power has failed, under any heel, powered by continuously-charged batteries inside the lighting units, so escape routes stay visible. On passenger ships with ro-ro or special category spaces, all public spaces and alleyways need supplementary electric lighting able to run at least 3 hours after all other power has failed, under any heel, powered by continuously-charged batteries inside the lighting units, so escape routes stay visible.

title: Fire precautions in periodically unattended machinery spaces
text: Fire precautions in periodically unattended machinery spaces Requires high-pressure fuel line jacketing, fuel leakage drain tanks with high-level alarms, and fire-prevention measures for unattended machinery spaces. Requires high-pressure fuel line jacketing, fuel leakage drain tanks with high-level alarms, and fire-prevention measures for unattended machinery spaces.

title: UMS fuel leakage precautions & line jacketing
text: UMS fuel leakage precautions & line jacketing High-pressure fuel injection lines in unattended machinery spaces must be jacketed, and fuel leakage collection tanks with high-level alarms must be provided. High-pressure fuel injection lines in unattended machinery spaces must be jacketed, and fuel leakage collection tanks with high-level alarms must be provided.

title: Control of propulsion machinery from the navigation bridge
text: Control of propulsion machinery from the navigation bridge Under all conditions including manoeuvring, speed, thrust direction and pitch must be fully controllable from the bridge through a single control device per independent propeller with overload prevention; the bridge must have an emergency stop independent of the bridge control system; remote control is possible from only one location at a time, and orders must be indicated in the machinery control room. Under all conditions including manoeuvring, speed, thrust direction and pitch must be fully controllable from the bridge through a single control device per independent propeller with overload prevention; the bridge must have an emergency stop independent of the bridge control system; remote control is possible from only one location at a time, and orders must be indicated in the machinery control room.

title: Periodically unattended machinery spaces — automation, alarms and safety systems
text: Periodically unattended machinery spaces — automation, alarms and safety systems The UMS backbone: automatic control must keep main propulsion services running through normal manoeuvres, load shedding or equivalent must protect remaining generators when one parallel set is lost, standby auxiliaries need automatic changeover with an alarm, a centralized control position must present alarms for all important pressures, temperatures and levels, and starting air pressure must be maintained automatically for internal combustion propulsion. The UMS backbone: automatic control must keep main propulsion services running through normal manoeuvres, load shedding or equivalent must protect remaining generators when one parallel set is lost, standby auxiliaries need automatic changeover with an alarm, a centralized control position must present alarms for all important pressures, temperatures and levels, and starting air pressure must be maintained automatically for internal combustion propulsion.

title: UMS centralized control station alarms
text: UMS centralized control station alarms A centralized alarm system must indicate all critical machinery pressures, temperatures, and fluid levels at the central control position with audible/visual annunciation. A centralized alarm system must indicate all critical machinery pressures, temperatures, and fluid levels at the central control position with audible/visual annunciation.

title: UMS standby auxiliary automatic changeover
text: UMS standby auxiliary automatic changeover Automatic changeover to standby auxiliary pumps must be provided upon failure of duty pumps, triggering immediate visual and audible alarms. Automatic changeover to standby auxiliary pumps must be provided upon failure of duty pumps, triggering immediate visual and audible alarms.

title: Alternative design and arrangements
text: Alternative design and arrangements Allows machinery and electrical installations to deviate from the prescriptive requirements if an engineering analysis (including fault/hazard-based risk assessment) is evaluated and approved by the Administration against IMO guidelines, with approved documentation carried on board and re-evaluation whenever assumptions or operational restrictions change. label: III
title: Life-saving appliances and arrangements
text: Life-saving appliances and arrangements Sets the carriage, stowage, manning, drill and maintenance requirements for life-saving appliances — survival craft, rescue boats, personal life-saving appliances and their launching arrangements — with the technical performance standards of the appliances themselves delegated to the LSA Code. Part B splits requirements between passenger ships and cargo ships; Part C mirrors Chapter II-1's alternative design route. Sets the carriage, stowage, manning, drill and maintenance requirements for life-saving appliances — survival craft, rescue boats, personal life-saving appliances and their launching arrangements — with the technical performance standards of the appliances themselves delegated to the LSA Code. Part B splits requirements between passenger ships and cargo ships; Part C mirrors Chapter II-1's alternative design route.

title: Exemptions
text: Exemptions The Administration may exempt ships that never proceed more than 20 miles from the nearest land from specific requirements where the sheltered voyage makes them unreasonable, and may exempt special-trade passenger ships (e.g. the pilgrim trade) provided they comply with the Special Trade Passenger Ships Agreement 1971 and its 1973 Space Requirements Protocol. title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines the chapter's terms, including anti-exposure suit (for rescue boat crews and marine evacuation system parties) and certificated person (holder of a certificate of proficiency in survival craft issued or recognized under STCW). Defines the chapter's terms, including anti-exposure suit (for rescue boat crews and marine evacuation system parties) and certificated person (holder of a certificate of proficiency in survival craft issued or recognized under STCW).

title: Communications (incl. public address system)
text: Communications (incl. public address system) Requires emergency communications including a public address system clearly audible above ambient noise in all required spaces, with bridge override so emergency messages broadcast even where loudspeakers are off or turned down; on newer passenger ships the PA needs two sufficiently-separated loops with independent amplifiers, and it must be connected to the emergency source of electrical power. title: Manning of survival craft and supervision
text: Manning of survival craft and supervision Requires enough trained persons aboard for mustering and assisting untrained persons, sufficient crew (deck officers or certificated persons) to operate all survival craft and launching arrangements for total persons on board, a person in charge of each survival craft with a crew list, and a nominated second-in-command for lifeboats. title: Rescue boat embarkation, launching and recovery arrangements
text: Rescue boat embarkation, launching and recovery arrangements Rescue boat arrangements must allow boarding and launching in the shortest possible time, including launching with the ship making headway using painters where necessary, and davit spans with at least two lifelines reaching the water under 10 degrees trim and 20 degrees list either way. Rescue boat arrangements must allow boarding and launching in the shortest possible time, including launching with the ship making headway using painters where necessary, and davit spans with at least two lifelines reaching the water under 10 degrees trim and 20 degrees list either way.

title: Rescue boat boarding & rapid launching arrangements
text: Rescue boat boarding & rapid launching arrangements The rescue boat embarkation and launching arrangements shall be such that the rescue boat can be boarded and launched in the shortest possible time; recovery time of the rescue boat shall not be more than 5 minutes in calm water when loaded with its full complement of persons and equipment. The rescue boat embarkation and launching arrangements shall be such that the rescue boat can be boarded and launched in the shortest possible time; recovery time of the rescue boat shall not be more than 5 minutes in calm water when loaded with its full complement of persons and equipment.

title: Recovery arrangements & headway launching
text: Recovery arrangements & headway launching Rapid recovery arrangements shall be provided for rescue boats; launching and recovery arrangements shall allow safe operation when the ship is making headway at speeds up to 5 knots in calm water. Rapid recovery arrangements shall be provided for rescue boats; launching and recovery arrangements shall allow safe operation when the ship is making headway at speeds up to 5 knots in calm water.

title: Emergency training and drills
text: Emergency training and drills Sets the abandon-ship and fire drill cycle, crew participation requirements, and lifeboat handling practice — including the constraints around drills with free-fall lifeboats, where crew boarding without launching is permitted under defined conditions. Sets the abandon-ship and fire drill cycle, crew participation requirements, and lifeboat handling practice — including the constraints around drills with free-fall lifeboats, where crew boarding without launching is permitted under defined conditions.

title: Abandon ship drill cycle & operational requirements
text: Abandon ship drill cycle & operational requirements Every crew member shall participate in at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill every month (or within 24 hours of leaving port if more than 25% of the crew have not participated in a drill on board that ship in the previous month); each lifeboat shall be launched and maneuvered in the water by its assigned operating crew at least once every 3 months. Every crew member shall participate in at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill every month (or within 24 hours of leaving port if more than 25% of the crew have not participated in a drill on board that ship in the previous month); each lifeboat shall be launched and maneuvered in the water by its assigned operating crew at least once every 3 months.

title: Free-fall lifeboat drill safety constraints
text: Free-fall lifeboat drill safety constraints During abandon ship drills with free-fall lifeboats, a simulated launching may be performed; free-fall launching with only the required operating crew on board shall be carried out at least once every 6 months. During abandon ship drills with free-fall lifeboats, a simulated launching may be performed; free-fall launching with only the required operating crew on board shall be carried out at least once every 6 months.

title: Survival craft and rescue boats (cargo ships)
text: Survival craft and rescue boats (cargo ships) Cargo-ship carriage requirements: lifeboats of aggregate capacity for the total persons on each side (or a free-fall lifeboat aft), liferafts for the total complement transferable across sides, and the alternatives available to cargo ships in lieu of the base requirement, scaled by ship type and length. Cargo-ship carriage requirements: lifeboats of aggregate capacity for the total persons on each side (or a free-fall lifeboat aft), liferafts for the total complement transferable across sides, and the alternatives available to cargo ships in lieu of the base requirement, scaled by ship type and length.

title: Cargo ship survival craft carriage rules
text: Cargo ship survival craft carriage rules Cargo ships shall carry one or more totally enclosed lifeboats of such aggregate capacity on each side as will accommodate the total number of persons on board; alternatively, a single free-fall lifeboat capable of being launched free-fall over the stern accommodating total complement may be fitted, supplemented by inflatable liferafts on each side. Cargo ships shall carry one or more totally enclosed lifeboats of such aggregate capacity on each side as will accommodate the total number of persons on board; alternatively, a single free-fall lifeboat capable of being launched free-fall over the stern accommodating total complement may be fitted, supplemented by inflatable liferafts on each side.

label: V
title: Safety of navigation
text: Safety of navigation Covers the operational navigation obligations that, unlike most of SOLAS, can extend to all ships on all voyages: carriage requirements for navigational equipment (radar, AIS, ECDIS, VDR) scaled by tonnage, steering-gear testing and drills, voyage planning, nautical charts and publications, and record-keeping of navigational activities. Covers the operational navigation obligations that, unlike most of SOLAS, can extend to all ships on all voyages: carriage requirements for navigational equipment (radar, AIS, ECDIS, VDR) scaled by tonnage, steering-gear testing and drills, voyage planning, nautical charts and publications, and record-keeping of navigational activities.

title: Carriage requirements for shipborne navigational systems and equipment
text: Carriage requirements for shipborne navigational systems and equipment The tonnage-tiered equipment ladder: AIS must automatically exchange identity, position, course, speed and navigational status with shore stations, other ships and aircraft; from 500 GT, single-equipment failure must not defeat basic requirements; from 3,000 GT a second (3 GHz or independent 9 GHz) radar and second automatic tracking aid are required; from 10,000 GT an ARPA plotting at least 20 targets connected to a speed/distance device. The tonnage-tiered equipment ladder: AIS must automatically exchange identity, position, course, speed and navigational status with shore stations, other ships and aircraft; from 500 GT, single-equipment failure must not defeat basic requirements; from 3,000 GT a second (3 GHz or independent 9 GHz) radar and second automatic tracking aid are required; from 10,000 GT an ARPA plotting at least 20 targets connected to a speed/distance device.

title: Use of heading and/or track control systems
text: Use of heading and/or track control systems Changeover between automatic and manual steering must be made by or under the supervision of a responsible officer, and manual steering must be tested after prolonged automatic operation and before entering areas demanding special caution. Changeover between automatic and manual steering must be made by or under the supervision of a responsible officer, and manual steering must be tested after prolonged automatic operation and before entering areas demanding special caution.

title: Operation of steering gear
text: Operation of steering gear In areas where navigation demands special caution, ships must run more than one steering gear power unit where the units are capable of simultaneous operation — a direct engine-room action item during river passages and port approaches. In areas where navigation demands special caution, ships must run more than one steering gear power unit where the units are capable of simultaneous operation — a direct engine-room action item during river passages and port approaches.

title: Steering gear: testing and drills
text: Steering gear: testing and drills Within 12 hours before departure the crew must check and test the steering gear — main and auxiliary gear, remote control systems, bridge steering positions, emergency power supply, rudder angle indicators against actual position, power-failure alarms, and automatic isolating arrangements — with the test and emergency-drill dates recorded. Within 12 hours before departure the crew must check and test the steering gear — main and auxiliary gear, remote control systems, bridge steering positions, emergency power supply, rudder angle indicators against actual position, power-failure alarms, and automatic isolating arrangements — with the test and emergency-drill dates recorded.

title: Nautical charts and nautical publications
text: Nautical charts and nautical publications Charts and publications for the intended voyage (sailing directions, lists of lights, notices to mariners, tide tables) must be adequate and up to date. Charts and publications for the intended voyage (sailing directions, lists of lights, notices to mariners, tide tables) must be adequate and up to date.

title: Records of navigational activities and daily reporting
text: Records of navigational activities and daily reporting All ships on international voyages must keep a record of navigational activities sufficient to restore a complete record of the voyage, and ships of 500 GT and above on voyages over 48 hours must send a daily report to their company (as defined in Ch. IX), which retains it for the voyage duration. IX), which retains it for the voyage duration.

label: VI
title: Carriage of cargoes and oil fuels
text: Carriage of cargoes and oil fuels Part A sets general cargo provisions (cargo information from shipper to master, oxygen analysis and gas detection, pesticide use, stowage and securing, oil-fuel safety data, the ban on blending bulk liquid cargoes at sea); Part B adds special provisions for solid bulk cargoes; Part C covers grain, delegating to the International Grain Code. This is the SOLAS hook for the IMSBC Code. This is the SOLAS hook for the IMSBC Code.

title: Cargo information
text: Cargo information The shipper must give the master appropriate cargo information sufficiently in advance of loading, confirmed in writing before loading: general description, gross mass and special properties for general/unitised cargo, and for solid bulk cargo the information required by the IMSBC framework — the legal basis for refusing cargo without proper declaration. title: Loading, unloading and stowage of solid bulk cargoes
text: Loading, unloading and stowage of solid bulk cargoes Loading/unloading must follow the agreed ship-terminal plan; the master may suspend operations and must notify the port State authority if ship limits are exceeded or threatened; personnel must continuously monitor operations, with draught checks against supplied tonnage figures recorded in a cargo logbook and deviations corrected. label: IX
title: Management for the safe operation of ships
text: Management for the safe operation of ships The five-regulation chapter that makes the ISM Code mandatory: it defines Company (owner, manager or bareboat charterer who has assumed responsibility and all ISM duties), requires company and ship to comply with the Code as mandatory, and establishes the Document of Compliance (company) and Safety Management Certificate (ship) issued by the Administration or a recognized organization. The five-regulation chapter that makes the ISM Code mandatory: it defines Company (owner, manager or bareboat charterer who has assumed responsibility and all ISM duties), requires company and ship to comply with the Code as mandatory, and establishes the Document of Compliance (company) and Safety Management Certificate (ship) issued by the Administration or a recognized organization.

title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines the ISM Code by reference to resolution A.741(18) as amended, and Company as the owner or any organization/person (manager, bareboat charterer) who has assumed responsibility for operation from the owner and agreed to take over all ISM Code duties; also defines oil tanker, chemical tanker, gas carrier and bulk carrier by cross-reference. title: Safety management requirements
text: Safety management requirements Company and ship must comply with the ISM Code, whose requirements are treated as mandatory for this purpose, and the ship must be operated by a company holding a Document of Compliance. Company and ship must comply with the ISM Code, whose requirements are treated as mandatory for this purpose, and the ship must be operated by a company holding a Document of Compliance.

title: Certification
text: Certification A Document of Compliance is issued to every compliant company (by the Administration, a recognized organization, or another Contracting Government at the Administration's request) with a copy kept on board for the master to produce; a Safety Management Certificate is issued to each ship after verifying the company and shipboard management operate per the approved safety management system. label: XI-2
title: Special measures to enhance maritime security
text: Special measures to enhance maritime security The post-9/11 security chapter that carries the ISPS Code: definitions and application, Contracting Government security-level obligations, company and ship compliance with ISPS Part A (guided by Part B), the ship security alert system, the master's overriding discretion for safety and security, control and compliance measures in port, and port facility requirements. The post-9/11 security chapter that carries the ISPS Code: definitions and application, Contracting Government security-level obligations, company and ship compliance with ISPS Part A (guided by Part B), the ship security alert system, the master's overriding discretion for safety and security, control and compliance measures in port, and port facility requirements.

title: Requirements for Companies and ships
text: Requirements for Companies and ships Companies and ships must comply with this chapter and ISPS Code Part A (taking Part B into account), with compliance verified and certified per Part A; ships must meet the security level set by a port's Contracting Government where higher than their Administration's, respond without undue delay to any level increase, and notify the competent authority before ship-to-ship activity if unable to comply. label: XII
title: Additional safety measures for bulk carriers
text: Additional safety measures for bulk carriers Born of the bulk-carrier loss casualties of the 1980s-90s: applies on top of all other chapters, with single-side-skin versus double-side-skin definitions, a phased implementation schedule keyed to ship age and the enhanced survey programme, damage stability and structural strength requirements for ships of 150 m and up, cargo density declaration/verification, loading instruments, and hold/ballast/dry-space water ingress alarms. title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines bulk carrier (a ship intended primarily to carry dry cargo in bulk, including ore and combination carriers), and distinguishes single-side-skin construction (any cargo hold bounded by the side shell, or double-skin narrower than 760/1,000 mm depending on build date) from double-side-skin construction (all holds bounded by a double skin of a longitudinal bulkhead connecting double bottom and deck). Defines bulk carrier (a ship intended primarily to carry dry cargo in bulk, including ore and combination carriers), and distinguishes single-side-skin construction (any cargo hold bounded by the side shell, or double-skin narrower than 760/1,000 mm depending on build date) from double-side-skin construction (all holds bounded by a double skin of a longitudinal bulkhead connecting double bottom and deck).

title: Implementation schedule
text: Implementation schedule Phases the retrofit obligations for pre-July-1999 bulk carriers by ship age on 1 July 1999 — 20 years and over by the first intermediate or periodical survey after that date; 15-20 years by the first periodical survey but no later than 1 July 2002; under 15 years by the survey after reaching age 15 but no later than age 17 — tied to the enhanced inspection programme of regulation XI-1/2. Phases the retrofit obligations for pre-July-1999 bulk carriers by ship age on 1 July 1999 — 20 years and over by the first intermediate or periodical survey after that date; 15-20 years by the first periodical survey but no later than 1 July 2002; under 15 years by the survey after reaching age 15 but no later than age 17 — tied to the enhanced inspection programme of regulation XI-1/2.

title: Structural strength of bulk carriers
text: Structural strength of bulk carriers Single-side-skin bulk carriers of 150 m and upwards built on or after 1 July 1999, carrying cargoes of density 1,000 kg/m3 and above, must have sufficient strength to withstand specified hold-flooding scenarios; for double-side construction from July 2006 the skin must keep primary stiffening outside the hold and maintain a minimum 1,000 mm clearance for inspection access. Single-side-skin bulk carriers of 150 m and upwards built on or after 1 July 1999, carrying cargoes of density 1,000 kg/m3 and above, must have sufficient strength to withstand specified hold-flooding scenarios; for double-side construction from July 2006 the skin must keep primary stiffening outside the hold and maintain a minimum 1,000 mm clearance for inspection access.

title: Solid bulk cargo density declaration
text: Solid bulk cargo density declaration Shippers must declare cargo density, and for ships subject to regulation 6, cargoes declared between 1,250 and 1,780 kg/m3 must have their density verified by an accredited testing organization unless the ship fully complies with the heavy-cargo requirements. Shippers must declare cargo density, and for ships subject to regulation 6, cargoes declared between 1,250 and 1,780 kg/m3 must have their density verified by an accredited testing organization unless the ship fully complies with the heavy-cargo requirements.

title: Loading instrument
text: Loading instrument Bulk carriers of 150 m and upwards must carry a loading instrument giving hull girder shear forces and bending moments (retrofitted to pre-1999 ships by their first intermediate/periodical survey after July 1999); smaller bulk carriers built from July 2006 need an instrument covering stability information. label: IV
title: Radiocommunications
text: Radiocommunications Sets GMDSS carriage and watchkeeping requirements: VHF DSC distress alerting on channel 70, EPIRBs capable of floating free and automatic activation, radar/AIS-SART, and sea-area-scaled equipment (A1-A4) up to satellite ship earth stations for A3/A4 areas. Also covers performance-standard type-approval, maintenance, radio record-keeping and automatic position updating of distress equipment. Also covers performance-standard type-approval, maintenance, radio record-keeping and automatic position updating of distress equipment.

title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines Maritime Safety Information (MSI), radar SART (9.2-9.5 GHz search and rescue transponder), the ITU Radio Regulations, recognized mobile satellite service, the 406 MHz EPIRB satellite service, and sea areas A1-A3 (A1: within VHF DSC coverage; A2: within MF DSC coverage; A3: satellite coverage beyond A1/A2) which drive the equipment carriage scale. title: Radio equipment: General
text: Radio equipment: General Every ship needs VHF DSC on channel 70 (distress alert initiation from the normal navigating position) plus radiotelephony on channels 6/13/16, a continuous DSC watch receiver, a radar or AIS-SART stowed for easy use, an MSI/SAR-information receiver for the whole voyage, and an EPIRB that is easily accessible, manually releasable into a survival craft, capable of floating free and automatically activating, and manually activatable. title: Radio equipment: Sea area A3
text: Radio equipment: Sea area A3 In addition to Regulation 7, ships on A3 voyages need a recognized mobile satellite service ship earth station capable of transmitting/receiving distress, urgency and safety communications and initiating/receiving distress priority calls. In addition to Regulation 7, ships on A3 voyages need a recognized mobile satellite service ship earth station capable of transmitting/receiving distress, urgency and safety communications and initiating/receiving distress priority calls.

title: Watchkeeping requirements
text: Watchkeeping requirements Requires a continuous DSC watch on the frequencies matching the ship's fitted equipment (VHF ch.70, MF 2187.5 kHz, MF/HF distress frequencies), a watch for MSI and SAR-related broadcasts on the area's frequencies, and, when practicable, a continuous listening watch on VHF channel 16 and other urgency/safety frequencies from the normal navigating position. title: Performance standards and maintenance requirements
text: Performance standards and maintenance requirements All GMDSS-chapter equipment must be Administration type-approved to IMO performance standards; equipment must be designed so main units can be replaced without elaborate recalibration, and constructed/installed for ready inspection and onboard maintenance access. title: Radio records and position-updating
text: Radio records and position-updating A record of all radiocommunication incidents of safety importance must be kept on board; two-way equipment that auto-includes ship's position in a distress alert must be fed automatically from a navigation receiver, with manual position updates at least every 4 hours if that receiver malfunctions while under way. label: VII
title: Carriage of dangerous goods
text: Carriage of dangerous goods Sets documentation, stowage and incident-reporting requirements for the carriage of dangerous goods, delegating detailed technical requirements to the IMDG Code (packaged form) and the IMSBC Code (solid form in bulk). title: Documents
text: Documents Transport information and the container/vehicle packing certificate for packaged dangerous goods must follow the IMDG Code and be available to the port State's designated person/organization; ships carrying such goods must have a special list, manifest or stowage plan showing what's aboard and where, with a copy available before departure. title: Cargo Securing Manual
text: Cargo Securing Manual Cargo, cargo units and cargo transport units must be loaded, stowed and secured throughout the voyage per an Administration-approved Cargo Securing Manual, drawn up to a standard at least equivalent to IMO guidelines. title: Reporting of incidents involving dangerous goods (packaged form)
text: Reporting of incidents involving dangerous goods (packaged form) When dangerous goods in packaged form are lost or likely lost overboard, the master (or person in charge) must report the incident's particulars. title: Reporting of incidents involving dangerous goods (solid bulk)
text: Reporting of incidents involving dangerous goods (solid bulk) The same reporting duty as Reg. 6 applies to loss or likely loss overboard of dangerous goods in solid form in bulk, reported to the nearest coastal State without delay; if the ship is abandoned or the report is incomplete/unobtainable, the company (as defined in Ch. IX Reg. 1.2) assumes the master's obligations to the fullest extent possible. Solid dangerous goods giving off dangerous vapours must be stowed in a well-ventilated cargo space. title: Requirements for the carriage of dangerous goods in solid form in bulk
text: Requirements for the carriage of dangerous goods in solid form in bulk Carriage of dangerous goods in solid form in bulk must comply with the relevant provisions of the IMSBC Code, as defined in Regulation VI/1-1.1. label: VIII
title: Nuclear ships
text: Nuclear ships A narrow, rarely-examined chapter setting extra requirements for nuclear-powered ships: an operating manual for the nuclear power plant kept current and on board, annual (minimum) surveys per Ch. I requirements as modified for radiation limitations plus any safety-assessment-specific items, a distinct Nuclear Ship Safety Certificate regime (Ch. I certificate provisions on duration/renewal don't apply), and an immediate casualty-reporting duty to the Administration and to the competent authority of waters the ship is in or approaching if damaged. title: Operating manual
text: Operating manual A fully detailed operating manual for the nuclear power plant must be prepared, kept up to date, approved by the Administration, and a copy kept on board for the operating personnel. title: Surveys
text: Surveys Nuclear ship surveys apply Ch. I Reg. 7 (passenger ships) or Regs. 8-10 (cargo ships) as far as radiation limits permit, plus any safety-assessment-specific items, and must be carried out at least annually regardless of the underlying Ch. title: Certificates
text: Certificates A distinct Nuclear (Passenger/Cargo) Ship Safety Certificate regime applies; the Ch. I Reg. 12 issuance and Reg. 14 duration/validity provisions do not apply to nuclear ships. title: Casualties
text: Casualties On any accident likely to lead to an environmental hazard, the master of a nuclear ship must immediately inform the Administration and the competent governmental authority of waters the ship is in, or approaching in a damaged condition. label: X
title: Safety measures for high-speed craft
text: Safety measures for high-speed craft A short, single-regulation chapter that operates by deeming compliance: a high-speed craft complying in its entirety with the applicable edition of the High-Speed Craft (HSC) Code (1994 for craft built 1996-2002, 2000 for craft built from July 2002) and surveyed/certified under that Code is deemed to comply with SOLAS Chapters I-IV and Regs. V/18-20, notwithstanding those chapters' own requirements — with HSC Code certificates carrying the same force as Chapter I certificates. title: Requirements for high-speed craft
text: Requirements for high-speed craft Craft built 1 Jan 1996-30 Jun 2002 complying fully with the 1994 HSC Code (treated as mandatory for this purpose) are deemed compliant with Chapters I-IV and Regs. V/18-20; craft built from 1 July 2002 achieve the same deeming under the 2000 HSC Code. HSC Code certificates and permits have the same force and recognition as Chapter I certificates. label: XI-1
title: Special measures to enhance maritime safety
text: Special measures to enhance maritime safety Covers the IMO ship identification number scheme (permanently marked on the hull, inserted on statutory certificates), port State control targeted at operational familiarity with safety procedures, the Continuous Synopsis Record documenting a ship's history (flag, owner, class, etc.), and the Casualty Investigation Code (resolution MSC.255(84)) governing marine casualty/incident investigations — Parts I/II mandatory, Part III explanatory. title: Ship identification number
text: Ship identification number Applies to passenger ships of 100 GT+ and cargo ships of 300 GT+: every ship gets an IMO ship identification number, inserted on Ch. I Reg. 12/13 certificates, and permanently marked in a visible external position (stern or hull sides, or superstructure) and an accessible internal position (machinery-space bulkhead, hatchway, pump-room for tankers, or ro-ro space bulkhead), painted to a defined standard. title: Port State control on operational requirements
text: Port State control on operational requirements A ship in another Contracting Government's port is subject to control on operational safety requirements where there are clear grounds the master or crew are unfamiliar with essential shipboard safety procedures; the controlling government must ensure the ship doesn't sail until the situation is corrected, following the Ch. I Reg. 19 port State control procedures. title: Continuous Synopsis Record
text: Continuous Synopsis Record Every ship to which Chapter I applies is issued a Continuous Synopsis Record, an on-board history of the ship (flag State, registration, owner/manager identity, class, etc.) intended to give port State control officers an at-a-glance ownership/history trail. title: Additional requirements for investigation of marine casualties and incidents
text: Additional requirements for investigation of marine casualties and incidents Each Administration must investigate marine casualties/incidents per the Casualty Investigation Code (resolution MSC.255(84)): Parts I and II are fully mandatory, Part III's guidance/explanatory material should be followed as far as possible for consistency, and amendment procedures differ between Parts I/II (Article VIII tacit acceptance) and Part III (amended directly by MSC under its own rules of procedure). label: XIII
title: Verification of compliance
text: Verification of compliance A short administrative chapter making the IMO Member State Audit Scheme and the IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code, resolution A.1070(28)) the mechanism by which Contracting Governments' own compliance with SOLAS is checked — this is a flag-State-level audit chapter, not a ship-level survey chapter. title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines Audit (a systematic, independent, documented process for obtaining and objectively evaluating audit evidence against audit criteria), Audit Scheme (the IMO Member State Audit Scheme), Code for Implementation (the III Code, resolution A.1070(28)), and Audit Standard (the Code for Implementation itself). title: Application
text: Application Contracting Governments must use the provisions of the Code for Implementation in executing their obligations and responsibilities under SOLAS. Contracting Governments must use the provisions of the Code for Implementation in executing their obligations and responsibilities under SOLAS.

title: Verification of compliance
text: Verification of compliance Every Contracting Government undergoes periodic audits by IMO against the Audit Standard to verify compliance with and implementation of SOLAS; the Secretary-General administers the Audit Scheme, and each Contracting Government must facilitate the audit and implement a programme of actions addressing the findings. label: XIV
title: Safety measures for ships operating in polar waters
text: Safety measures for ships operating in polar waters The SOLAS hook making Part I-A of the Polar Code mandatory for ships operating in Arctic/Antarctic waters, on top of the ordinary Ch. I survey/certification regime, with Part I-B treated as additional (non-mandatory) guidance. Government non-commercial-service ships are excluded but encouraged to comply voluntarily. I survey/certification regime, with Part I-B treated as additional (non-mandatory) guidance. Government non-commercial-service ships are excluded but encouraged to comply voluntarily.

title: Requirements for ships to which this chapter applies
text: Requirements for ships to which this chapter applies Ships within scope must comply with the Polar Code's safety-related introduction provisions and Part I-A, and be surveyed/certified under that Code in addition to the ordinary Ch. I Reg. 7-10 survey requirements; the resulting certificate is treated as a Ch. I Reg. 12/13 certificate for port State control purposes under Regs. I/19 and XI-1/4. Part I-B additional guidance should also be considered. The chapter does not apply to government non-commercial-service ships (though voluntary compliance is encouraged), and does not prejudice States' rights/obligations under international law. label: XV
title: Safety measures for ships carrying industrial personnel
text: Safety measures for ships carrying industrial personnel A 2024-vintage chapter (the newest in SOLAS at time of writing) making the International Code of Safety for Ships Carrying Industrial Personnel (IP Code) mandatory for cargo ships and high-speed cargo craft carrying more than 12 industrial personnel — a direct response to the growth of offshore wind and similar industrial-crew-transfer operations. Phases compliance in via survey milestones tied to construction/authorization date rather than a single hard cutover. title: Application and phase-in of IP Code compliance
text: Application and phase-in of IP Code compliance Cargo ships already authorized before 1 July 2024 to carry more than 12 industrial personnel must comply with IP Code regulations III/1, III/2 (except para. 2.1.7), IV/7 and IV/8 by their first intermediate or renewal survey after that date; high-speed cargo craft under the equivalent authorization get the same regulations (V/7, V/8 instead of IV/7, IV/8) by their third periodical or first renewal survey. Ships not previously authorized must comply and be certified under this chapter and the IP Code before carrying more than 12 industrial personnel at all. "Constructed" is defined by cross-reference to Ch. II-2/1.1.2.1 (cargo ships) and Ch. X/1.4 (high-speed cargo craft). Cargo ships already authorized before 1 July 2024 to carry more than 12 industrial personnel must comply with IP Code regulations III/1, III/2 (except para. 2.1.7), IV/7 and IV/8 by their first intermediate or renewal survey after that date; high-speed cargo craft under the equivalent authorization get the same regulations (V/7, V/8 instead of IV/7, IV/8) by their third periodical or first renewal survey. Ships not previously authorized must comply and be certified under this chapter and the IP Code before carrying more than 12 industrial personnel at all. "Constructed" is defined by cross-reference to Ch. II-2/1.1.2.1 (cargo ships) and Ch. X/1.4 (high-speed cargo craft).

title: International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), 1973, as modified by the 1978 Protocol
text: International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), 1973, as modified by the 1978 Protocol MARPOL marpol annex vi oil record book eexi cii air pollution

label: I
title: Prevention of Pollution by Oil
text: Prevention of Pollution by Oil The oldest and, for an engine-room officer, the most operationally central annex: it sets the equipment (oily-water separators, sludge tanks), discharge criteria and record-keeping (Oil Record Book Part I) that govern day-to-day handling of oil and oily mixtures in machinery spaces, plus construction rules (double hulls, segregated ballast) aimed at preventing pollution from tanker cargo operations and casualties. title: Tanks for oil residues (sludge)
text: Tanks for oil residues (sludge) Requires ships of 400 GT and above to have dedicated sludge tank(s) sized for the machinery and voyage length to hold oil residues that cannot otherwise be disposed of, with piping kept isolated from the bilge system and from any direct overboard connection other than the standard discharge connection.
