title: Sludge tank sizing & capacity requirements
text: Sludge tank sizing & capacity requirements Every ship of 400 GT and above must be provided with a tank or tanks of adequate capacity, having regard to the type of machinery and length of voyage, to receive oil residues (sludge) such as those resulting from the purification of fuel and lubricating oils and oil leakages in machinery spaces. Every ship of 400 GT and above must be provided with a tank or tanks of adequate capacity, having regard to the type of machinery and length of voyage, to receive oil residues (sludge) such as those resulting from the purification of fuel and lubricating oils and oil leakages in machinery spaces.

title: Piping isolation requirements
text: Piping isolation requirements Oil residue (sludge) tanks must be designed and constructed so that sludge piping has no direct connection overboard other than the standard discharge connection referred to in Regulation 13, and has no direct connection to bilge discharge piping. Oil residue (sludge) tanks must be designed and constructed so that sludge piping has no direct connection overboard other than the standard discharge connection referred to in Regulation 13, and has no direct connection to bilge discharge piping.

title: Standard discharge connection flange dimensions
text: Standard discharge connection flange dimensions To enable pipes of reception facilities to be connected with the ship's discharge pipe for oil residues, the discharge pipe must be fitted with a standard discharge connection flange having 215 mm outer diameter, 183 mm bolt circle diameter, 6 slots of 22 mm diameter, 16 mm flange thickness, designed for 6 bar working pressure. title: Oil filtering equipment
text: Oil filtering equipment Requires ships to carry an approved oily-water separating/filtering system (and, where applicable, an oil discharge monitoring and control system) so that any oily bilge water discharged overboard is treated to remain within the 15 ppm oil-content limit this annex sets. Requires ships to carry an approved oily-water separating/filtering system (and, where applicable, an oil discharge monitoring and control system) so that any oily bilge water discharged overboard is treated to remain within the 15 ppm oil-content limit this annex sets.

title: 15 ppm oil filtering equipment carriage
text: 15 ppm oil filtering equipment carriage Ships of 400 GT and above but less than 10,000 GT must be fitted with oil filtering equipment complying with Resolution MEPC.107(49) ensuring that any oil mixture discharged into the sea after passing through the system has an oil content not exceeding 15 ppm. Ships of 400 GT and above but less than 10,000 GT must be fitted with oil filtering equipment complying with Resolution MEPC.107(49) ensuring that any oil mixture discharged into the sea after passing through the system has an oil content not exceeding 15 ppm.

title: Automatic 15 ppm alarm & stopping device
text: Automatic 15 ppm alarm & stopping device Ships of 10,000 GT and above must be fitted with oil filtering equipment provided with an alarm arrangement to indicate when the 15 ppm oil content limit cannot be maintained, and an automatic 3-way stopping device to stop any discharge of oily mixture when effluent oil content exceeds 15 ppm. Ships of 10,000 GT and above must be fitted with oil filtering equipment provided with an alarm arrangement to indicate when the 15 ppm oil content limit cannot be maintained, and an automatic 3-way stopping device to stop any discharge of oily mixture when effluent oil content exceeds 15 ppm.

title: Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System (ODME)
text: Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System (ODME) Oil tankers of 150 GT and above must be fitted with an approved Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System (ODME) that continuously records discharge flow rate, vessel speed, and oil content in ppm, automatically stopping discharge if allowable rates are exceeded. Oil tankers of 150 GT and above must be fitted with an approved Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System (ODME) that continuously records discharge flow rate, vessel speed, and oil content in ppm, automatically stopping discharge if allowable rates are exceeded.

title: Control of discharge of oil
text: Control of discharge of oil Sets the operational conditions under which any discharge of oil or oily mixtures from machinery spaces is permitted — the 15 ppm concentration limit, the requirement that the ship be en route, and distance-from-land/special-area restrictions — underpinning day-to-day bilge and slop-handling decisions. Sets the operational conditions under which any discharge of oil or oily mixtures from machinery spaces is permitted — the 15 ppm concentration limit, the requirement that the ship be en route, and distance-from-land/special-area restrictions — underpinning day-to-day bilge and slop-handling decisions.

title: Machinery space discharge criteria outside special areas
text: Machinery space discharge criteria outside special areas Discharge into the sea of oil or oily mixtures from machinery spaces of ships of 400 GT and above outside special areas is prohibited unless the ship is proceeding en route, oil content of effluent without dilution does not exceed 15 ppm, and effluent is processed through approved 15 ppm oil filtering equipment. Discharge into the sea of oil or oily mixtures from machinery spaces of ships of 400 GT and above outside special areas is prohibited unless the ship is proceeding en route, oil content of effluent without dilution does not exceed 15 ppm, and effluent is processed through approved 15 ppm oil filtering equipment.

title: Special area discharge criteria
text: Special area discharge criteria In special areas (including the Mediterranean Sea, Baltic Sea, Black Sea, Red Sea, Gulfs area, Gulf of Aden, Antarctic area, NW European waters, Oman area, and Southern African waters), any discharge of oil or oily mixtures is prohibited unless the ship is en route and fitted with 15 ppm equipment provided with an automatic stopping device. In special areas (including the Mediterranean Sea, Baltic Sea, Black Sea, Red Sea, Gulfs area, Gulf of Aden, Antarctic area, NW European waters, Oman area, and Southern African waters), any discharge of oil or oily mixtures is prohibited unless the ship is en route and fitted with 15 ppm equipment provided with an automatic stopping device.

title: Oil tanker cargo area discharge criteria
text: Oil tanker cargo area discharge criteria Discharge into the sea of oily mixture from cargo area of oil tankers is prohibited unless tanker is more than 50 NM from nearest land, proceeding en route, instantaneous rate of discharge does not exceed 30 litres per nautical mile, total quantity does not exceed 1/30,000 of total cargo volume, and ODME is operational. Discharge into the sea of oily mixture from cargo area of oil tankers is prohibited unless tanker is more than 50 NM from nearest land, proceeding en route, instantaneous rate of discharge does not exceed 30 litres per nautical mile, total quantity does not exceed 1/30,000 of total cargo volume, and ODME is operational.

title: Oil Record Book, Part I (Machinery space operations)
text: Oil Record Book, Part I (Machinery space operations) Requires oil tankers of 150 GT and above and other ships of 400 GT and above to maintain an Oil Record Book Part I recording machinery-space operations (bilge transfers, sludge disposal, bunkering, OWS operation) chronologically, signed by the responsible officer and the master, retained on board for at least three years. title: Double hull and double bottom requirements for oil tankers
text: Double hull and double bottom requirements for oil tankers Sets phased-in structural requirements for oil tankers to be built with double hulls (or an equivalent design approved by IMO), with separate provisions and phase-out timetables depending on tanker size and delivery date, aimed at reducing outflow in the event of grounding or collision. title: Shipboard oil pollution emergency plan (SOPEP)
text: Shipboard oil pollution emergency plan (SOPEP) Requires oil tankers of 150 GT and above and all ships of 400 GT and above to carry an approved Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP) containing operational procedures for reporting oil spills and initial response measures. title: SOPEP mandatory carriage thresholds
text: SOPEP mandatory carriage thresholds Every oil tanker of 150 GT and above and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 GT and above must carry on board a Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP) approved by the Administration. Every oil tanker of 150 GT and above and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 GT and above must carry on board a Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP) approved by the Administration.

title: SOPEP plan structure and initial response procedures
text: SOPEP plan structure and initial response procedures The SOPEP plan must be written in the working language of the master and officers and contain detailed procedures to report an oil pollution incident, lists of national and local coastal contacts, actions to be taken immediately by persons on board to reduce or control the discharge of oil, and procedures for coordinating with coastal authorities. label: II
title: Control of Pollution by Noxious Liquid Substances in Bulk
text: Control of Pollution by Noxious Liquid Substances in Bulk Governs chemical tankers and any ship carrying noxious liquid substances (NLS) in bulk, built around a hazard-based categorisation of substances (X/Y/Z) that in turn drives discharge criteria, tank-cleaning (prewash) procedures and record-keeping — the Annex II counterpart to Annex I's oil regime, cross-referenced to the IBC Code for the ship construction/equipment standards. Governs chemical tankers and any ship carrying noxious liquid substances (NLS) in bulk, built around a hazard-based categorisation of substances (X/Y/Z) that in turn drives discharge criteria, tank-cleaning (prewash) procedures and record-keeping — the Annex II counterpart to Annex I's oil regime, cross-referenced to the IBC Code for the ship construction/equipment standards.

title: Categorization of noxious liquid substances
text: Categorization of noxious liquid substances Sorts NLS cargoes into hazard Categories X, Y and Z (plus 'Other Substances') according to the hazard they present to marine resources or human health if discharged from tank cleaning or deballasting, with the category assigned to each substance driving how strictly its discharge is controlled. title: Control of discharges of residues of noxious liquid substances
text: Control of discharges of residues of noxious liquid substances Sets the conditions (ship speed/en route, distance from land, discharge rate, tank residue quantity, prewash where required) under which residues of Category X, Y or Z substances may be discharged into the sea, and prohibits discharge of substances that have not been categorized. title: Cargo Record Book
text: Cargo Record Book Requires every ship carrying NLS in bulk to keep a Cargo Record Book (which may be electronic) recording loading, internal transfer, unloading, tank cleaning, ballasting/deballasting of cargo tanks and residue discharge/disposal operations, with each entry signed by the responsible officer and each page by the master. title: Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan for noxious liquid substances
text: Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan for noxious liquid substances Requires ships of 150 GT and above certified to carry NLS in bulk to carry an approved emergency plan (often combined with the Annex I SOPEP into a single Shipboard Marine Pollution Emergency Plan) setting out the procedures the master and crew follow to prevent, contain and control a discharge of noxious liquid substances. label: III
title: Prevention of Pollution by Harmful Substances Carried by Sea in Packaged Form
text: Prevention of Pollution by Harmful Substances Carried by Sea in Packaged Form The shortest and least engine-room-relevant annex: it does not set discharge limits at all, instead requiring that harmful substances carried in packaged form (drums, containers, etc., as identified via the IMDG Code's marine pollutant criteria) be packed, marked, labelled, documented and stowed so as to minimise the risk of marine pollution if a package is lost or damaged. title: Application
text: Application Confines the Annex to substances identified as marine pollutants under the IMDG Code (or meeting the Annex's own hazard criteria) when carried in packaged form, distinguishing this Annex's scope from the bulk-cargo regimes of Annexes I and II. Confines the Annex to substances identified as marine pollutants under the IMDG Code (or meeting the Annex's own hazard criteria) when carried in packaged form, distinguishing this Annex's scope from the bulk-cargo regimes of Annexes I and II.

title: Marking and labelling
text: Marking and labelling Requires packages containing harmful substances to be durably marked with the correct technical name and marked/labelled to show they are a marine pollutant, so the hazard is identifiable throughout stowage, handling and any emergency response. Requires packages containing harmful substances to be durably marked with the correct technical name and marked/labelled to show they are a marine pollutant, so the hazard is identifiable throughout stowage, handling and any emergency response.

title: Stowage
text: Stowage Requires harmful substances to be properly stowed and secured to minimise the risk to the marine environment, while not compromising the safety of the ship or the persons on board — a balance between pollution prevention and conventional cargo-securing safety. Requires harmful substances to be properly stowed and secured to minimise the risk to the marine environment, while not compromising the safety of the ship or the persons on board — a balance between pollution prevention and conventional cargo-securing safety.

title: Quantity limitations
text: Quantity limitations Allows certain harmful substances to be prohibited from carriage altogether or limited in the quantity carried on a single ship, for sound scientific/technical reasons, having regard to the ship's size, construction and equipment as well as the packaging and nature of the substance. Allows certain harmful substances to be prohibited from carriage altogether or limited in the quantity carried on a single ship, for sound scientific/technical reasons, having regard to the ship's size, construction and equipment as well as the packaging and nature of the substance.

label: IV
title: Prevention of Pollution by Sewage from Ships
text: Prevention of Pollution by Sewage from Ships Covers black-water (sewage) discharge, requiring ships above defined size/passenger thresholds to be fitted with an approved sewage treatment plant, comminuting/disinfecting system, or holding tank, and setting the distance-from-land and treatment conditions under which sewage may be discharged. title: Surveys and issue of the International Sewage Pollution Prevention Certificate
text: Surveys and issue of the International Sewage Pollution Prevention Certificate Requires an initial survey of the sewage treatment plant, comminuting/disinfecting equipment, holding tank, discharge pipework and standard shore connection before an International Sewage Pollution Prevention Certificate is issued, with renewal surveys keeping the certificate valid (nominally five years, subject to the harmonised survey system). title: Sewage systems
text: Sewage systems Requires every ship to be fitted with one of: an approved sewage treatment plant, a comminuting and disinfecting system with holding facility, or a holding tank of adequate capacity, sized and equipped so sewage can be retained until it can be discharged in compliance with this Annex. Requires every ship to be fitted with one of: an approved sewage treatment plant, a comminuting and disinfecting system with holding facility, or a holding tank of adequate capacity, sized and equipped so sewage can be retained until it can be discharged in compliance with this Annex.

title: Discharge of sewage
text: Discharge of sewage Sets the conditions under which sewage may be discharged — untreated sewage only beyond a specified distance from the nearest land and at a moderate rate while en route, or treated/comminuted-and-disinfected sewage under less restrictive distance conditions — with tighter limits applying in designated special areas. label: V
title: Prevention of Pollution by Garbage from Ships
text: Prevention of Pollution by Garbage from Ships Regulates disposal of ship-generated garbage, built around a general prohibition on discharging plastics of any kind and distance-graduated rules for other garbage categories, backed up by a Garbage Management Plan, placards and a Garbage Record Book so compliance can be demonstrated to port State control. title: Application
text: Application Applies the Annex to all ships, with the Garbage Record Book and Garbage Management Plan duties keyed to gross tonnage and persons-carried thresholds, and extends coverage to fixed and floating platforms. title: Discharge of garbage outside special areas
text: Discharge of garbage outside special areas Sets minimum distances from the nearest land at which different garbage categories may be discharged outside special areas while the ship is en route — including ground food waste at 3 nautical miles and cargo residues not harmful to the marine environment at 12 nautical miles — while maintaining a complete ban on plastics. title: Placards, garbage management plans and garbage record-keeping
text: Placards, garbage management plans and garbage record-keeping Requires ships of 12 m or more in length to display placards on discharge requirements, ships of 100 GT and above (or certified to carry 15+ persons) to carry a written Garbage Management Plan naming who is responsible for it, and a Garbage Record Book logging every discharge, incineration or shore-disposal of garbage. label: VI
title: Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships
text: Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships The newest and, since the 2010s, fastest-evolving annex: it limits NOx from marine diesel engines and SOx/particulate matter from fuel oil combustion, bans deliberate emission of ozone-depleting substances, and — since 2013/2023 — layers on a mandatory energy-efficiency and carbon-intensity regime (EEDI/EEXI/SEEMP/CII) aimed at IMO's decarbonisation targets. title: Nitrogen oxides (NOx)
text: Nitrogen oxides (NOx) Sets tiered NOx emission limits (Tier I/II/III, tightening with engine installation date and, for Tier III, requiring designated Emission Control Areas) for marine diesel engines above 130 kW, verified against the NOx Technical Code and recorded on the Engine International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate. Sets tiered NOx emission limits (Tier I/II/III, tightening with engine installation date and, for Tier III, requiring designated Emission Control Areas) for marine diesel engines above 130 kW, verified against the NOx Technical Code and recorded on the Engine International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate.

title: Marine diesel engine NOx applicability threshold
text: Marine diesel engine NOx applicability threshold Regulation 13 applies to each marine diesel engine with a power output of more than 130 kW installed on a ship constructed on or after 1 January 2000, or undergoing a major conversion; emergency diesel engines and lifeboat engines are exempt. Regulation 13 applies to each marine diesel engine with a power output of more than 130 kW installed on a ship constructed on or after 1 January 2000, or undergoing a major conversion; emergency diesel engines and lifeboat engines are exempt.

title: Tier I NOx emission limits (2000-2011)
text: Tier I NOx emission limits (2000-2011) Marine diesel engines installed on ships constructed between 1 January 2000 and 1 January 2011 shall comply with Tier I NOx limits: 17.0 g/kWh for rated engine speed n < 130 rpm, 45.0 * n^(-0.2) g/kWh for 130 <= n < 2000 rpm, and 9.8 g/kWh for n >= 2000 rpm. Marine diesel engines installed on ships constructed between 1 January 2000 and 1 January 2011 shall comply with Tier I NOx limits: 17.0 g/kWh for rated engine speed n < 130 rpm, 45.0 * n^(-0.2) g/kWh for 130 <= n < 2000 rpm, and 9.8 g/kWh for n >= 2000 rpm.

title: Tier II NOx emission limits (2011-2016)
text: Tier II NOx emission limits (2011-2016) Marine diesel engines installed on ships constructed on or after 1 January 2011 shall comply with Tier II NOx limits: 14.4 g/kWh for n < 130 rpm, 44.0 * n^(-0.23) g/kWh for 130 <= n < 2000 rpm, and 7.7 g/kWh for n >= 2000 rpm. Marine diesel engines installed on ships constructed on or after 1 January 2011 shall comply with Tier II NOx limits: 14.4 g/kWh for n < 130 rpm, 44.0 * n^(-0.23) g/kWh for 130 <= n < 2000 rpm, and 7.7 g/kWh for n >= 2000 rpm.

title: Tier III NOx emission limits inside ECAs
text: Tier III NOx emission limits inside ECAs Marine diesel engines operating inside designated Emission Control Areas (ECAs) installed on ships constructed on or after 1 January 2016 (North American/US Caribbean ECA) or 1 January 2021 (Baltic/North Sea ECA) shall comply with Tier III NOx limits: 3.4 g/kWh for n < 130 rpm, 9.0 * n^(-0.2) g/kWh for 130 <= n < 2000 rpm, and 2.0 g/kWh for n >= 2000 rpm, typically achieved via Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) or Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR). Marine diesel engines operating inside designated Emission Control Areas (ECAs) installed on ships constructed on or after 1 January 2016 (North American/US Caribbean ECA) or 1 January 2021 (Baltic/North Sea ECA) shall comply with Tier III NOx limits: 3.4 g/kWh for n < 130 rpm, 9.0 * n^(-0.2) g/kWh for 130 <= n < 2000 rpm, and 2.0 g/kWh for n >= 2000 rpm, typically achieved via Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) or Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR).

title: Sulphur oxides (SOx) and particulate matter
text: Sulphur oxides (SOx) and particulate matter Caps the sulphur content of fuel oil used on board — 0.50% m/m globally since 2020 ('IMO 2020'), tightened to 0.10% m/m inside designated Emission Control Areas — applicable to all fuel-oil-burning equipment on board (main/auxiliary engines, boilers, inert gas generators), with exhaust gas cleaning systems (scrubbers) as an approved equivalent compliance method. title: Global fuel oil sulphur content cap (0.50% m/m)
text: Global fuel oil sulphur content cap (0.50% m/m) The sulphur content of any fuel oil used on board ships shall not exceed 0.50% m/m on and after 1 January 2020 (IMO 2020 global sulphur cap), applicable to all main/auxiliary engines, boilers, and inert gas generators. The sulphur content of any fuel oil used on board ships shall not exceed 0.50% m/m on and after 1 January 2020 (IMO 2020 global sulphur cap), applicable to all main/auxiliary engines, boilers, and inert gas generators.

title: Emission Control Area (ECA) sulphur cap (0.10% m/m)
text: Emission Control Area (ECA) sulphur cap (0.10% m/m) While operating within designated SOx Emission Control Areas (Baltic Sea, North Sea, North American, US Caribbean ECAs), the sulphur content of fuel oil shall not exceed 0.10% m/m; ships using separate fuels shall complete fuel changeover prior to entry and record volumes, date, time, and position in an approved log book. While operating within designated SOx Emission Control Areas (Baltic Sea, North Sea, North American, US Caribbean ECAs), the sulphur content of fuel oil shall not exceed 0.10% m/m; ships using separate fuels shall complete fuel changeover prior to entry and record volumes, date, time, and position in an approved log book.

title: Exhaust gas cleaning system (scrubber) equivalence
text: Exhaust gas cleaning system (scrubber) equivalence Exhaust Gas Cleaning Systems (EGCS / Scrubbers) approved per IMO Guidelines (MEPC.259(68)/MEPC.340(77)) are accepted as an equivalent compliance method to reduce SOx emissions to levels equivalent to 0.50% m/m or 0.10% m/m fuel sulphur limits. Exhaust Gas Cleaning Systems (EGCS / Scrubbers) approved per IMO Guidelines (MEPC.259(68)/MEPC.340(77)) are accepted as an equivalent compliance method to reduce SOx emissions to levels equivalent to 0.50% m/m or 0.10% m/m fuel sulphur limits.

title: Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI)
text: Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) Requires most existing cargo, cruise and gas-carrier ships above 400 GT to calculate a one-off 'attained EEXI' and demonstrate it meets a required technical efficiency level, achieved by engine power limitation, retrofit, or other technical/operational measures — a one-time technical check rather than the annually-rated CII. title: Attained EEXI calculation requirement
text: Attained EEXI calculation requirement Each ship of 400 GT and above shall calculate an attained Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) specific to its ship type and capacity, verified by the Administration against the EEXI Technical File. Each ship of 400 GT and above shall calculate an attained Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) specific to its ship type and capacity, verified by the Administration against the EEXI Technical File.

title: Required EEXI compliance & Engine Power Limitation
text: Required EEXI compliance & Engine Power Limitation The attained EEXI shall be less than or equal to the required EEXI calculated using baseline reduction factors; compliance may be achieved via Engine Power Limitation (EPL/Shaft Power Limitation) or technical retrofits. The attained EEXI shall be less than or equal to the required EEXI calculated using baseline reduction factors; compliance may be achieved via Engine Power Limitation (EPL/Shaft Power Limitation) or technical retrofits.

title: Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP)
text: Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) Requires every ship to carry a SEEMP; ships of 5,000 GT and above carry an expanded SEEMP with Part II (fuel-consumption data collection for the IMO Data Collection System) and Part III (the ship's plan for meeting its CII targets), making the SEEMP the operational document tying day-to-day fuel/efficiency management to the Annex's data-reporting and CII regimes. title: SEEMP Part I carriage requirement (400 GT)
text: SEEMP Part I carriage requirement (400 GT) Each ship of 400 GT and above shall keep on board a ship-specific Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP Part I) providing operational measures to improve energy efficiency. Each ship of 400 GT and above shall keep on board a ship-specific Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP Part I) providing operational measures to improve energy efficiency.

title: SEEMP Part II (DCS) & Part III (CII plan)
text: SEEMP Part II (DCS) & Part III (CII plan) Ships of 5,000 GT and above shall include in their SEEMP Part II (methodologies for collecting fuel oil consumption data for the IMO DCS) and Part III (the ship operational carbon intensity plan detailing required CII targets and implementation plans). Ships of 5,000 GT and above shall include in their SEEMP Part II (methodologies for collecting fuel oil consumption data for the IMO DCS) and Part III (the ship operational carbon intensity plan detailing required CII targets and implementation plans).

title: Operational carbon intensity (CII)
text: Operational carbon intensity (CII) Requires ships of 5,000 GT and above to calculate an annual attained operational Carbon Intensity Indicator and receive an A-to-E rating against a required reference line; ships rated D for three consecutive years or E in any year must submit a corrective action plan, making this the recurring operational counterpart to the one-off Regulation 23 EEXI check. title: Annual attained operational CII calculation
text: Annual attained operational CII calculation Ships of 5,000 GT and above shall calculate an annual attained operational Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) over a 12-month calendar year period, expressed in g CO2 per DWT-nautical mile. Ships of 5,000 GT and above shall calculate an annual attained operational Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) over a 12-month calendar year period, expressed in g CO2 per DWT-nautical mile.

title: Annual operational CII rating (A to E)
text: Annual operational CII rating (A to E) The attained operational CII shall be documented and rated against required reference lines into five carbon intensity ratings: A (major superior), B (minor superior), C (moderate), D (minor inferior), or E (inferior). title: Corrective action plan for D & E ratings
text: Corrective action plan for D & E ratings A ship rated D for three consecutive years or rated E in any single year shall develop a Corrective Action Plan as a revised SEEMP Part III detailing actions to achieve the required operational CII. A ship rated D for three consecutive years or rated E in any single year shall develop a Corrective Action Plan as a revised SEEMP Part III detailing actions to achieve the required operational CII.

title: International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW), 1978, as amended (Manila Amendments 2010)

label: I
title: General Provisions
text: General Provisions Carries the Convention's administrative machinery — definitions, flag-State certification and control duties, quality-standards system, and the certificate lifecycle (issue, endorsement, revalidation) that every other chapter's competence tables plug into. title: Revalidation of certificates
text: Revalidation of certificates Requires certificate holders to establish continued professional competence at intervals not exceeding five years, normally through a combination of approved seagoing service, refresher/updating training (e.g. safety and firefighting refreshers) and, where applicable, demonstrated maintenance of standards of competence, before a certificate can be revalidated. label: III
title: Engine Department
text: Engine Department Sets the mandatory minimum certification requirements for engineer officers by main-propulsion power band and management/operational level — the direct source of the MEO Class 1 (management level, unlimited kW) and MEO Class 2/4 (operational level) certification hierarchy — plus the parallel electro-technical officer track introduced by the 2010 Manila Amendments. Sets the mandatory minimum certification requirements for engineer officers by main-propulsion power band and management/operational level — the direct source of the MEO Class 1 (management level, unlimited kW) and MEO Class 2/4 (operational level) certification hierarchy — plus the parallel electro-technical officer track introduced by the 2010 Manila Amendments.

title: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of officers in charge of an engineering watch
text: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of officers in charge of an engineering watch Sets the operational-level certification (Officer in Charge of an Engineering Watch, or Designated Duty Engineer on periodically unattended machinery spaces) for engineers on ships with main propulsion machinery of 750 kW or more, requiring approved seagoing service, education/training and demonstrated competence per Code Table A-III/1. Sets the operational-level certification (Officer in Charge of an Engineering Watch, or Designated Duty Engineer on periodically unattended machinery spaces) for engineers on ships with main propulsion machinery of 750 kW or more, requiring approved seagoing service, education/training and demonstrated competence per Code Table A-III/1.

title: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of chief engineer officers and second engineer officers (ships powered by 3,000 kW propulsion power or more)
text: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of chief engineer officers and second engineer officers (ships powered by 3,000 kW propulsion power or more) Sets the management-level certification for chief and second engineer officers on ships of 3,000 kW or more — the STCW basis for the MEO Class 1 certificate of competency — requiring prior certification as OICEW plus not less than 36 months' approved seagoing service (at least 12 months as a qualified second engineer officer) and competence per Code Table A-III/2. Sets the management-level certification for chief and second engineer officers on ships of 3,000 kW or more — the STCW basis for the MEO Class 1 certificate of competency — requiring prior certification as OICEW plus not less than 36 months' approved seagoing service (at least 12 months as a qualified second engineer officer) and competence per Code Table A-III/2.

title: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of chief engineer officers and second engineer officers (ships powered by between 750 kW and 3,000 kW propulsion power)
text: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of chief engineer officers and second engineer officers (ships powered by between 750 kW and 3,000 kW propulsion power) Sets the equivalent management-level certification for smaller ships (750 kW to 3,000 kW) — broadly the MEO Class 2/4 tier — requiring not less than 24 months' approved seagoing service (at least 12 months as a qualified second engineer officer) and competence per Code Table A-III/3. Sets the equivalent management-level certification for smaller ships (750 kW to 3,000 kW) — broadly the MEO Class 2/4 tier — requiring not less than 24 months' approved seagoing service (at least 12 months as a qualified second engineer officer) and competence per Code Table A-III/3.

title: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of electro-technical officers
text: Mandatory minimum requirements for certification of electro-technical officers A Manila 2010 addition requiring electro-technical officers on ships with 750 kW or more propulsion power to hold a dedicated certificate of competency, with training/service pathways (combined workshop and seagoing service, or longer engine-department service) and competence per Code Table A-III/6 covering electrical, electronic and control-engineering duties. label: V
title: Special Training Requirements for Personnel on Certain Types of Ships
text: Special Training Requirements for Personnel on Certain Types of Ships Layers additional, ship-type-specific training on top of the general certification of Chapters II/III/VII for personnel serving on tankers and passenger ships, recognising that cargo/vessel-specific hazards (flammable/toxic cargo, mass evacuation) are not adequately covered by generic deck/engine competence tables alone. title: Mandatory minimum requirements for the training and qualification of masters, officers and ratings on oil and chemical tankers
text: Mandatory minimum requirements for the training and qualification of masters, officers and ratings on oil and chemical tankers Requires basic tanker-familiarization training (cargo hazards, layouts, equipment, operational sequence) for anyone assigned shipboard duties on an oil or chemical tanker, and a further advanced-level course and seagoing service for those assigned cargo-handling responsibility. title: Mandatory minimum requirements for the training and qualification of masters, officers and ratings on liquefied gas tankers
text: Mandatory minimum requirements for the training and qualification of masters, officers and ratings on liquefied gas tankers Parallels Regulation V/1-1 for liquefied gas carriers, requiring basic (and, for those with cargo responsibility, advanced) training in gas-tanker-specific hazards — cargo containment, gas safety measures, pollution prevention and emergency response — held as a distinct certificate from oil/chemical tanker endorsements. label: VIII
title: Watchkeeping
text: Watchkeeping Sets the framework for safe watchkeeping arrangements and, critically, mandatory minimum rest-hour limits for watchkeepers and other safety-critical personnel, aimed squarely at preventing fatigue-related accidents. title: Fitness for duty
text: Fitness for duty Requires Administrations to establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and others with designated safety/security/pollution-prevention duties — minimum 10 hours' rest in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period (rest divisible into no more than two periods, one at least 6 hours) — with the master retaining a limited power to suspend the rest schedule for immediate safety needs, followed by compensatory rest. label: B
title: Steering and Sailing Rules
text: Steering and Sailing Rules The operational core of COLREG: how vessels must behave to avoid collision, split into rules applying in any condition of visibility (lookout, safe speed, risk assessment, action to avoid collision, narrow channels, traffic separation schemes), rules for vessels in sight of one another (overtaking, head-on, crossing, give-way/stand-on duties), and a separate rule for restricted visibility where the usual sight-based give-way/stand-on roles do not apply. title: Look-out
text: Look-out Requires every vessel to maintain a proper look-out by sight, hearing and all available means appropriate to the prevailing circumstances, so as to make a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision — the foundational duty underlying every other Part B rule. title: Risk of collision
text: Risk of collision Requires vessels to use all available means, including radar where fitted, to determine whether risk of collision exists, treating risk as present if a large vessel's compass bearing does not appreciably change, and cautioning against assuming safety from scanty information. Requires vessels to use all available means, including radar where fitted, to determine whether risk of collision exists, treating risk as present if a large vessel's compass bearing does not appreciably change, and cautioning against assuming safety from scanty information.

title: Narrow channels
text: Narrow channels Requires vessels proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway to keep as near the outer limit on their starboard side as is safe and practicable, restricts crossing and anchoring in narrow channels, and imposes special caution/signalling duties near bends and on vessels engaged in overtaking within the channel. title: Crossing situation
text: Crossing situation Where two power-driven vessels are crossing so as to involve risk of collision, requires the vessel that has the other on her own starboard side to give way and, if circumstances permit, avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel. title: Conduct of vessels in restricted visibility
text: Conduct of vessels in restricted visibility Applies to vessels not in sight of one another navigating in or near restricted visibility, requiring safe speed adapted to the conditions and, if collision risk is detected mainly by radar, action taken in ample time while avoiding an alteration towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam or an alteration towards a vessel forward of the beam other than one being overtaken. label: C
title: Lights and Shapes
text: Lights and Shapes Specifies the navigation lights and day shapes each type/condition of vessel must exhibit so that another vessel's type, aspect and activity (underway, at anchor, aground, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, engaged in specific operations) can be identified visually at night or by shape in daylight. title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines the technical terms used throughout Part C — masthead light, sidelights, sternlight, towing light, all-round light and flashing light — including their required arcs of visibility and colours, which every subsequent lighting rule builds on. title: Power-driven vessels underway
text: Power-driven vessels underway Sets the standard light configuration for a power-driven vessel underway (masthead light(s), sidelights, sternlight), with size-based variations in number/height of masthead lights and a reduced configuration permitted for vessels under a specified length. title: Anchored vessels and vessels aground
text: Anchored vessels and vessels aground Requires vessels at anchor to exhibit an all-round white light (or ball shape by day) forward, and a further light/shape aft on larger vessels, while a vessel aground exhibits the anchor light/shape configuration plus additional distinctive lights/shapes signalling that she is not under command in the ordinary sense. label: D
title: Sound and Light Signals
text: Sound and Light Signals Defines the whistle, bell/gong and light signals vessels use to communicate manoeuvring intentions, warn another vessel, signal in restricted visibility, or indicate distress — the audible/visual counterpart to Part B's steering rules and Part C's lights/shapes. title: Manoeuvring and warning signals
text: Manoeuvring and warning signals Defines the short-blast whistle signals power-driven vessels in sight of one another use to indicate an alteration of course (one/two/three short blasts) or, in a narrow channel, intention to overtake, plus a light-signal alternative, and the prolonged-blast warning signal used when in doubt about another vessel's actions or intentions. title: Sound signals in restricted visibility
text: Sound signals in restricted visibility Prescribes the specific whistle/bell (and, for vessels of 100 m or more, gong) signals vessels must sound at intervals not exceeding two minutes in or near restricted visibility, with distinct signal patterns for power-driven vessels making way, power-driven vessels underway but stopped, vessels not under command, vessels at anchor and vessels aground. title: Distress signals
text: Distress signals Points to Annex IV's list of recognised distress signals (e.g. continuous sounding of a fog signal apparatus, rockets/red flares, SOS, MAYDAY radiotelephony, orange smoke signal) to be used or exhibited only to indicate that a vessel is in distress and requires assistance. title: Conditions of Assignment of Freeboard

title: Information to be supplied to the master
text: Information to be supplied to the master Requires the master to be supplied with sufficient information, in an approved form, to allow rapid and simple determination of the ship's stability under varying conditions of service — the load-line-side counterpart of the loading/stability information required under SOLAS. title: Terms and Definitions

title: Organization and Co-ordination

title: Inventory of Hazardous Materials (IHM)
text: Inventory of Hazardous Materials (IHM) Requires each ship to carry a ship-specific Inventory of Hazardous Materials — Part I listing materials present in the ship's structure and equipment (asbestos, ozone-depleting substances, heavy metals, certain flame retardants and the like) — established at construction for new ships and compiled for existing ships, and kept up to date throughout the ship's operating life as materials and equipment change. title: Ship Recycling Plan
text: Ship Recycling Plan Requires a ship-specific Ship Recycling Plan to be prepared by the ship recycling facility before any recycling begins, drawing on information the shipowner provides and the ship's completed IHM, setting out how that particular ship will be recycled given its structure, materials and inventory, and requiring approval by the facility's competent authority where the recycling State so provides. title: London Convention 1972 — the black/grey list approach
text: London Convention 1972 — the black/grey list approach The original 1972 dumping treaty took a permissive approach: everything could in principle be dumped at sea unless a control applied, with a 'black list' of substances banned outright and a 'grey list' of substances that could be dumped only under a special permit, everything else needing a general permit. title: Establishment and purpose of the Fund
text: Establishment and purpose of the Fund Sets up the IOPC Fund 1992 as an organisation with legal personality in each member State and defines its purpose — to provide compensation for pollution damage to the extent that the CLC regime is inadequate, and to give effect to the related aims of the Convention — for damage suffered in the territory, territorial sea and EEZ of member States. title: Compensation payable and the overall ceiling
text: Compensation payable and the overall ceiling Obliges the Fund to pay compensation to any claimant who cannot obtain full recovery under the CLC, subject to an overall maximum per incident that is expressed as a single ceiling combining the amount actually available from the shipowner under the CLC with the Fund's own contribution, so that the two tiers together cap the compensation for one incident. title: Conduct barring limitation
text: Conduct barring limitation Sets the high threshold at which the right to limit is forfeited: the person liable loses the ceiling only if it is proved the loss resulted from their own personal act or omission committed either with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result — a deliberately demanding test that makes breaking limitation rare. title: Definitions and scope

title: Strict liability of the shipowner

text: Salvage contracts Confirms that the Convention applies to any salvage operation save where a contract provides otherwise, leaving parties free to agree their own terms (as they do under standard forms such as Lloyd's Open Form) while the Convention supplies the default rules and preserves the power to annul or modify a contract reached under undue influence or on inequitable terms. text: Duties of the salvor and of the owner and master Imposes reciprocal duties: the salvor must carry out the operation with due care, exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment, seek help from other salvors when reasonable and accept intervention when reasonably requested; the owner and master of the ship in danger owe the salvor corresponding duties to cooperate fully and to likewise act to prevent or minimise environmental damage. title: Conditions for reward — no cure, no pay

title: Criteria for fixing the reward
text: Criteria for fixing the reward Lists the factors used to set the salvage reward so as to encourage salvage — among them the salved value of the ship and property, the salvor's skill and efforts (including in preventing environmental damage), the measure of success, the nature and degree of danger, the time and expenses incurred, and the risk of liability run — with the reward not to exceed the salved value of the property. title: Special compensation and the SCOPIC alternative

title: Carrier Liability, Limits and Compulsory Insurance
text: Carrier Liability, Limits and Compulsory Insurance The regime governing what a passenger can recover when killed, injured or deprived of luggage at sea: the 2002 Protocol layers strict liability for major 'shipping incidents' onto the older fault-based scheme, caps the carrier's exposure, and — crucially for enforceability — requires insurance backed by a direct right of action against the insurer. title: Two-tier liability for death and personal injury
text: Two-tier liability for death and personal injury For death or personal injury caused by a 'shipping incident' (such as shipwreck, capsizing, collision, stranding, explosion, fire or defect in the ship) the carrier is strictly liable up to 250,000 SDR per passenger unless it proves a narrow defence such as an act of war or an exceptional natural phenomenon or the wholly intentional act of a third party; above that, up to 400,000 SDR per passenger, the carrier is liable unless it proves the incident occurred without its fault or neglect. For death or personal injury caused by a 'shipping incident' (such as shipwreck, capsizing, collision, stranding, explosion, fire or defect in the ship) the carrier is strictly liable up to 250,000 SDR per passenger unless it proves a narrow defence such as an act of war or an exceptional natural phenomenon or the wholly intentional act of a third party; above that, up to 400,000 SDR per passenger, the carrier is liable unless it proves the incident occurred without its fault or neglect.

label: 4bis
title: Compulsory insurance and direct action
text: Compulsory insurance and direct action Requires carriers of ships licensed to carry more than twelve passengers to maintain insurance or other financial security to cover their liability for passenger death and personal injury — at least 250,000 SDR per passenger per occasion — evidenced by a certificate carried on board, and gives the claimant a direct right of action against the insurer providing that cover. Requires carriers of ships licensed to carry more than twelve passengers to maintain insurance or other financial security to cover their liability for passenger death and personal injury — at least 250,000 SDR per passenger per occasion — evidenced by a certificate carried on board, and gives the claimant a direct right of action against the insurer providing that cover.

title: Limits for luggage and vehicles
text: Limits for luggage and vehicles Sets separate, lower liability limits for loss of or damage to a passenger's luggage — distinguishing cabin luggage, vehicles and the luggage carried in or on them, and other luggage — with the carrier able to deduct an agreed excess, complementing the death/personal-injury limits under the two-tier regime. label: Title 1
title: Minimum Requirements for Seafarers to Work on a Ship
text: Minimum Requirements for Seafarers to Work on a Ship Sets the gatekeeping conditions a person must satisfy before working at sea: a minimum age, a valid medical fitness certificate, appropriate training and qualification for the job, and access to a properly regulated recruitment and placement service that does not charge the seafarer fees for finding work. Sets the gatekeeping conditions a person must satisfy before working at sea: a minimum age, a valid medical fitness certificate, appropriate training and qualification for the job, and access to a properly regulated recruitment and placement service that does not charge the seafarer fees for finding work.

label: Title 2
title: Conditions of Employment
text: Conditions of Employment Governs the terms on which seafarers serve: a written seafarers' employment agreement, regular payment of wages, limits on hours of work and minimum hours of rest, entitlement to paid annual leave, and the right to repatriation at the employer's expense at the end of the engagement — plus manning-level and career/skill-development provisions. Governs the terms on which seafarers serve: a written seafarers' employment agreement, regular payment of wages, limits on hours of work and minimum hours of rest, entitlement to paid annual leave, and the right to repatriation at the employer's expense at the end of the engagement — plus manning-level and career/skill-development provisions.

title: Repatriation and financial security for abandonment
text: Repatriation and financial security for abandonment Guarantees a seafarer the right to be repatriated without cost at the end of service or when the employment agreement is terminated, and — as strengthened by the 2014 amendments in force from 2017 — requires ships to carry evidence of a financial-security arrangement (typically an insurer's certificate posted on board) that will cover outstanding wages, repatriation and essential needs of a seafarer who is abandoned. label: Title 3
title: Accommodation, Recreational Facilities, Food and Catering
text: Accommodation, Recreational Facilities, Food and Catering Sets standards for seafarers' living conditions on board — the size, layout, lighting, heating/ventilation and sanitary arrangements of accommodation and recreational spaces (with the detailed construction requirements applying to newly-built ships) — and requires an adequate supply of good-quality food and drinking water served free of charge, prepared by trained catering staff. Sets standards for seafarers' living conditions on board — the size, layout, lighting, heating/ventilation and sanitary arrangements of accommodation and recreational spaces (with the detailed construction requirements applying to newly-built ships) — and requires an adequate supply of good-quality food and drinking water served free of charge, prepared by trained catering staff.

label: Title 4
title: Health Protection, Medical Care, Welfare and Social Security Protection
text: Health Protection, Medical Care, Welfare and Social Security Protection Covers seafarers' health and welfare: access to on-board and ashore medical care at no cost, occupational health and safety and accident prevention, the shipowner's liability to meet the costs of sickness and injury arising in service, access to shore-based welfare facilities, and entitlement to social-security protection. title: Shipowners' liability and financial security for compensation
text: Shipowners' liability and financial security for compensation Makes the shipowner responsible for the costs of a seafarer's sickness, injury or death occurring in connection with employment, including medical care and a period of wages; the 2014 amendments (in force from 2017) added a requirement to carry financial security ensuring compensation is paid for contractual claims arising from a seafarer's death or long-term disability due to occupational injury, illness or hazard. Makes the shipowner responsible for the costs of a seafarer's sickness, injury or death occurring in connection with employment, including medical care and a period of wages; the 2014 amendments (in force from 2017) added a requirement to carry financial security ensuring compensation is paid for contractual claims arising from a seafarer's death or long-term disability due to occupational injury, illness or hazard.

label: Title 5
title: Compliance and Enforcement
text: Compliance and Enforcement The machinery that makes the other four Titles enforceable: flag-State responsibilities for inspection and certification of ships, port-State control of foreign ships, a labour-supplying State's responsibilities, and on-board and onshore complaint procedures — with certification evidenced by the Maritime Labour Certificate and its accompanying Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance. The machinery that makes the other four Titles enforceable: flag-State responsibilities for inspection and certification of ships, port-State control of foreign ships, a labour-supplying State's responsibilities, and on-board and onshore complaint procedures — with certification evidenced by the Maritime Labour Certificate and its accompanying Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance.

title: Maritime Labour Certificate and Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance
text: Maritime Labour Certificate and Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance Requires ships of 500 GT and above on international voyages (or operating from a foreign port) to hold a Maritime Labour Certificate, backed by a Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance in two parts — Part I in which the flag State sets out the national requirements, and Part II in which the shipowner describes the measures adopted to meet them — together giving prima facie evidence of compliance to port-State inspectors. title: General objectives, safety and environmental protection policy, company responsibilities and authority
text: General objectives, safety and environmental protection policy, company responsibilities and authority Sets the Code's overall objectives (safe practices, safeguarding against identified risks, continuous improvement of safety-management skills) and requires the Company to establish a documented safety and environmental-protection policy that it, in turn, implements and monitors at all levels, shore and shipboard. title: Designated Person(s) Ashore
text: Designated Person(s) Ashore Requires the Company to designate a person or persons ashore (the DPA) with direct access to top management, responsible for monitoring the safety and environmental-protection aspects of ship operation and ensuring adequate resources/shore support are provided. title: Direct access to top management
text: Direct access to top management The DPA's defining feature: a reporting line to the highest level of company management that does not pass through the ordinary operational chain, so safety concerns cannot be filtered out before reaching decision-makers. title: Master's Responsibility and Authority
text: Master's Responsibility and Authority Confirms the master's overriding authority and responsibility to make decisions on safety and pollution prevention, and to request Company assistance as necessary — the Company must not constrain this authority. title: Resources and Personnel
text: Resources and Personnel Covers manning, qualification, and familiarization/training requirements so shipboard personnel are adequately resourced and prepared to operate the Safety Management System. title: Shipboard Operations and Emergency Preparedness
text: Shipboard Operations and Emergency Preparedness Requires procedures for key shipboard operations affecting safety/environmental protection, plus identification of potential emergencies and drill/response procedures to deal with them. title: Reports and Analysis of Non-Conformities, Accidents and Hazardous Occurrences
text: Reports and Analysis of Non-Conformities, Accidents and Hazardous Occurrences Requires the SMS to include procedures for reporting non-conformities, accidents and hazardous situations, investigating them, and taking corrective action — the feedback loop that drives continuous improvement. title: Company Verification, Review and Certification (DOC/SMC)
text: Company Verification, Review and Certification (DOC/SMC) Sets the internal audit and management-review cycle the Company must run on its own SMS, and the external verification/certification cycle (Document of Compliance for the Company, Safety Management Certificate for each ship) that confirms the SMS meets the Code. title: International Ship and Port Facility Security Code (ISPS Code)
text: International Ship and Port Facility Security Code (ISPS Code) ISPS Code isps code maritime security ssp cso sso security levels

label: A
title: Mandatory requirements regarding the provisions of chapter XI-2 of the Annex to SOLAS 1974
text: Mandatory requirements regarding the provisions of chapter XI-2 of the Annex to SOLAS 1974 The mandatory half of the Code, given legal force through SOLAS chapter XI-2: nineteen numbered sections that set the ship-side and port-facility-side security regime — objectives and functional requirements, definitions, application thresholds, Contracting Government duties (including setting security levels), the Declaration of Security, company obligations, ship security measures, assessment and plan requirements, the CSO/SSO roles, training and drills, port facility security counterparts, and the verification/certification machinery ending in the International Ship Security Certificate. The mandatory half of the Code, given legal force through SOLAS chapter XI-2: nineteen numbered sections that set the ship-side and port-facility-side security regime — objectives and functional requirements, definitions, application thresholds, Contracting Government duties (including setting security levels), the Declaration of Security, company obligations, ship security measures, assessment and plan requirements, the CSO/SSO roles, training and drills, port facility security counterparts, and the verification/certification machinery ending in the International Ship Security Certificate.

title: Responsibilities of Contracting Governments
text: Responsibilities of Contracting Governments Places the levers of the security regime with governments: they set the prevailing security level (level 1 normal operations, level 2 heightened risk, level 3 exceptional/imminent threat), communicate level changes and threat information to ships and port facilities, and may delegate defined duties to recognized security organizations — though setting security levels and approving port facility security assessments/plans cannot be delegated. Places the levers of the security regime with governments: they set the prevailing security level (level 1 normal operations, level 2 heightened risk, level 3 exceptional/imminent threat), communicate level changes and threat information to ships and port facilities, and may delegate defined duties to recognized security organizations — though setting security levels and approving port facility security assessments/plans cannot be delegated.

title: Declaration of Security
text: Declaration of Security Creates the Declaration of Security (DoS) mechanism — a signed agreement between a ship and a port facility (or another ship) recording which party will carry out which security measures during an interface, used when the Contracting Government deems it necessary, when the two sides are operating at different security levels, or after security threats/incidents, with completed DoS documents kept for a government-specified minimum period. Creates the Declaration of Security (DoS) mechanism — a signed agreement between a ship and a port facility (or another ship) recording which party will carry out which security measures during an interface, used when the Contracting Government deems it necessary, when the two sides are operating at different security levels, or after security threats/incidents, with completed DoS documents kept for a government-specified minimum period.

title: Obligations of the Company
text: Obligations of the Company Makes the shipping company accountable for the regime working on board: the company must ensure the ship security plan clearly states the master's overriding authority and responsibility for safety and security decisions (including the right to request company or government assistance), and must give the CSO, master and SSO the support they need to discharge their duties. Makes the shipping company accountable for the regime working on board: the company must ensure the ship security plan clearly states the master's overriding authority and responsibility for safety and security decisions (including the right to request company or government assistance), and must give the CSO, master and SSO the support they need to discharge their duties.

title: Ship security
text: Ship security Requires every ship to act on the security level set by its Administration (and, in port, at least the level set by the port's Contracting Government): at level 1 the plan's baseline protective activities run (access control, monitoring restricted areas and deck, supervising cargo and stores handling, security communications); levels 2 and 3 trigger the plan's additional and further-specific protective measures, with the ship acknowledging receipt of level-change instructions and reporting if it cannot comply. title: Ship security assessment
text: Ship security assessment Makes a documented ship security assessment (SSA) the mandatory foundation of the ship security plan: carried out by persons with appropriate skills under CSO responsibility, it must include an on-scene security survey and identify existing measures, key shipboard operations needing protection, possible threats and their likelihood, and weaknesses (including human factors) in the ship's infrastructure, policies and procedures. title: Ship security plan
text: Ship security plan Requires every ship to carry an Administration-approved ship security plan (SSP) built on the SSA and covering all three security levels — measures against weapons and dangerous substances, restricted areas, responses to threats and to government level-3 instructions, evacuation, security duties of personnel, audit and drill arrangements, plan review and reporting — written in the working language plus a translation where needed, protected from unauthorized access, and amendable only per Administration-set procedures. Requires every ship to carry an Administration-approved ship security plan (SSP) built on the SSA and covering all three security levels — measures against weapons and dangerous substances, restricted areas, responses to threats and to government level-3 instructions, evacuation, security duties of personnel, audit and drill arrangements, plan review and reporting — written in the working language plus a translation where needed, protected from unauthorized access, and amendable only per Administration-set procedures.

title: Company security officer
text: Company security officer Requires the company to designate a company security officer (CSO) — one person may cover several ships if each is identified — whose duties run from advising on threat levels and ensuring SSAs are carried out, through developing, submitting and maintaining the SSP, to arranging internal audits, verifications and crew security awareness, and coordinating with the ship security officer and port facility security officers. title: Ship security officer
text: Ship security officer Requires a ship security officer (SSO) to be designated on each ship, accountable to the master, with duties including regular security inspections of the ship, implementing and maintaining the SSP, proposing plan amendments, coordinating cargo and stores security handling with shipboard personnel and the relevant PFSO, enhancing security awareness on board, ensuring security equipment is operated, tested and calibrated, and reporting deficiencies and incidents to the CSO. title: Training, drills and exercises on ship security
text: Training, drills and exercises on ship security Requires the CSO, appropriate shore staff and the SSO to have knowledge and training per the Part B guidance, shipboard personnel with security duties to understand their SSP responsibilities, and drills to be held at appropriate intervals so the plan actually works in practice — with the CSO ensuring effective coordination and implementation of ship security plans through participation in exercises. title: Verification and certification for ships
text: Verification and certification for ships Closes the loop with certification: ships undergo initial, renewal and at least one intermediate verification by the Administration (or a recognized security organization), after which an International Ship Security Certificate (ISSC) is issued for a period not exceeding five years, with detailed duration/validity rules mirroring other statutory certificates and an Interim ISSC (valid six months, not renewable consecutively) covering new ships, flag transfers and company changes. Closes the loop with certification: ships undergo initial, renewal and at least one intermediate verification by the Administration (or a recognized security organization), after which an International Ship Security Certificate (ISSC) is issued for a period not exceeding five years, with detailed duration/validity rules mirroring other statutory certificates and an Interim ISSC (valid six months, not renewable consecutively) covering new ships, flag transfers and company changes.

label: B
title: Guidance regarding the provisions of chapter XI-2 of the Annex to SOLAS 1974 and Part A of this Code
text: Guidance regarding the provisions of chapter XI-2 of the Annex to SOLAS 1974 and Part A of this Code The recommendatory half of the Code: section-by-section guidance mirroring Part A's numbering that fleshes out how to conduct security assessments, what ship and port facility security plans should address at each security level, the knowledge expected of CSOs, SSOs and PFSOs, and the Statement of Compliance of a Port Facility — formally non-mandatory under SOLAS, but SOLAS XI-2/4 requires it to be taken into account, and some jurisdictions (notably the EU under Regulation 725/2004) have made selected Part B paragraphs binding. title: International Life-Saving Appliance (LSA) Code
text: International Life-Saving Appliance (LSA) Code LSA Code lsa code life-saving appliances lifeboats liferafts davits solas iii

label: I
title: General
text: General Defines Code-specific terms used mainly in the free-fall lifeboat provisions (free-fall acceleration, certification height, launching ramp angle/length, water-entry angle, effective clearing) and lays down baseline performance demanded of every life-saving appliance: sound workmanship, undamaged across a -30 to +65 degC stowage range and (personal appliances) operable across -15 to +40 degC air and -1 to +30 degC seawater, rot/corrosion/fungal resistance, high-visibility colour with retro-reflective material, approval markings, and — for anything that deteriorates with age — a marked expiry/replacement date. Defines Code-specific terms used mainly in the free-fall lifeboat provisions (free-fall acceleration, certification height, launching ramp angle/length, water-entry angle, effective clearing) and lays down baseline performance demanded of every life-saving appliance: sound workmanship, undamaged across a -30 to +65 degC stowage range and (personal appliances) operable across -15 to +40 degC air and -1 to +30 degC seawater, rot/corrosion/fungal resistance, high-visibility colour with retro-reflective material, approval markings, and — for anything that deteriorates with age — a marked expiry/replacement date.

label: II
title: Personal life-saving appliances
text: Personal life-saving appliances Sets performance standards for the appliances worn or held by an individual: lifebuoys, lifejackets, immersion suits, anti-exposure suits and thermal protective aids. Sets performance standards for the appliances worn or held by an individual: lifebuoys, lifejackets, immersion suits, anti-exposure suits and thermal protective aids.

title: Lifebuoys
text: Lifebuoys Fixes size (400-800 mm diameter), buoyant construction (no loose granulated fill), minimum 14.5 kg iron support in fresh water for 24 h, minimum mass, 30 m drop-test survival, a grabline geometry, and the separate performance specs for the self-igniting light and self-activating smoke signal a lifebuoy may carry. Fixes size (400-800 mm diameter), buoyant construction (no loose granulated fill), minimum 14.5 kg iron support in fresh water for 24 h, minimum mass, 30 m drop-test survival, a grabline geometry, and the separate performance specs for the self-igniting light and self-activating smoke signal a lifebuoy may carry.

title: Lifejackets
text: Lifejackets Sizes lifejackets into infant/child/adult bands by weight or height, sets don-ability and in-water righting/floating-angle performance verified against a reference test device, requires a jump-height survival test, bars knot-tying closures, and specifies the separate light and inflatable-lifejacket requirements, including automatic inflation on immersion. Sizes lifejackets into infant/child/adult bands by weight or height, sets don-ability and in-water righting/floating-angle performance verified against a reference test device, requires a jump-height survival test, bars knot-tying closures, and specifies the separate light and inflatable-lifejacket requirements, including automatic inflation on immersion.

title: Immersion suits
text: Immersion suits Covers the watertight/insulating garments intended to protect a person's core temperature in cold water, including don-ability and buoyancy/thermal-protection performance requirements. Covers the watertight/insulating garments intended to protect a person's core temperature in cold water, including don-ability and buoyancy/thermal-protection performance requirements.

title: Anti-exposure suits
text: Anti-exposure suits Covers the lighter working suits intended for rescue-boat and marshalling crew that need mobility as well as some thermal/immersion protection, distinct from a full immersion suit. Covers the lighter working suits intended for rescue-boat and marshalling crew that need mobility as well as some thermal/immersion protection, distinct from a full immersion suit.

title: Thermal protective aids
text: Thermal protective aids Covers the lightweight bag/covering used to reduce heat loss from a survivor's body once in a survival craft or rescue boat, supplementing rather than replacing a suit. Covers the lightweight bag/covering used to reduce heat loss from a survivor's body once in a survival craft or rescue boat, supplementing rather than replacing a suit.

label: III
title: Visual signals
text: Visual signals Sets performance standards for the three pyrotechnic/smoke distress signals ships must carry. Sets performance standards for the three pyrotechnic/smoke distress signals ships must carry.

title: Rocket parachute flares
text: Rocket parachute flares Requires a water-resistant, self-igniting casing that fires a rocket to at least 300 m altitude, ejecting a parachute flare that burns bright red at not less than 30,000 cd for at least 40 seconds while descending no faster than 5 m/s. Requires a water-resistant, self-igniting casing that fires a rocket to at least 300 m altitude, ejecting a parachute flare that burns bright red at not less than 30,000 cd for at least 40 seconds while descending no faster than 5 m/s.

title: Hand flares
text: Hand flares Requires a water-resistant, self-ignited hand-held flare burning bright red at not less than 15,000 cd for at least one minute, safe to hold, and able to keep burning after brief immersion under 100 mm of water. Requires a water-resistant, self-ignited hand-held flare burning bright red at not less than 15,000 cd for at least one minute, safe to hold, and able to keep burning after brief immersion under 100 mm of water.

title: Buoyant smoke signals
text: Buoyant smoke signals Requires a water-resistant floating signal that emits highly visible smoke (no flame) at a steady rate for at least three minutes in calm water, without exploding on use and without being swamped or extinguished by brief submersion. Requires a water-resistant floating signal that emits highly visible smoke (no flame) at a steady rate for at least three minutes in calm water, without exploding on use and without being swamped or extinguished by brief submersion.

label: IV
title: Survival craft
text: Survival craft The Code's largest and most heavily examined chapter: liferafts and lifeboats of every design variant, each section building on the general requirements of the section before it. The Code's largest and most heavily examined chapter: liferafts and lifeboats of every design variant, each section building on the general requirements of the section before it.

title: General requirements for liferafts
text: General requirements for liferafts Baseline liferaft standards that both inflatable and rigid liferafts build on, covering strength, capacity calculation basis and general seaworthiness that every liferaft type must meet before its section-specific extras apply. Baseline liferaft standards that both inflatable and rigid liferafts build on, covering strength, capacity calculation basis and general seaworthiness that every liferaft type must meet before its section-specific extras apply.

title: Inflatable liferafts
text: Inflatable liferafts Adds the requirements specific to gas-inflated liferafts on top of section 4.1's baseline, including buoyancy-chamber subdivision and canopy/inflation performance. title: Rigid liferafts
text: Rigid liferafts Requires fire-retardant, near-periphery buoyant material and a floor that keeps occupants out of the water; carrying capacity is the lowest of three calculations (buoyancy-material volume, floor area, or seated headroom for 82.5 kg occupants in immersion suits/lifejackets). title: General requirements for lifeboats
text: General requirements for lifeboats The baseline every lifeboat design must meet: rigid, stable, holed-and-still-floating hulls; an approval plate and conformity certificate recording manufacturer, model, capacity and hull material; strength to be launched and towed at speed; seating that survives drop/impact loading; and a heavily engineered on-load release system — dual reset-confirmation methods, colour-coded warning markings, a factor of safety of 6 on the release mechanism and painter, plus exterior/interior lighting requirements. title: Lifeboat construction & structural drop tests
text: Lifeboat construction & structural drop tests Every lifeboat shall be of rigid construction and capable of maintaining positive stability in calm water when filled with water and open to the sea; lifeboats shall be capable of withstanding a drop test from a height of at least 3.0 metres into the water without damage. Every lifeboat shall be of rigid construction and capable of maintaining positive stability in calm water when filled with water and open to the sea; lifeboats shall be capable of withstanding a drop test from a height of at least 3.0 metres into the water without damage.

title: Lifeboat propulsion, cold-start & fuel capacity
text: Lifeboat propulsion, cold-start & fuel capacity Every lifeboat shall be powered by a compression-ignition engine capable of starting at an ambient temperature of -15°C within 2 minutes of starting procedure initiation; fuel tanks shall have a capacity sufficient to run the fully loaded lifeboat at 6 knots for at least 24 hours, with towing capability at 5 knots. Every lifeboat shall be powered by a compression-ignition engine capable of starting at an ambient temperature of -15°C within 2 minutes of starting procedure initiation; fuel tanks shall have a capacity sufficient to run the fully loaded lifeboat at 6 knots for at least 24 hours, with towing capability at 5 knots.

title: On-load / off-load release mechanism & safety factor
text: On-load / off-load release mechanism & safety factor Lifeboat release mechanisms shall be capable of off-load release when fully waterborne and on-load release under emergency load; the mechanism shall feature a mechanical hydrostatic interlock, dual reset indicators, and structural components maintaining a factor of safety of at least 6. title: Partially enclosed lifeboats
text: Partially enclosed lifeboats Adds partial-canopy protection requirements on top of section 4.4's general lifeboat baseline. Adds partial-canopy protection requirements on top of section 4.4's general lifeboat baseline.

title: Totally enclosed lifeboats
text: Totally enclosed lifeboats Requires a rigid watertight enclosure with closeable hatches usable from inside and outside, capable of supporting the fully loaded, fully manned lifeboat while capsized, and (with hatches shut and engine running) keeping cabin pressure within 20 hPa of ambient. Occupants must be secured by contrasting-colour safety belts, and the hull must be inherently or automatically self-righting when fully or partly loaded. title: Totally enclosed lifeboat self-righting & enclosure
text: Totally enclosed lifeboat self-righting & enclosure Every totally enclosed lifeboat shall be fitted with a rigid watertight enclosure providing total shelter for occupants; the lifeboat shall be inherently or automatically self-righting when fully or partially loaded, with occupants secured by safety belts. title: Air support system & fire protection in lifeboats
text: Air support system & fire protection in lifeboats Lifeboats with a self-contained air support system shall supply breathable air for all occupants with engine running for at least 10 minutes, maintaining positive internal cabin pressure not exceeding 20 hPa above ambient.
