title: Free-fall lifeboats
text: Free-fall lifeboats Builds on section 4.6's totally enclosed requirements with free-fall-specific rules: positive headway and no ship contact after launch at up to 10 degrees trim/20 degrees list from certification height across various loading conditions; a hull strong enough for a launch from 1.3 times its certification height; harmful-acceleration protection at the certified height/trim/list; a dual-activation release system operable only from inside; and a certificate of approval that additionally records the certified free-fall height, ramp length and ramp angle. title: Lifeboats with a self-contained air support system
text: Lifeboats with a self-contained air support system Requires that when all entrances/openings are closed and the air-support system is running, the atmosphere inside stays safe and breathable and the engine runs normally for at least 10 minutes, with cabin pressure never more than 20 hPa above or below ambient and a visual indicator of air-supply pressure at all times. title: Fire-protected lifeboats
text: Fire-protected lifeboats Adds fire-survival requirements on top of the enclosed-lifeboat baseline for craft that must be capable of launching through and surviving a period in a surface fire, relevant chiefly to tankers. label: V
title: Rescue boats
text: Rescue boats Rescue boats largely inherit the general lifeboat requirements of section 4.4 (with an 82.5 kg seating basis) but add their own rules: 3.8-8.5 m length, capacity for at least five seated persons plus a stretcher case, a minimum 6-knot speed sustained 4 hours fully loaded, at least 2-knot towing ability for the largest liferaft aboard, inboard or outboard propulsion (including permitted petrol outboards with protected fuel systems), self-bailing, all-round visibility from the control position, and a defined standard equipment list (oars, bailer, compass, sea-anchor, painter with release device, tow line, torch, whistle, first-aid kit, rescue quoits, searchlight, radar reflector, thermal protective aids). label: VI
title: Launching and embarkation appliances
text: Launching and embarkation appliances Covers the davits, winches, falls and marine evacuation systems used to get survival craft and rescue boats safely into the water. title: Launching and embarkation appliances
text: Launching and embarkation appliances Requires a launching appliance to work safely at up to 10 degrees trim/20 degrees list, powered only by gravity or stored mechanical power independent of the ship's supplies (with a narrow manual-hoist exception for very light cargo-ship rescue boats), built for minimal routine maintenance, and strong enough to survive a static proof load of 2.2 times working load with factors of safety of at least 4.5 on structural members and 6 on falls/chains/blocks. Falls-and-winch appliances must additionally use rotation- and corrosion-resistant wire, wind evenly on multi-drum winches, and brake against both static (1.5x) and dynamic (1.1x) proof loads, among other controls. title: Launching appliance strength & list/trim rules
text: Launching appliance strength & list/trim rules Launching appliances shall operate safely under adverse conditions of up to 10 degrees trim and 20 degrees list either way with the craft fully loaded; structural members shall have a factor of safety of at least 4.5 on ultimate tensile strength, with wire falls having a factor of safety of 6. title: Winch brake holding capacity & speed governor
text: Winch brake holding capacity & speed governor Davit winches shall be fitted with brakes capable of stopping and holding the craft when loaded with full complement and equipment under a static proof load test of 1.5 times maximum working load. title: Marine evacuation systems
text: Marine evacuation systems Covers slide/chute evacuation systems: the passage/platform must safely take people of varying ages and abilities down to a floating platform or survival craft, the platform must be stable, self-draining, sub-divided against total buoyancy loss, and sized for at least two liferafts; deployment must be achievable by one person and complete the evacuation within 30 minutes (passenger ship) or 10 minutes (cargo ship), under up to 10 degrees trim/20 degrees list, with at least 50% of installed systems trial-deployed after installation. label: VII
title: Other life-saving appliances
text: Other life-saving appliances Covers the two remaining shipboard life-saving items not addressed elsewhere: line-throwing appliances and the general emergency alarm/public address system. title: Line-throwing appliances
text: Line-throwing appliances Requires reasonably accurate throwing performance, at least four projectiles each able to carry a line 230 m in calm weather, at least four lines of at least 2 kN breaking strength, weatherproof stowage, and (for pistol-fired rockets) a water-resistant casing. title: General alarm and public address system
text: General alarm and public address system The general emergency alarm (seven-plus short blasts and one long blast on the ship's whistle/siren plus an electrically powered bell/klaxon, on main and emergency power) must be operable from the bridge and other strategic points and keep sounding until manually silenced or interrupted by a PA announcement, meeting minimum sound-pressure levels in interior/exterior spaces and cabins. The public address system must reach all crew/passenger spaces and muster stations, be broadcastable from the bridge, and be protected against unauthorized use. title: International Code for Application of Fire Test Procedures (FTP Code)
text: International Code for Application of Fire Test Procedures (FTP Code) FTP Code ftp code fire test procedures solas ii-2 fire safety msc.61(67) msc.307(88)

title: Scope, application and definitions
text: Scope, application and definitions Establishes that the Code is the tool Administrations and their competent authorities use to approve products against SOLAS Chapter II-2's fire-safety requirements, and that testing laboratories must use it when testing and evaluating those products. Wherever the Convention calls for something to be tested 'in accordance with the Fire Test Procedures Code', or simply requires low flame-spread/fire-resistance performance, the applicable part of Annex 1 governs. Key terms are defined, including the standard time-temperature curve a furnace must follow during a standard fire test. title: Testing and approval procedures
text: Testing and approval procedures Requires fire tests to be run only in laboratories the Administration recognizes as independent of the product's manufacturer/vendor and operating under an audited quality-control system, with prescribed content for test reports. Products are then approved either by type approval — a certificate valid up to five years, renewable on fresh test reports, requiring the manufacturer's own audited quality system — or by one-off case-by-case approval limited to a specific ship, without a type-approval certificate. title: Products exempt from testing, equivalents and transitional test procedures
text: Products exempt from testing, equivalents and transitional test procedures Annex 2 lists product groups that may be installed without any testing or approval at all because their fire performance is already assured by their composition. Administrations may also accept modern products tested and verified by methods not spelled out in the Code, provided they notify the Organization with a written justification. A limited period of grace lets Administrations keep using pre-existing (legacy) test procedures and acceptance criteria instead of Annex 1 while labs and industry catch up, with the applicable expiry dates fixed in Annex 3. label: Annex 1, Part 1
title: Non-combustibility test
text: Non-combustibility test Sets the pass/fail furnace test (based on ISO 1182) for materials that must be classed non-combustible: limits on furnace/surface thermocouple temperature rise, duration of sustained flaming, and mass loss, plus the minimum data a test report must record. label: P1.1
title: Non-combustibility test criteria (750°C furnace)
text: Non-combustibility test criteria (750°C furnace) Material is non-combustible if in 750°C furnace test: furnace/surface temp rise ≤ 30°C, sustained flaming ≤ 10 seconds, and mass loss ≤ 50%. label: Annex 1, Part 2
title: Smoke and toxicity test
text: Smoke and toxicity test Covers materials that must not generate excessive smoke or toxic gases at elevated temperature: specimens are exposed to defined radiant-heat conditions with and without a pilot flame, smoke density is tracked and averaged against limits that vary by application (bulkhead/lining, primary deck covering, floor covering, pipes/cables), and toxic-gas concentrations (CO, HCl, HF, NOx, HBr, HCN, SO2) are capped. label: P2.1
title: Smoke density and toxicity acceptance criteria
text: Smoke density and toxicity acceptance criteria Specific optical smoke density Dm and toxic gas limits: CO ≤ 1450 ppm, HCl ≤ 600 ppm, HF ≤ 600 ppm, NOx ≤ 350 ppm, HCN ≤ 140 ppm, SO2 ≤ 120 ppm. label: Annex 1, Part 3
title: Test for 'A', 'B' and 'F' class divisions
text: Test for 'A', 'B' and 'F' class divisions Governs fire-resistance testing of decks, bulkheads, doors, ceilings, linings, windows, fire dampers and pipe/cable penetrations that must meet an 'A', 'B' or 'F' class rating, fixing minimum specimen sizes and confirming that 'B' class integrity depends on non-combustible materials at joints and supports. Two appendices add an optional thermal-radiation test for windows in fire divisions and a procedure for verifying 'continuous B class' linings/ceilings/constructions. title: 'A' Class division fire resistance test
text: 'A' Class division fire resistance test A-Class bulkheads/decks must prevent flame/smoke passage for 60 min; unexposed temp rise ≤ 140°C avg / 180°C max within specified time (A-60: 60 min, A-30: 30 min, A-15: 15 min, A-0: 0 min). label: Annex 1, Part 4
title: Test for fire door control systems
text: Test for fire door control systems Prescribes a prototype furnace test for the control systems (pneumatic, hydraulic or electrical) that must close fire doors automatically in a fire: the door model must survive 60 minutes without failing, then remain closed as the furnace temperature climbs further, and an automatic switchover must isolate the control system from power at 300 degC while keeping the door shut up to 945 degC. label: Annex 1, Parts 5-6
title: Surface flammability and primary deck covering tests
text: Surface flammability and primary deck covering tests Part 5 tests bulkhead/ceiling/deck finish materials, floor coverings and combustible ventilation-duct or cold-service insulation surfaces for low flame-spread characteristics, with a companion appendix giving uniform guidance on interpreting unusual specimen behaviour (melting, spalling, premature flame-out) during the test. Part 6 applies the ignitability test to primary deck coverings — the layer applied directly onto the deck plating beneath any floor covering. title: Surface flammability test criteria

label: Annex 1, Parts 7-9
title: Tests for textiles/films, upholstered furniture and bedding
text: Tests for textiles/films, upholstered furniture and bedding Part 7 tests vertically supported curtains, draperies and similar textiles/films for flame-propagation resistance at least equal to 0.8 kg/m2 wool; Part 8 tests upholstered furniture and Part 9 tests bedding components for resistance to ignition and flame spread — in all three, a new test is required whenever the base product or treatment changes, not merely its colour. label: A-1
title: Specific requirements for ships using natural gas as fuel
text: Specific requirements for ships using natural gas as fuel Chapters 5-15 set detailed goal-based regulations for LNG/CNG-fuelled ships: ship design and fuel-tank location/protection (Ch.5, in real detail below), fuel containment system engineering including inerting (Ch.6), material/pipe design (Ch.7), bunkering (Ch.8), fuel supply to consumers (Ch.9), power generation via ICEs/boilers/gas turbines (Ch.10), fire safety (Ch.11), explosion prevention and hazardous-area zoning (Ch.12), ventilation (Ch.13), electrical installations (Ch.14), and control/monitoring/safety systems (Ch.15) — plus an annex standard for limit-state design methodologies for novel fuel-containment configurations. Chapters 5-15 set detailed goal-based regulations for LNG/CNG-fuelled ships: ship design and fuel-tank location/protection (Ch.5, in real detail below), fuel containment system engineering including inerting (Ch.6), material/pipe design (Ch.7), bunkering (Ch.8), fuel supply to consumers (Ch.9), power generation via ICEs/boilers/gas turbines (Ch.10), fire safety (Ch.11), explosion prevention and hazardous-area zoning (Ch.12), ventilation (Ch.13), electrical installations (Ch.14), and control/monitoring/safety systems (Ch.15) — plus an annex standard for limit-state design methodologies for novel fuel-containment configurations.

title: Ship design and arrangement
text: Ship design and arrangement Requires fuel tanks located to minimize collision/grounding damage probability, fuel containment/piping arranged so released gas vents to open air, access openings arranged to prevent gas escaping to non-designed spaces, mechanically protected piping, and machinery-space design minimizing gas-explosion probability. Sets precise fuel-tank protective-distance formulas (B/5 or 11.5m inboard from ship side; passenger-ship minimum B/10 or 0.8m from shell/aft terminal; cargo-ship minimum scaled by tank volume from 0.8m up to 2m; B/15 or 2m minimum from the bottom shell) with an alternative risk-based fCN calculation method, plus a two-machinery-space-concept framework (gas-safe machinery spaces, inherently safe under all conditions; ESD-protected machinery spaces, non-hazardous normally but with automatic emergency shutdown on abnormal gas conditions) and detailed regulations for bilge systems, drip trays, entrance/airlock arrangements, and fuel-piping location/protection. Requires fuel tanks located to minimize collision/grounding damage probability, fuel containment/piping arranged so released gas vents to open air, access openings arranged to prevent gas escaping to non-designed spaces, mechanically protected piping, and machinery-space design minimizing gas-explosion probability. Sets precise fuel-tank protective-distance formulas (B/5 or 11.5m inboard from ship side; passenger-ship minimum B/10 or 0.8m from shell/aft terminal; cargo-ship minimum scaled by tank volume from 0.8m up to 2m; B/15 or 2m minimum from the bottom shell) with an alternative risk-based fCN calculation method, plus a two-machinery-space-concept framework (gas-safe machinery spaces, inherently safe under all conditions; ESD-protected machinery spaces, non-hazardous normally but with automatic emergency shutdown on abnormal gas conditions) and detailed regulations for bilge systems, drip trays, entrance/airlock arrangements, and fuel-piping location/protection.

title: Fuel tank protective location distances
text: Fuel tank protective location distances Fuel storage tanks must be located at least B/5 or 11.5m inboard from ship side, B/15 or 2.0m from bottom shell centreline, and abaft 0.08L from forward perpendicular. Fuel storage tanks must be located at least B/5 or 11.5m inboard from ship side, B/15 or 2.0m from bottom shell centreline, and abaft 0.08L from forward perpendicular.

title: Gas-safe machinery space concept
text: Gas-safe machinery space concept Gas-safe machinery spaces are inherently safe; a single failure cannot release gas fuel into the space; all gas piping within the space must be double-walled or enclosed. Gas-safe machinery spaces are inherently safe; a single failure cannot release gas fuel into the space; all gas piping within the space must be double-walled or enclosed.

title: ESD-protected machinery space concept
text: ESD-protected machinery space concept ESD-protected machinery spaces are non-hazardous normally, but automatic emergency shutdown isolates non-certified electrical equipment and gas fuel supply upon 40% LEL gas detection. ESD-protected machinery spaces are non-hazardous normally, but automatic emergency shutdown isolates non-certified electrical equipment and gas fuel supply upon 40% LEL gas detection.

title: Airlock design and door interlocks
text: Airlock design and door interlocks Airlocks between hazardous and non-hazardous areas must be gastight, fitted with two self-closing doors 1.5m to 2.5m apart, 300mm sill, and positive pressure ventilation. Airlocks between hazardous and non-hazardous areas must be gastight, fitted with two self-closing doors 1.5m to 2.5m apart, 300mm sill, and positive pressure ventilation.

title: Fuel containment system
text: Fuel containment system Sets goal-based engineering requirements for the physical storage of gas fuel: general regulations plus specific rules for liquefied-gas containment, portable liquefied-gas tanks, CNG containment, pressure relief systems, loading limits, maintaining fuel storage condition, atmospheric control within the containment system and surrounding fuel storage hold spaces, environmental control around type C independent tanks, inerting, and on-board inert gas production/storage — including an annex standard for limit-state design methodologies applicable to novel containment configurations. Sets goal-based engineering requirements for the physical storage of gas fuel: general regulations plus specific rules for liquefied-gas containment, portable liquefied-gas tanks, CNG containment, pressure relief systems, loading limits, maintaining fuel storage condition, atmospheric control within the containment system and surrounding fuel storage hold spaces, environmental control around type C independent tanks, inerting, and on-board inert gas production/storage — including an annex standard for limit-state design methodologies applicable to novel containment configurations.

title: Type C independent pressure tank design
text: Type C independent pressure tank design Type C independent fuel tanks are pressure vessels designed per recognized standards for MARVS > 2 bar, with vacuum insulation and no secondary barrier required. Type C independent fuel tanks are pressure vessels designed per recognized standards for MARVS > 2 bar, with vacuum insulation and no secondary barrier required.

title: Pressure relief systems and BOG management
text: Pressure relief systems and BOG management Fuel tanks must be fitted with at least two pressure relief valves venting to open deck; boil-off gas (BOG) must be managed via re-liquefaction, gas consumption, or thermal oxidizer. Fuel tanks must be fitted with at least two pressure relief valves venting to open deck; boil-off gas (BOG) must be managed via re-liquefaction, gas consumption, or thermal oxidizer.

title: Fuel tank loading and filling limits
text: Fuel tank loading and filling limits Maximum filling limit for fuel tanks must be determined based on fuel expansion at reference temperature, typically capped at 95% volume limit. Maximum filling limit for fuel tanks must be determined based on fuel expansion at reference temperature, typically capped at 95% volume limit.

title: Material and general pipe design
text: Material and general pipe design Sets goal-based requirements for general pipe design and material selection suitable for low-flashpoint fuel service. Sets goal-based requirements for general pipe design and material selection suitable for low-flashpoint fuel service.

title: Bunkering
text: Bunkering Sets goal-based requirements for the bunkering station, manifold, and bunkering system used to transfer fuel from shore/floating facilities or portable tanks into the ship's permanent fuel tanks. Sets goal-based requirements for the bunkering station, manifold, and bunkering system used to transfer fuel from shore/floating facilities or portable tanks into the ship's permanent fuel tanks.

title: Bunkering station arrangement and manifold isolation
text: Bunkering station arrangement and manifold isolation Bunkering stations must be located on open deck or in dedicated spaces, fitted with remote-operated isolation valves, dry-break couplings, emergency release couplers (ERC), and drip trays. Bunkering stations must be located on open deck or in dedicated spaces, fitted with remote-operated isolation valves, dry-break couplings, emergency release couplers (ERC), and drip trays.

title: Bunkering line nitrogen inerting and purging
text: Bunkering line nitrogen inerting and purging Bunkering lines must be provided with nitrogen purging connections to enable complete inerting prior to and following fuel transfer operations. Bunkering lines must be provided with nitrogen purging connections to enable complete inerting prior to and following fuel transfer operations.

title: Fuel supply to consumers
text: Fuel supply to consumers Covers redundancy of fuel supply, safety functions of the gas supply system, fuel distribution outside the machinery space, fuel supply to consumers in both gas-safe and ESD-protected machinery spaces, ventilated-duct/double-pipe design against inner-pipe gas leakage, and requirements for compressors and pumps. Covers redundancy of fuel supply, safety functions of the gas supply system, fuel distribution outside the machinery space, fuel supply to consumers in both gas-safe and ESD-protected machinery spaces, ventilated-duct/double-pipe design against inner-pipe gas leakage, and requirements for compressors and pumps.

title: Gas fuel supply redundancy
text: Gas fuel supply redundancy Redundancy of gas fuel supply must ensure continuous propulsion power following a single failure in the gas fuel supply system. Redundancy of gas fuel supply must ensure continuous propulsion power following a single failure in the gas fuel supply system.

title: Master gas fuel valve and double block and bleed
text: Master gas fuel valve and double block and bleed A Master Gas Fuel Valve outside the machinery space and double block and bleed valve arrangement must vent gas fuel lines within 3 seconds of trip signal. A Master Gas Fuel Valve outside the machinery space and double block and bleed valve arrangement must vent gas fuel lines within 3 seconds of trip signal.

title: Double-wall gas fuel piping and ducting design
text: Double-wall gas fuel piping and ducting design Gas fuel piping passing through enclosed spaces must be enclosed in a secondary duct continuously ventilated at 30 air changes/hour or inerted with nitrogen. Gas fuel piping passing through enclosed spaces must be enclosed in a secondary duct continuously ventilated at 30 air changes/hour or inerted with nitrogen.

title: Power generation including propulsion and other gas consumers
text: Power generation including propulsion and other gas consumers Sets goal-based requirements for internal combustion engines of piston type, main and auxiliary boilers, and gas turbines burning gas or low-flashpoint fuel. Sets goal-based requirements for internal combustion engines of piston type, main and auxiliary boilers, and gas turbines burning gas or low-flashpoint fuel.

title: Fire safety
text: Fire safety Sets goal-based requirements for fire protection, the fire main, water spray systems, dry chemical powder fire-extinguishing systems, and fire detection/alarm systems specific to gas-fuelled machinery and fuel spaces. Sets goal-based requirements for fire protection, the fire main, water spray systems, dry chemical powder fire-extinguishing systems, and fire detection/alarm systems specific to gas-fuelled machinery and fuel spaces.

title: Water spray deluge systems for fuel storage
text: Water spray deluge systems for fuel storage A fixed water spray deluge system providing at least 10 L/min/m2 must protect fuel tank exposed surfaces, tank domes, and bunkering manifolds. A fixed water spray deluge system providing at least 10 L/min/m2 must protect fuel tank exposed surfaces, tank domes, and bunkering manifolds.

title: Dry chemical powder fire-extinguishing systems
text: Dry chemical powder fire-extinguishing systems A fixed dry chemical powder fire-extinguishing system with at least 3.5 kg/s output rate must protect the bunkering station area, supplemented by 5 kg portable units. A fixed dry chemical powder fire-extinguishing system with at least 3.5 kg/s output rate must protect the bunkering station area, supplemented by 5 kg portable units.

title: Explosion prevention
text: Explosion prevention Sets general requirements plus area-classification regulations and hazardous-area zoning to minimize explosion risk around gas fuel systems. Sets general requirements plus area-classification regulations and hazardous-area zoning to minimize explosion risk around gas fuel systems.

title: Hazardous area Zone 0 classification
text: Hazardous area Zone 0 classification Zone 0 includes fuel tank interiors, fuel pipe interiors, and pressure relief valve discharge pipe interiors where explosive gas is continuously present. Zone 0 includes fuel tank interiors, fuel pipe interiors, and pressure relief valve discharge pipe interiors where explosive gas is continuously present.

title: Hazardous area Zone 1 classification
text: Hazardous area Zone 1 classification Zone 1 includes fuel tank connection spaces, enclosed fuel preparation rooms, airlocks, and enclosed bunkering manifold spaces where explosive gas is likely during normal operation. Zone 1 includes fuel tank connection spaces, enclosed fuel preparation rooms, airlocks, and enclosed bunkering manifold spaces where explosive gas is likely during normal operation.

title: Hazardous area Zone 2 classification
text: Hazardous area Zone 2 classification Zone 2 includes open deck areas within 1.5m to 3m of Zone 1 boundaries, fuel tank vents, and gas fuel flanges where explosive gas is not likely during normal operation. Zone 2 includes open deck areas within 1.5m to 3m of Zone 1 boundaries, fuel tank vents, and gas fuel flanges where explosive gas is not likely during normal operation.

title: Ventilation
text: Ventilation Sets general ventilation regulations plus specific requirements for tank connection spaces, machinery spaces, the fuel preparation room, the bunkering station, and ducts/double pipes. Sets general ventilation regulations plus specific requirements for tank connection spaces, machinery spaces, the fuel preparation room, the bunkering station, and ducts/double pipes.

title: Fuel preparation room mechanical extraction ventilation
text: Fuel preparation room mechanical extraction ventilation Fuel preparation rooms must be provided with dedicated mechanical extraction ventilation maintaining negative pressure at a rate of at least 30 air changes/hour. Fuel preparation rooms must be provided with dedicated mechanical extraction ventilation maintaining negative pressure at a rate of at least 30 air changes/hour.

title: Double-wall gas fuel duct continuous ventilation
text: Double-wall gas fuel duct continuous ventilation Outer secondary ducting around gas fuel pipes must be provided with continuous mechanical extraction ventilation at 30 air changes/hour with gas detection. Outer secondary ducting around gas fuel pipes must be provided with continuous mechanical extraction ventilation at 30 air changes/hour with gas detection.

title: Electrical installations
text: Electrical installations Sets general regulations for electrical installations in and around gas fuel systems and hazardous areas. Sets general regulations for electrical installations in and around gas fuel systems and hazardous areas.

title: Control, monitoring and safety systems
text: Control, monitoring and safety systems Sets general regulations plus specific requirements for bunkering/liquefied-gas-tank monitoring, bunkering control, gas compressor/engine monitoring, gas detection, fire detection, ventilation control, and the safety functions of fuel supply systems. Sets general regulations plus specific requirements for bunkering/liquefied-gas-tank monitoring, bunkering control, gas compressor/engine monitoring, gas detection, fire detection, ventilation control, and the safety functions of fuel supply systems.

title: Gas detection alarm activation (20% LEL)
text: Gas detection alarm activation (20% LEL) Gas detectors in fuel preparation rooms, double-wall ducts, and airlocks must trigger audible and visual alarms at 20% Lower Explosive Limit (LEL). Gas detectors in fuel preparation rooms, double-wall ducts, and airlocks must trigger audible and visual alarms at 20% Lower Explosive Limit (LEL).

title: Automatic Master Gas Fuel Valve trip and ESD (40% LEL)
text: Automatic Master Gas Fuel Valve trip and ESD (40% LEL) Gas detection reaching 40% Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) must automatically close the Master Gas Fuel Valve and trigger ESD isolation of the space. Gas detection reaching 40% Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) must automatically close the Master Gas Fuel Valve and trigger ESD isolation of the space.

label: B-1
title: Manufacture, workmanship and testing
text: Manufacture, workmanship and testing Sets general test regulations, welding/non-destructive-testing requirements for the fuel containment system's metallic materials, other construction regulations, and testing regulations (including post-weld heat treatment). Sets general test regulations, welding/non-destructive-testing requirements for the fuel containment system's metallic materials, other construction regulations, and testing regulations (including post-weld heat treatment).

title: Manufacture, workmanship and testing
text: Manufacture, workmanship and testing Covers general test regulations/specifications, welding of metallic materials and non-destructive testing for the fuel containment system, other regulations for construction in metallic materials, testing, welding/post-weld heat treatment/non-destructive testing, and further testing regulations. Covers general test regulations/specifications, welding of metallic materials and non-destructive testing for the fuel containment system, other regulations for construction in metallic materials, testing, welding/post-weld heat treatment/non-destructive testing, and further testing regulations.

label: C-1
title: Operating requirements
text: Operating requirements Covers drills and emergency exercises plus operational requirements: maintenance, bunkering operations, enclosed space entry, inerting/purging of fuel systems, and hot work on or near fuel systems — with an annex LNG-bunker delivery note. Covers drills and emergency exercises plus operational requirements: maintenance, bunkering operations, enclosed space entry, inerting/purging of fuel systems, and hot work on or near fuel systems — with an annex LNG-bunker delivery note.

title: Drills and emergency exercises
text: Drills and emergency exercises Requires drills and emergency exercises specific to gas-fuel system hazards, in addition to standard SOLAS fire/abandon-ship drills. Requires drills and emergency exercises specific to gas-fuel system hazards, in addition to standard SOLAS fire/abandon-ship drills.

title: Operation
text: Operation Sets goal-based requirements for maintenance, bunkering operations, enclosed space entry, inerting and purging of fuel systems, and hot work on or near fuel systems, with an annex LNG-bunker delivery note documenting each bunkering transfer. Sets goal-based requirements for maintenance, bunkering operations, enclosed space entry, inerting and purging of fuel systems, and hot work on or near fuel systems, with an annex LNG-bunker delivery note documenting each bunkering transfer.

label: D
title: Training
text: Training Sets the goal and functional requirements for crew training on ships using gases or other low-flashpoint fuels, linked to STCW. Sets the goal and functional requirements for crew training on ships using gases or other low-flashpoint fuels, linked to STCW.

title: Training
text: Training Sets the goal (ensuring crew are properly trained and qualified to operate gas/low-flashpoint fuel systems safely) and functional requirements for training, cross-referenced to STCW. Sets the goal (ensuring crew are properly trained and qualified to operate gas/low-flashpoint fuel systems safely) and functional requirements for training, cross-referenced to STCW.

title: International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk (IBC Code)
text: International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk (IBC Code) IBC Code ibc code chemical tanker noxious liquid cargo containment

title: Ship survival capability and location of cargo tanks
text: Ship survival capability and location of cargo tanks The chapter that gives the Code its type 1/2/3 ship philosophy: cargoes are assigned a ship type according to hazard severity, and each type must survive prescribed collision/grounding damage assumptions in a defined loading condition, with type 1 (most hazardous products) demanding the greatest damage resistance and cargo tanks kept furthest inboard and away from the shell, relaxing progressively through types 2 and 3. The chapter that gives the Code its type 1/2/3 ship philosophy: cargoes are assigned a ship type according to hazard severity, and each type must survive prescribed collision/grounding damage assumptions in a defined loading condition, with type 1 (most hazardous products) demanding the greatest damage resistance and cargo tanks kept furthest inboard and away from the shell, relaxing progressively through types 2 and 3.

title: Cargo containment
text: Cargo containment Defines the tank types available for chemical cargoes — independent tanks, integral tanks, gravity tanks and pressure tanks — and sets which containment arrangement a product requires, so that tank structure, design pressure and separation from the hull match the cargo's hazards; the individual product's tank-type requirement is then read off the chapter 17 table. Defines the tank types available for chemical cargoes — independent tanks, integral tanks, gravity tanks and pressure tanks — and sets which containment arrangement a product requires, so that tank structure, design pressure and separation from the hull match the cargo's hazards; the individual product's tank-type requirement is then read off the chapter 17 table.

title: Cargo tank venting and gas-freeing arrangements
text: Cargo tank venting and gas-freeing arrangements Requires each cargo tank to have a venting system matched to the cargo carried — open venting only where the product allows it, controlled venting with pressure/vacuum valves and prescribed vent outlet heights and distances from accommodation openings for more hazardous products — plus arrangements for safely gas-freeing tanks so that flammable or toxic vapour concentrations on deck and in working areas stay controlled during cargo and tank-cleaning operations. Requires each cargo tank to have a venting system matched to the cargo carried — open venting only where the product allows it, controlled venting with pressure/vacuum valves and prescribed vent outlet heights and distances from accommodation openings for more hazardous products — plus arrangements for safely gas-freeing tanks so that flammable or toxic vapour concentrations on deck and in working areas stay controlled during cargo and tank-cleaning operations.

title: Electrical installations
text: Electrical installations Controls ignition and shock risk from electrical equipment where flammable or corrosive chemical vapours may be present: equipment in gas-dangerous zones must be of certified safe type appropriate to the products carried (with the product-specific electrical apparatus data taken from the chapter 17 table), and installations must be designed, protected and maintained so cargo vapours cannot be ignited by normal operation or fault conditions. Controls ignition and shock risk from electrical equipment where flammable or corrosive chemical vapours may be present: equipment in gas-dangerous zones must be of certified safe type appropriate to the products carried (with the product-specific electrical apparatus data taken from the chapter 17 table), and installations must be designed, protected and maintained so cargo vapours cannot be ignited by normal operation or fault conditions.

title: Fire protection and fire extinction
text: Fire protection and fire extinction Builds on the SOLAS II-2 tanker fire regime but adapts it to chemical cargoes: the cargo area must be protected by a fixed deck foam system using foam concentrates effective for the products carried (alcohol-resistant foam for foam-destructive cargoes), supplemented where the chapter 17 table requires by alternative media, since some chemicals react with water or are not amenable to standard hydrocarbon fire-fighting methods. Builds on the SOLAS II-2 tanker fire regime but adapts it to chemical cargoes: the cargo area must be protected by a fixed deck foam system using foam concentrates effective for the products carried (alcohol-resistant foam for foam-destructive cargoes), supplemented where the chapter 17 table requires by alternative media, since some chemicals react with water or are not amenable to standard hydrocarbon fire-fighting methods.

title: Mechanical ventilation in the cargo area
text: Mechanical ventilation in the cargo area Requires powered ventilation of cargo pump-rooms and other normally-entered spaces in the cargo area, with prescribed air-change capacity, extraction from where vapours accumulate, non-sparking fans, and ducting arranged so vented cargo vapour cannot re-enter accommodation, service or machinery spaces — the engineering defence that keeps enclosed cargo-area spaces safe to enter and work in. Requires powered ventilation of cargo pump-rooms and other normally-entered spaces in the cargo area, with prescribed air-change capacity, extraction from where vapours accumulate, non-sparking fans, and ducting arranged so vented cargo vapour cannot re-enter accommodation, service or machinery spaces — the engineering defence that keeps enclosed cargo-area spaces safe to enter and work in.

title: Instrumentation
text: Instrumentation Requires cargo tanks to be fitted with gauging appropriate to the product — from open gauging up to closed gauging where the cargo must never be exposed to the atmosphere — together with high-level alarms/overflow control and vapour detection instruments capable of monitoring the flammable and/or toxic vapours of the products carried, the product-by-product requirements again being assigned through the chapter 17 table. title: Special requirements
text: Special requirements Adds product-family-specific safeguards that the general chapters cannot capture — for example inhibitor/stabilisation certificates for polymerising monomers, segregation and dedicated pumping/piping for particularly reactive or toxic products, temperature and overpressure safeguards for substances like hydrogen peroxide, and handling controls for acids — each triggered for an individual cargo only when the chapter 17 table points to the relevant paragraph of this chapter. title: Summary of minimum requirements
text: Summary of minimum requirements The working heart of the Code: a product-by-product table listing every chemical the Code covers with its pollution category (X/Y/Z under MARPOL Annex II), required ship type (1/2/3), tank type, venting and gauging requirements, electrical apparatus data, fire-fighting media and applicable chapter 15/16 special provisions — the single reference an officer consults to establish the complete carriage conditions for a named cargo. title: List of products to which the Code does not apply
text: List of products to which the Code does not apply The companion table to chapter 17: products assessed as falling outside the Code's safety-hazard scope (typically Category Z or 'Other Substances' cargoes presenting only pollution, not safety, hazards) are listed here with their pollution categories, so a cargo found in chapter 18 rather than chapter 17 may be carried without the Code's construction requirements while still remaining subject to MARPOL Annex II discharge control. title: Criteria for assigning carriage requirements for products subject to the IBC Code
text: Criteria for assigning carriage requirements for products subject to the IBC Code The rule-book behind the tables: it sets out the safety and pollution criteria (toxicity, flammability, reactivity, marine environmental hazard profiles drawn from GESAMP hazard evaluation) used to decide a candidate product's ship type, tank type, venting, gauging, electrical and special-requirement assignments — the complete revision of these criteria under the 2019 amendments (MEPC.318(74)/MSC.460(101), in force 1 January 2021) drove the wholesale re-issue of the chapter 17 and 18 product tables. title: International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Liquefied Gases in Bulk (IGC Code)
text: International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Liquefied Gases in Bulk (IGC Code) IGC Code igc code gas carrier lng lpg cargo containment

title: Ship survival capability and location of cargo tanks
text: Ship survival capability and location of cargo tanks Assigns each gas cargo a ship type (1G, 2G, 2PG or 3G in descending order of hazard) and requires the ship to survive prescribed side and bottom damage assumptions, with cargo tanks set progressively further inboard and above the bottom shell the more hazardous the cargo — type 1G ships (e.g. for chlorine) getting the greatest separation between cargo and the sea. Assigns each gas cargo a ship type (1G, 2G, 2PG or 3G in descending order of hazard) and requires the ship to survive prescribed side and bottom damage assumptions, with cargo tanks set progressively further inboard and above the bottom shell the more hazardous the cargo — type 1G ships (e.g. for chlorine) getting the greatest separation between cargo and the sea.

title: Cargo containment
text: Cargo containment The design core of the Code: it classifies containment systems into independent tanks (type A designed by classical ship-structural analysis with a full secondary barrier, type B by refined fatigue/crack-propagation analysis with only a partial secondary barrier, and pressure-vessel type C needing no secondary barrier) plus membrane and integral tanks, and sets the design loads, secondary-barrier and structural analysis requirements for each — the basis for distinguishing LNG membrane ships, Moss-sphere ships and pressurised LPG carriers. title: Process pressure vessels and liquid, vapour and pressure piping systems
text: Process pressure vessels and liquid, vapour and pressure piping systems Sets the mechanical standards for everything the cargo flows through outside the tanks — cargo and process piping, valves, expansion arrangements, and process pressure vessels — including design pressure/temperature selection, material and welding/NDT requirements, pressure and tightness testing, and emergency shutdown valving, so the piping system offers the same integrity philosophy as the containment system it serves. title: Materials of construction and quality control
text: Materials of construction and quality control Matches materials to cryogenic and chemical service: it specifies steel grades and other materials acceptable for tanks, secondary barriers, piping and adjacent hull structure according to design temperature (with toughness/impact-test requirements tightening as temperatures fall towards LNG's -163°C), plus welding, fabrication and quality-control standards — the chapter amended from 2026 (MSC.523(106)) to accept high-manganese austenitic steel for cryogenic cargo service. Matches materials to cryogenic and chemical service: it specifies steel grades and other materials acceptable for tanks, secondary barriers, piping and adjacent hull structure according to design temperature (with toughness/impact-test requirements tightening as temperatures fall towards LNG's -163°C), plus welding, fabrication and quality-control standards — the chapter amended from 2026 (MSC.523(106)) to accept high-manganese austenitic steel for cryogenic cargo service.

title: Cargo pressure/temperature control
text: Cargo pressure/temperature control The gas engineer's chapter: cargo tank pressure and temperature must be kept within design limits by an accepted method — reliquefaction of boil-off vapour, thermal oxidation (burning boil-off, e.g. in the ship's propulsion plant or a gas combustion unit), pressure-accumulation within tank design margins, or cargo cooling — with system redundancy/availability requirements and specific safeguards, and with segregation rules preventing incompatible cargoes sharing a refrigeration system. The gas engineer's chapter: cargo tank pressure and temperature must be kept within design limits by an accepted method — reliquefaction of boil-off vapour, thermal oxidation (burning boil-off, e.g. in the ship's propulsion plant or a gas combustion unit), pressure-accumulation within tank design margins, or cargo cooling — with system redundancy/availability requirements and specific safeguards, and with segregation rules preventing incompatible cargoes sharing a refrigeration system.

title: Vent systems for cargo containment
text: Vent systems for cargo containment Requires every cargo tank to be protected by pressure relief valves sized for fire exposure and other overpressure scenarios, discharging through vent masts of prescribed height and location so relieved gas disperses clear of accommodation and ignition sources, together with vacuum protection arrangements — the last-resort safety system that keeps tank pressure inside design limits when normal boil-off management fails. Requires every cargo tank to be protected by pressure relief valves sized for fire exposure and other overpressure scenarios, discharging through vent masts of prescribed height and location so relieved gas disperses clear of accommodation and ignition sources, together with vacuum protection arrangements — the last-resort safety system that keeps tank pressure inside design limits when normal boil-off management fails.

title: Electrical installations
text: Electrical installations Requires electrical equipment in gas-dangerous spaces and zones to be certified safe for the gases carried (or excluded altogether), with hazardous areas classified and equipment selected so that neither normal operation nor fault conditions can ignite flammable cargo vapour — supplemented by bonding/earthing provisions against electrostatic ignition. Requires electrical equipment in gas-dangerous spaces and zones to be certified safe for the gases carried (or excluded altogether), with hazardous areas classified and equipment selected so that neither normal operation nor fault conditions can ignite flammable cargo vapour — supplemented by bonding/earthing provisions against electrostatic ignition.

title: Fire protection and extinction
text: Fire protection and extinction Adapts the SOLAS tanker fire regime to gas cargoes: the cargo area is protected by a fixed water-spray system for cooling and crew protection over tank domes, manifolds and boundaries facing the cargo area, plus fixed dry chemical powder systems for gas fires on deck — reflecting that burning gas releases are fought by cutting off flow and controlling surroundings rather than by foam blanketing. title: Instrumentation and automation systems
text: Instrumentation and automation systems Requires each cargo tank to have closed-type level gauging, independent high-level alarm and overflow protection, and pressure/temperature monitoring, and — critically for watchkeepers — a fixed gas detection system continuously monitoring spaces such as hold/interbarrier spaces, cargo compressor rooms, motor rooms and ventilation ducts, alarming well below the lower flammable limit (and at toxic thresholds where applicable) so leakage is caught before it becomes an ignitable or harmful atmosphere. title: Filling limits for cargo tanks
text: Filling limits for cargo tanks Prevents liquid-full tanks: cargo tanks may only be loaded to a limit that leaves room for the liquid to expand as it warms towards the temperature corresponding to the relief valve set pressure, with the loading limit derived from the cargo's reference density conditions — the reason LNG and LPG tanks are never pressed completely full and why filling-limit calculations feature in gas-carrier loading plans. title: Use of cargo as fuel
text: Use of cargo as fuel The chapter that lets a gas carrier burn its own cargo: it sets the conditions for using cargo boil-off as fuel in machinery spaces — gas fuel supply via double-walled/ducted piping with ventilation and gas detection in the annular space, automatic master gas valve shutdown on leakage or loss of ventilation, and engine/boiler safeguards — historically limited to methane (LNG), with the 2026 amendment (MSC.566(109)) opening a flag-approved path for toxic cargoes such as ammonia carried on type 2G/2PG ships to be used as fuel. title: Operating requirements
text: Operating requirements Turns the design chapters into shipboard practice: cargo operations require approved cargo handling information and loading/cooldown procedures on board, crews must be trained in the properties and emergency response for the cargoes carried, and operational controls cover matters such as cargo transfer, use of protective equipment, and keeping essential cargo systems available — the operations counterpart to the construction-focused body of the Code. title: EmS Guide — emergency response procedures for FIRE
text: EmS Guide — emergency response procedures for FIRE Gives shipboard fire-response guidance for packaged dangerous goods, meant for the master and crew to use without external help: identify the dangerous good involved from its UN number (cross-referenced to an EmS FIRE schedule number in the IMDG Code's Dangerous Goods List and on the Dangerous Goods Manifest/Stowage Plan), then follow the matching schedule, which differs for on-deck versus under-deck stowage. It stresses crew safety (breathing apparatus, protective clothing, escape routes), protecting accommodation spaces from toxic smoke, and integrating this procedure into the ship's contingency plan and Safety Management System before any incident occurs. title: General provisions
text: General provisions Frames the whole Code: definitions and the Group A/B/C cargo classification (A may liquefy, B possesses chemical hazards, C neither), application to all SOLAS ships carrying solid bulk cargoes, the mandatory/recommendatory split (security provisions, conversion tables, references and the descriptive parts of individual schedules remain non-mandatory), how listed and unlisted cargoes are handled — unlisted cargoes needing a tripartite assessment between the load port, discharge port and flag State authorities — and the exemption/equivalence machinery. title: General loading, carriage and unloading precautions
text: General loading, carriage and unloading precautions Sets the shipboard precautions common to all bulk cargoes: cargo distribution to avoid overstressing the structure (loading high-density cargoes per the ship's loading manual so tanktop limits and stability are respected), and care during loading/unloading — including grab, bulldozer and hammering damage to structure — so the ship's strength and stability margins survive the terminal as well as the sea passage. title: Safety of personnel and ship
text: Safety of personnel and ship The human-safety section: poisoning, corrosive and asphyxiation hazards from bulk cargoes (oxygen depletion in and adjacent to cargo spaces, toxic gas evolution), health hazards from cargo dust, flammable atmospheres and the precautions before entering enclosed cargo-linked spaces, plus fumigation controls — the reason engine-room and deck staff treat holds and adjacent trunkings as enclosed spaces with atmosphere testing before entry. title: Assessment of acceptability of consignments for safe shipment
text: Assessment of acceptability of consignments for safe shipment Places the information burden on the shipper: before loading, the master must receive a written cargo declaration covering the bulk cargo shipping name, group, IMO class where applicable, TML and actual moisture content for Group A cargoes, stowage factor, angle of repose and any special properties — supported by test certificates from sampling and testing conducted within prescribed intervals (moisture testing within seven days of loading, retested after significant rain or snow) — giving the master the legal footing to refuse cargo presented without proper documentation. title: Trimming procedures
text: Trimming procedures Requires cargoes to be trimmed reasonably level to the boundaries of the cargo space as necessary, with trimming reducing the risk of cargo shift (especially for cargoes with a low angle of repose or partly-filled holds), limiting air ingress into self-heating cargoes, and matching each cargo's schedule requirements — the stability-protecting counterpart to the moisture controls of sections 7 and 8. title: Cargoes that may liquefy
text: Cargoes that may liquefy The Group A regime at the heart of bulk-carrier casualty prevention: fine-particled cargoes carried with moisture above their Transportable Moisture Limit can pass into a viscous fluid state, and the resulting free-surface/cargo-shift effect can capsize a ship rapidly — so such cargoes must not be accepted for loading when their moisture content exceeds the TML, unless carried in a specially constructed or fitted ship, with exposure to precipitation during loading controlled. title: Test procedures for cargoes that may liquefy
text: Test procedures for cargoes that may liquefy Links the Group A rules to evidence: the shipper's declared TML and moisture content must come from testing under the procedures of appendix 2, and it gives the master a shipboard screening tool — the complementary 'can test', half-filling a cylindrical can with sample and striking it against a hard surface; free moisture or fluid appearing on the surface warns that the cargo may exceed its TML and calls for full laboratory testing before acceptance. title: Materials possessing chemical hazards
text: Materials possessing chemical hazards The Group B framework: bulk cargoes with chemical hazards are classified using the dangerous-goods class system (flammable solids, spontaneously combustible materials, materials dangerous when wet, oxidizers, toxics, corrosives) plus the residual 'materials hazardous only in bulk' (MHB) category for substances like coal and DRI whose hazards — self-heating, oxygen depletion, flammable gas evolution — appear only in bulk quantities, with stowage and segregation requirements keyed to those classifications. title: Individual schedules of solid bulk cargoes
text: Individual schedules of solid bulk cargoes The cargo-by-cargo body of the Code: a schedule for each listed bulk cargo giving its bulk cargo shipping name, group, characteristics (angle of repose, bulk density, stowage factor), hazards, stowage and segregation requirements, hold cleanliness, weather and loading precautions, ventilation, carriage and discharge requirements and emergency procedures — the schedule's operative carriage requirements are mandatory, while its descriptive DESCRIPTION/CHARACTERISTICS/HAZARD/EMERGENCY text is informative; amendment cycles keep adding schedules (e.g. for direct reduced iron variants and newer battery-material cargoes). label: Appendix 2
title: Laboratory test procedures, associated apparatus and standards
text: Laboratory test procedures, associated apparatus and standards The laboratory backbone of the Group A regime: it specifies the three recognized methods for determining a cargo's transportable moisture limit — the flow table test (fine materials, determining moisture content and flow moisture point, with the TML derived from the FMP), the penetration test, and the Proctor/Fagerberg test — together with the associated apparatus and standards, plus procedures such as the trough test and self-heating test used for chemical-hazard classification; the choice among TML methods rests with local practice or the appropriate authorities. label: I-A
title: Safety measures (mandatory)
text: Safety measures (mandatory) The mandatory safety half of the Code, made binding through SOLAS chapter XIV: twelve chapters running from general provisions (ship categories A/B/C by ice capability, the operational assessment, and the Polar Ship Certificate) through the Polar Water Operational Manual, structure, stability, watertight integrity, machinery, fire safety, life-saving, navigation and communication, to voyage planning and manning/training — each chapter framed as goals and functional requirements backed by prescriptive regulations, addressing the hazard chain unique to polar service: ice, icing, low temperature, darkness, remoteness and scarce SAR resources. title: Polar water operational manual (PWOM)
text: Polar water operational manual (PWOM) Requires every ship to carry a ship-specific Polar Water Operational Manual giving the master and officers the information needed to operate within the ship's assessed capabilities and limitations — procedures for normal polar operations, for managing conditions that exceed the ship's limitations, for use of icebreaker escort, and for contact with emergency response providers — so the operational-assessment output becomes a working bridge/engine-room document rather than a certificate entry; the associated ice-regime methodology (POLARIS, issued as IMO guidance) is the accepted tool for setting those ice limitations. title: Ship structure
text: Ship structure Requires the structure to withstand the global and local loads anticipated under the foreseen ice conditions: ships intended for ice operation are assigned an ice class — Polar Classes per the IACS Polar Class unified requirements or an equivalent standard acceptable to the Administration — and materials of exposed structure must remain adequate at the polar service temperature, tying scantlings and steel grades to the ship's category and intended ice regime. Requires the structure to withstand the global and local loads anticipated under the foreseen ice conditions: ships intended for ice operation are assigned an ice class — Polar Classes per the IACS Polar Class unified requirements or an equivalent standard acceptable to the Administration — and materials of exposed structure must remain adequate at the polar service temperature, tying scantlings and steel grades to the ship's category and intended ice regime.

title: Machinery installations
text: Machinery installations The engineer's chapter: machinery must deliver its required functionality under the expected environmental conditions — accounting for ice accretion and snow ingestion, freezing and increased viscosity of liquids, sea-water inlet temperature and ice ingestion into cooling systems, and cold-degraded battery and starting performance — with materials, working fluids and arrangements (e.g. sea chests, ballast systems, exposed machinery) chosen so propulsion and essential auxiliaries remain available at the polar service temperature and in the ship's assessed ice conditions. title: Fire safety/protection
text: Fire safety/protection Keeps the fire main, extinguishers, pumps, hydrants and firefighting outfits effective in the cold: systems and appliances must remain operable at the polar service temperature, isolating and freeze-protection measures must cover exposed fire-fighting equipment, hydrants and sections of the fire main, and extinguishing media must suit polar temperatures — recognising that a frozen fire line or an unusable extinguisher turns a manageable machinery-space fire into a casualty far from help. title: Life-saving appliances and arrangements
text: Life-saving appliances and arrangements Reframes abandonment for remoteness: escape, evacuation and survival arrangements must remain usable under icing and low temperature, and survival resources — fully or partially enclosed survival craft, personal and group survival equipment, thermal protection and rations — must sustain survivors for the maximum expected time of rescue, which by the Code's own definition is never less than five days, a figure that drives the polar survival-kit and life-raft capacity planning. title: Voyage planning
text: Voyage planning Extends the standard voyage-planning duty for polar transits: the master must plan a safe route accounting for current ice and iceberg information and its expected evolution, the ship's assessed capabilities and limitations, remoteness from SAR and salvage resources, places of refuge, and environmentally sensitive features such as marine mammal concentrations and protected areas — making the passage plan the operational proof that the ship will stay inside its certificate limitations. title: Manning and training
text: Manning and training Adds a polar layer on top of STCW: masters, chief mates and officers in charge of a navigational watch on ships operating in polar waters must hold basic or advanced polar-water training qualifications graduated by ship category and ice conditions, and companies must ensure crews are adequately qualified for the intended operation — the manning counterpart to the ship-side certification, implemented through corresponding STCW amendments. label: II-A
title: Pollution prevention measures (mandatory)
text: Pollution prevention measures (mandatory) The mandatory environmental half of the Code, given force through amendments to MARPOL: five chapters tracking the MARPOL annex structure — oil (chapter 1), noxious liquid substances (chapter 2), harmful substances in packaged form (chapter 3, kept blank intentionally), sewage (chapter 4) and garbage (chapter 5) — that tighten the parent-annex discharge regimes for polar waters, in most cases to outright prohibition or to discharges conditioned on distance from land, ice-shelf and fast ice. title: Prevention of pollution by oil
text: Prevention of pollution by oil Goes beyond MARPOL Annex I's 15 ppm regime: in Arctic waters any discharge into the sea of oil or oily mixtures from any ship is prohibited (the Antarctic already being covered by Annex I special-area rules), operation in polar waters must be reflected in the Oil Record Book, SOPEP and manuals, and category A and B ships built from 2017 must keep oil fuel and cargo/residue tanks separated from the outer shell — pushing engine-room practice towards full retention on board and shore/reception disposal. title: Control of pollution by noxious liquid substances in bulk
text: Control of pollution by noxious liquid substances in bulk Prohibits any discharge of noxious liquid substances or NLS-containing mixtures into Arctic waters, requires polar operation to be reflected in the Cargo Record Book, Procedures and Arrangements Manual and NLS emergency plan, and makes carriage of certain ship-type-3 products in type 3 tank arrangements on new category A and B ships subject to Administration approval recorded on the ship's NLS certificate or Certificate of Fitness. Prohibits any discharge of noxious liquid substances or NLS-containing mixtures into Arctic waters, requires polar operation to be reflected in the Cargo Record Book, Procedures and Arrangements Manual and NLS emergency plan, and makes carriage of certain ship-type-3 products in type 3 tank arrangements on new category A and B ships subject to Administration approval recorded on the ship's NLS certificate or Certificate of Fitness.

title: Prevention of pollution by sewage from ships
text: Prevention of pollution by sewage from ships Tightens MARPOL Annex IV for polar waters: sewage discharge is prohibited except under narrow conditions — comminuted and disinfected sewage well clear of land, ice-shelf and fast ice and away from areas of specified ice concentration, or discharge via an approved sewage treatment plant — with distances defined against polar features (ice-shelf and fast ice are defined terms) rather than shoreline alone. Tightens MARPOL Annex IV for polar waters: sewage discharge is prohibited except under narrow conditions — comminuted and disinfected sewage well clear of land, ice-shelf and fast ice and away from areas of specified ice concentration, or discharge via an approved sewage treatment plant — with distances defined against polar features (ice-shelf and fast ice are defined terms) rather than shoreline alone.

title: Prevention of pollution by garbage from ships
text: Prevention of pollution by garbage from ships Layers polar restrictions over MARPOL Annex V: only narrow categories such as food waste may be discharged, and then only ground/comminuted, away from land, ice-shelf and fast ice and from areas of specified ice concentration — never onto the ice — with cargo residues and other Annex V categories effectively retained on board, reflected in the ship's Garbage Record Book and Garbage Management Plan. title: General
text: General Sets the Code's scope (fire safety systems required by SOLAS Ch. II-2), applies it to ships whose keels are laid on or after 1 July 2002, defines Administration/Convention/Fire Safety Systems Code, allows Administration-approved equivalents under modern technology, and bans fire-extinguishing media that give off toxic gases in quantities endangering persons. title: Application
text: Application The Code applies to fire safety systems referred to in SOLAS Ch. II-2; applicable to ships whose keels are laid (or at a similar stage of construction) on or after 1 July 2002, with later amendments applying only to ships built on or after each amendment's own entry-into-force date unless expressly stated otherwise. title: Use of equivalents and modern technology
text: Use of equivalents and modern technology The Administration may approve fire safety systems not specified in this Code, provided the equivalence requirements of SOLAS Ch. II-2 Part F are met. title: Use of toxic extinguishing media
text: Use of toxic extinguishing media A fire-extinguishing medium that, in the Administration's opinion, gives off toxic gases/liquids/substances in quantities endangering persons shall not be permitted. title: International shore connections
text: International shore connections Sets standard dimensions (178mm outside diameter, 64mm inside diameter, 132mm bolt circle, 4x19mm slotted holes, 14.5mm minimum flange thickness) and material/accessory requirements for the international shore connection required by SOLAS Ch. II-2, so any ship's fire main can connect to shore or another ship's fire-fighting water supply. title: Engineering specifications
text: Engineering specifications Standard flange dimensions per Table 2.1 (178mm OD, 64mm ID, 132mm bolt circle, 4 holes of 19mm spaced equidistantly, 14.5mm minimum thickness, 4 bolts/nuts of 16mm diameter x 50mm length); connections shall be of steel or equivalent material designed for 1 N/mm2 service, with a flat face on one side permanently attached to a coupling fitting the ship's hydrant and hose, kept aboard with a gasket and spare bolts/nuts/washers. title: Personnel protection
text: Personnel protection Specifies the firefighter's outfit (protective clothing, boots, rigid helmet, electric safety lamp, insulated axe, self-contained breathing apparatus of at least 1,200 l air capacity or 30 min duration, a 30m fireproof lifeline) and Emergency Escape Breathing Devices (EEBD) — supplied-air/oxygen devices for escape only, not firefighting, with at least 10 min service duration. title: Firefighter's outfit
text: Firefighter's outfit Personal equipment (water-resistant protective clothing, non-conducting rubber boots, rigid helmet, explosion-proof electric safety lamp with 3h minimum burning period, insulated-handle axe) plus breathing apparatus (self-contained compressed-air type of at least 1,200 l air volume or otherwise capable of 30 min minimum function, fitted with a low-air audible/visual alarm) and a 30m fireproof lifeline rated to a 3.5kN static load for 5 min. title: Emergency escape breathing devices (EEBD)
text: Emergency escape breathing devices (EEBD) An EEBD is an approved supplied-air/oxygen device used only to escape a hazardous atmosphere (never for firefighting or entering oxygen-deficient spaces); must have at least 10 min service duration, a hood or full face piece of flame-resistant material, be capable of hands-free carry when inactive, and be clearly marked with maintenance/manufacture/shelf-life information. An EEBD is an approved supplied-air/oxygen device used only to escape a hazardous atmosphere (never for firefighting or entering oxygen-deficient spaces); must have at least 10 min service duration, a hood or full face piece of flame-resistant material, be capable of hands-free carry when inactive, and be clearly marked with maintenance/manufacture/shelf-life information.

title: Fire extinguishers
text: Fire extinguishers Requires Administration type-approval for all portable fire extinguishers, sets minimum capacities (5kg for powder/CO2, 9l for foam, mass not exceeding 23kg) and portable foam applicator unit requirements (self-inducing nozzle/branch pipe, at least 20l foam concentrate plus a spare tank, 200 l/min minimum foam solution flow rate). title: Fire extinguishers
text: Fire extinguishers Each powder/CO2 extinguisher shall hold at least 5kg, each foam extinguisher at least 9l; total portable extinguisher mass shall not exceed 23kg with fire-extinguishing capability at least equivalent to a 9l fluid extinguisher; only approved refills may be used for recharging. title: Portable foam applicators
text: Portable foam applicators A portable foam applicator unit needs a self-inducing (or separately inducted) nozzle/branch pipe connectable to the fire main by hose, at least 20l foam concentrate plus one spare tank of equal capacity, and must produce effective oil-fire-extinguishing foam at a minimum 200 l/min solution flow rate at fire-main nominal pressure. A portable foam applicator unit needs a self-inducing (or separately inducted) nozzle/branch pipe connectable to the fire main by hose, at least 20l foam concentrate plus one spare tank of equal capacity, and must produce effective oil-fire-extinguishing foam at a minimum 200 l/min solution flow rate at fire-main nominal pressure.

title: Fixed gas fire-extinguishing systems
text: Fixed gas fire-extinguishing systems Sets general requirements (medium quantity calculation, container/piping design, control valve marking, pre-discharge alarms) plus specific requirements for carbon dioxide systems (30% free-gas volume for cargo spaces, 40%/35% for machinery spaces depending on casing geometry, two-control-releasing sequence for occupied ro-ro/container spaces) including low-pressure CO2 system provisions (working pressure 1.8-2.2 N/mm2, dual refrigeration units, dual safety relief valves). title: General
text: General Where medium protects more than one space, only the largest single-space quantity need be carried; starting-air-receiver volume is added to machinery-space gross volume for medium calculations; crew must be able to check medium quantity without fully removing containers; pressure containers are sited outside protected spaces per SOLAS II-2/10.4.3; discharge piping must withstand 925°C and pass a 5 N/mm2 pressure test where routed through accommodation; audible/visual pre-discharge alarms (at least 20s before release) are required for ro-ro/container-hold/accessible spaces; automatic release is not permitted except as the Administration allows. title: Medium quantity calculation and multi-space sharing
text: Medium quantity calculation and multi-space sharing Where a fixed gas system protects more than one space, the total quantity of medium stored need only equal the maximum required for any single space so protected; starting-air receiver free-air volume must be added to gross machinery-space volume when calculating medium quantity. title: Pre-discharge audible and visual release alarm
text: Pre-discharge audible and visual release alarm An automatic audible and visual warning device must sound and flash automatically in protected ro-ro, container, or accessible spaces for a minimum of 20 seconds before the extinguishing medium is discharged, giving crew time to evacuate; automatic release without manual initiation is barred. title: Distribution piping and container siting
text: Distribution piping and container siting Storage containers must be located outside protected spaces per SOLAS II-2/10.4.3; distribution pipes passing through accommodation must withstand 925°C temperatures and pass a 5 N/mm² hydraulic pressure test. title: Carbon dioxide systems
text: Carbon dioxide systems Cargo spaces need a minimum 30% free-gas volume of the largest space (45% for non-special-category vehicle/ro-ro spaces, two-thirds delivered within 10 min); machinery spaces need the larger of 40% (excluding upper casing) or 35% (including casing) of gross volume, reduced to 35%/30% for cargo ships under 2,000 GT with adjoining spaces, with 85% dischargeable within 2 min; occupied ro-ro/container/accessible spaces need two separate sequential controls (piping valve, then storage-container release) inside an identified, break-glass-key release box. title: High-pressure CO2 machinery space calculations
text: High-pressure CO2 machinery space calculations Machinery space CO2 systems must deliver a minimum free-gas volume equal to the larger of 40% of gross machinery space volume excluding casing, or 35% including casing; 85% of the total required CO2 volume must be discharged into the space within 2 minutes. title: Cargo & vehicle space CO2 calculations
text: Cargo & vehicle space CO2 calculations Dry cargo spaces require a minimum CO2 free-gas volume equal to 30% of the gross volume of the largest cargo hold; ro-ro vehicle spaces require 45% gross volume, with two-thirds discharged within 10 minutes. title: Dual-control release sequence and break-glass box
text: Dual-control release sequence and break-glass box Two separate controls must be operated to release CO2 into protected spaces: the first opens the main distribution line stop valve, and the second opens the cylinder storage release valves; both controls must be located inside an identified release cabinet provided with a break-glass key lock. title: Low pressure CO2 systems
text: Low pressure CO2 systems Liquid CO2 is stored at a working pressure of 1.8-2.2 N/mm2, filled to at most 95% of vessel volumetric capacity; requires pressure gauges, high/low pressure alarms, filling/discharge pipes, a level indicator, and two safety valves; two independent automated refrigerating units (each with compressor, evaporator, condenser) maintain temperature under continuous 24h operation at up to 45°C ambient; cooling water comes from at least two sea connections (preferably port and starboard) with a stand-by circulating pump. title: Low-pressure CO2 storage and volumetric fill limits
text: Low-pressure CO2 storage and volumetric fill limits Liquid CO2 must be stored in pressure vessels under a controlled working pressure of 1.8 to 2.2 N/mm²; the storage vessel must not be filled beyond 95% of its volumetric capacity to allow liquid expansion. Liquid CO2 must be stored in pressure vessels under a controlled working pressure of 1.8 to 2.2 N/mm²; the storage vessel must not be filled beyond 95% of its volumetric capacity to allow liquid expansion.

title: Low-pressure CO2 refrigeration units and relief valves
text: Low-pressure CO2 refrigeration units and relief valves Storage vessels must be served by two independent, automatically controlled refrigerating units capable of maintaining liquid CO2 pressure up to 45°C ambient temperature; two safety relief valves must be fitted so that either valve can be isolated for servicing while the other remains operational. title: Fixed foam fire-extinguishing systems

title: Fixed high-expansion foam fire-extinguishing systems
text: Fixed high-expansion foam fire-extinguishing systems System shall release manually and produce foam at the required rate within one minute (automatic release generally not permitted); foam concentrate and system performance require Administration approval per IMO guidelines; components must withstand ambient/vibration/humidity/shock/corrosion, with piping in contact with concentrate built of corrosion-resistant material; the quantity of concentrate must produce foam equal to 5x the protected space's volume or support 30 min of full operation, whichever is greater; audible/visual alarms warn of release with at least 20s evacuation time. title: High-expansion foam release and application
text: High-expansion foam release and application Fixed high-expansion foam systems must release manually and produce foam at the required application rate within one minute; the quantity of foam concentrate supplied must produce a volume of foam equal to at least 5 times the gross volume of the largest protected space or support 30 minutes of continuous full-capacity operation, whichever is greater. title: Foam concentrate and piping specifications
text: Foam concentrate and piping specifications Foam concentrates must be approved by the Administration based on guidelines adopted by the IMO; supply piping in contact with concentrate must be constructed of corrosion-resistant materials (or hot-dip galvanized steel) and withstand 925°C temperatures. title: Fixed low-expansion foam fire-extinguishing systems
text: Fixed low-expansion foam fire-extinguishing systems Fixed low-expansion foam systems for cargo pump-rooms and tanker deck cargo areas must deliver foam solution at specified application rates (minimum 6 L/min/m² for deck cargo areas) with sufficient concentrate for at least 20 minutes of continuous discharge. title: Low-expansion deck foam solution delivery rates
text: Low-expansion deck foam solution delivery rates Deck foam systems on tankers must supply foam monitors and hand hose nozzles capable of delivering foam solution to any part of the deck cargo area at a rate of at least 6 litres per minute per square metre of protected area for at least 20 minutes. title: Fixed pressure water-spraying and water mist fire-extinguishing systems
text: Fixed pressure water-spraying and water mist fire-extinguishing systems Requires Administration approval (based on IMO guidelines) for fixed pressure water-spraying systems and equivalent water mist systems protecting machinery spaces and cargo pump-rooms, water-spraying systems for cabin balconies, and water-based fire-fighting systems for ro-ro/vehicle/special category spaces; controls must be accessible, simple to operate, and grouped in as few locations as possible. title: Machinery space pressure water-spraying & water-mist approval
text: Machinery space pressure water-spraying & water-mist approval Fixed pressure water-spraying and equivalent water-mist systems protecting Category A machinery spaces and cargo pump-rooms must be approved by the Administration based on guidelines adopted by the IMO (such as MSC/Circ.1165 as amended).
