title: Cabin balcony & ro-ro vehicle space water-based systems
text: Cabin balcony & ro-ro vehicle space water-based systems Fixed water-based fire-extinguishing systems protecting cabin balconies, ro-ro spaces, and vehicle spaces must provide effective coverage across all protected decks with controls grouped in accessible locations outside protected spaces. title: Automatic sprinkler, fire detection and fire alarm systems
text: Automatic sprinkler, fire detection and fire alarm systems Requires wet-pipe sprinkler systems (dry-pipe permitted for small exposed sections or control stations; saunas need dry-pipe with 140C-rated heads); at least two independent power sources for the seawater pump and alarm/detection system on both passenger and cargo ships (one main, one emergency, with automatic changeover on passenger ships); sprinklers must resist marine-atmosphere corrosion and activate between 68-79C in accommodation/service spaces. title: Wet-pipe and dry-pipe sprinkler system rules
text: Wet-pipe and dry-pipe sprinkler system rules Sprinklers in accommodation and service spaces must be of the wet-pipe type, activating between 68°C and 79°C (saunas require dry-pipe systems with heads rated up to 140°C); dry-pipe systems are permitted only where unheated spaces risk freezing. title: Dual power sources and automatic sea pump starting
text: Dual power sources and automatic sea pump starting At least two independent power sources must be provided for the seawater pump and automatic fire alarm system (one main generator and one emergency source); the seawater pump must start automatically upon a pressure drop in the sprinkler main before the fresh-water pressure tank is exhausted. title: Fixed fire detection and fire alarm systems
text: Fixed fire detection and fire alarm systems Applies to ships built on/after 1 July 2012; defines Section (a monitored group of detectors/call points), section identification capability, and individually identifiable devices; the detection system must control/monitor all connected detectors and call points, output signals to the bridge/central control station/safety centre, monitor its own power supplies/circuits for faults, and may interface with paging/fire doors/dampers/sprinklers/smoke extraction/low-location lighting/local-application extinguishing/CCTV systems. title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines Section (a group of detectors/manually-operated call points reported at the indicating unit), section identification capability, and individually identifiable (the capability to identify the exact location/type/signal of the activated device). title: System control, power supply monitoring, and fault signaling
text: System control, power supply monitoring, and fault signaling The fire detection control panel must continuously monitor all connected loops, detectors, manual call points, and power supply circuits for faults; any fault or fire signal must activate audible/visual alarms on the navigation bridge and in the central control station. title: Detector loop zoning & section limits
text: Detector loop zoning & section limits A single section or loop of fire detectors must not serve more than 50 enclosed spaces; manual call points must be installed at all accommodation exits, service corridors, and stairways. title: Detector installation & thermal/smoke activation thresholds
text: Detector installation & thermal/smoke activation thresholds Smoke detectors must be installed in all stairways, corridors, and escape routes; heat detectors must activate before temperature exceeds 78°C in normal spaces or 130°C in boiler rooms and drying rooms. title: Sample extraction smoke detection systems
text: Sample extraction smoke detection systems Applies to cargo-space smoke detection on ships built on/after 1 January 2012; a system comprises smoke accumulators (air collection devices at sampling-pipe ends in each cargo hold, which may double as gas-extinguishing discharge nozzles), sampling pipes (sectioned so a fire's location can be identified), three-way valves (redirecting sampling pipes to a fixed gas-extinguishing manifold on fire detection), and a control panel providing continuous monitoring. title: Low-location lighting systems
text: Low-location lighting systems Requires any low-location lighting system to be Administration-approved based on IMO guidelines (resolution A.752(18)) or an acceptable international standard, guiding evacuation along escape routes close to deck level where smoke obscures normal lighting. title: Fixed emergency fire pumps
text: Fixed emergency fire pumps Not applicable to passenger ships of 1,000 GT and above (covered instead by SOLAS II-2/10.2.2.3.1.1); requires an independently driven power-operated pump with capacity at least 40% of the total required fire-pump capacity (minimum 25 m3/h for smaller passenger/larger cargo ships, 15 m3/h for smaller cargo ships); diesel-driven pumps must cold-start by hand cranking down to 0C (or via compressed air/electric/hydraulic/cartridge start if hand-starting is impracticable) and carry sufficient fuel for 3h full-load running plus 15h of reserve fuel outside the machinery space. title: Arrangement of means of escape
text: Arrangement of means of escape Sets passenger-ship stairway width calculations (minimum 900mm, +10mm per person above 90, based on a formula considering consecutive stairway loading by main vertical zone) and means-of-escape plan requirements (occupancy counts, escape routes, assembly stations, primary/secondary escape means, dimensions); cargo ships need stairways/corridors of at least 700mm clear width with handrails (both sides if 1,800mm or wider), stairway inclination generally 45 degrees (up to 60 degrees in machinery/small spaces). title: Passenger ships
text: Passenger ships Stairway width is calculated from occupancy (two-thirds of crew plus all passengers in the served area) via a formula accounting for consecutive stairways feeding into each other by main vertical zone; means-of-escape plans must show occupancy counts, expected escape routes, assembly stations/embarkation positions, primary/secondary escape means, and stairway/door/corridor widths, backed by detailed width calculations; routes from assembly station to embarkation position need not exceed 1,500mm width unless normal-condition evacuation requires more. title: Cargo ships
text: Cargo ships Stairways/corridors used as escape routes must be at least 700mm clear width with a handrail on one side (both sides if 1,800mm or wider); stairway inclination should generally be 45 degrees, not exceeding 50 degrees (60 degrees in machinery/small spaces); escape doorways must match their stairway's width. title: Fixed deck foam systems
text: Fixed deck foam systems Requires tanker deck foam systems capable of delivering foam across the entire cargo-tank deck (including a ruptured tank deck) via simple, rapid operation; sets monitor/applicator coverage (at least 4 applicators on all tankers, monitors positioned so throw covers at least 75% of the distance to the farthest protected point, port-and-starboard placement forward of accommodation) and isolation-valve requirements to segregate damaged main sections. title: Inert gas systems
text: Inert gas systems Defines cargo tanks (flashpoint under 60C), inert gas system, gas-safe space, and gas-free condition; requires the system to render/maintain cargo-tank atmosphere non-flammable — inerting empty tanks to at most 8% oxygen at positive pressure, purging without creating a flammable atmosphere, delivering inert gas at 125% of maximum discharge rate (80%/lower-capacity allowance for chemical tankers) with at most 5% oxygen content; inert gas may come from treated flue gas, an oil/gas-fired generator, or nitrogen generators (stored CO2 systems are barred unless static-ignition risk is minimized). title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines cargo tanks (including slop tanks, carrying cargo/residues with flashpoint under 60C), inert gas system (plant, distribution, backflow prevention, measuring/control devices — using flue gas, gas generators, or nitrogen generators), gas-safe space, and gas-free (hydrocarbon/flammable vapour under 1% LFL, oxygen at least 21%, no toxic gases). title: Requirements for all systems
text: Requirements for all systems The system must be designed/constructed/tested to the Administration's satisfaction, capable of inerting empty cargo tanks to at most 8% oxygen at positive pressure, eliminating tank-entry air needs except when gas-freeing, purging without creating a flammable atmosphere, delivering inert gas at 125% of maximum discharge capacity (reduced allowance permitted for chemical/product tankers) at at most 5% oxygen content; materials must resist gas/liquid corrosion; supply may be treated flue gas, an oil/gas-fired generator, or nitrogen generators, with stored-CO2 systems barred unless static-electricity ignition risk is minimized. title: Gas-free condition & non-flammable atmosphere criteria
text: Gas-free condition & non-flammable atmosphere criteria Inert gas systems must maintain a positive-pressure non-flammable atmosphere in cargo tanks with oxygen content not exceeding 8% by volume; gas-freeing must reduce hydrocarbon concentration to under 1% LFL with oxygen content of at least 21%. title: Blower capacity & oxygen delivery limits
text: Blower capacity & oxygen delivery limits Inert gas blowers must deliver inert gas at a rate of at least 125% of the maximum rated cargo discharge capacity of the ship; the oxygen content of inert gas delivered to cargo tanks must not exceed 5% by volume under any operating condition. title: Flue gas, oil-fired generator, and nitrogen generator specifications
text: Flue gas, oil-fired generator, and nitrogen generator specifications Inert gas may be produced from boiler flue gas, an oil-fired gas generator, or nitrogen generators; flue gas systems must include a cooling gas scrubber, two blowers, a deck water seal, and a non-return valve to prevent backflow of cargo gases into machinery spaces. title: System monitoring, alarms, and automatic shutdown valves
text: System monitoring, alarms, and automatic shutdown valves Continuous oxygen and pressure monitoring instruments must activate visual and audible alarms on the bridge and cargo control room if oxygen exceeds 5% or pressure drops below positive levels; an automatic regulating valve must close automatically if blower failure or low water seal pressure occurs. title: Fixed hydrocarbon gas detection systems
text: Fixed hydrocarbon gas detection systems Requires a central gas measurement/analysis unit with sampling pipes in all double-hull/double-bottom ballast tanks and void spaces adjacent to cargo tanks (including the forepeak); gas sampling lines must resist restriction/clogging (non-metallic materials must be electrically conductive, aluminium barred), generally need two sampling points per space (upper and lower) with exceptions for smaller/lower-deadweight ships; the analysis unit must be sited in a safe space with flame-arrested sampling lines, sequential 30-min sampling intervals, portable-instrument backup, and audible/visual alarms at 30% of the lower flammable limit. title: Gas sampling lines
text: Gas sampling lines Common sampling lines are barred except for paired sampling points; lines must prevent restriction (non-metallic materials must be electrically conductive, no aluminium); generally two sampling points per space (upper at least 1m below tank top, lower above the bottom-shell girder height but at least 0.5m from the tank bottom); ships under 50,000 DWT may use one sampling location per tank; double-bottom ballast tanks not intended for partial filling and void spaces don't need an upper sampling point; anti-clogging compressed-air flushing and a clog alarm are required. title: Gas analysis unit and detection equipment
text: Gas analysis unit and detection equipment The analysis unit sits in a safe space (e.g. cargo control room/bridge), with sampling lines avoiding gas-safe spaces except via flame-arrested, ignition-clear outlets; a manual isolating valve sits at the gas-safe-side bulkhead; equipment is housed in a gas-tight cabinet that auto-shuts-down above 30% LFL internally; detection equipment sequentially samples every protected space at intervals not exceeding 30 min, backed by portable-instrument procedures if the fixed system fails, with audible/visual alarms at the control room/bridge/analysing unit triggering at or below 30% LFL. Requirements for pipes and tubes used in piping systems and boilers: general manufacture/testing conditions, seamless pressure pipes, welded pressure pipes, boiler and superheater tubes, tubes/pipes for low-temperature service, and austenitic stainless steel tubes and pipes.

title: Iron Castings
text: Iron Castings General requirements for cast-iron components accepted for classed work, covering manufacture, chemical composition, and mechanical test requirements distinct from the steel-casting requirements of Chapter 4. General requirements for cast-iron components accepted for classed work, covering manufacture, chemical composition, and mechanical test requirements distinct from the steel-casting requirements of Chapter 4.

title: Copper Alloys
text: Copper Alloys Requirements for copper-alloy components: general manufacture/testing conditions, castings for valves and fittings, castings for propellers, and copper-alloy tubes — covering the chemical composition and mechanical test requirements for these non-ferrous castings. Requirements for copper-alloy components: general manufacture/testing conditions, castings for valves and fittings, castings for propellers, and copper-alloy tubes — covering the chemical composition and mechanical test requirements for these non-ferrous castings.

title: Aluminium Alloys
text: Aluminium Alloys Requirements for aluminium-alloy hull/superstructure material: general conditions, wrought aluminium alloys, aluminium alloy castings, and the aluminium/steel transition joints used where an aluminium superstructure lands on a steel hull. Requirements for aluminium-alloy hull/superstructure material: general conditions, wrought aluminium alloys, aluminium alloy castings, and the aluminium/steel transition joints used where an aluminium superstructure lands on a steel hull.

title: Equipment
text: Equipment Requirements for shipboard mooring/anchoring hardware as manufactured items (distinct from Part 3 Chapter 14's structural/arrangement requirements for the same equipment): anchors, stud-link chain cables, short-link chain cables, steel wire ropes, and offshore mooring chains — each section setting manufacture, chemical composition, and proof/breaking-load test requirements. Requirements for shipboard mooring/anchoring hardware as manufactured items (distinct from Part 3 Chapter 14's structural/arrangement requirements for the same equipment): anchors, stud-link chain cables, short-link chain cables, steel wire ropes, and offshore mooring chains — each section setting manufacture, chemical composition, and proof/breaking-load test requirements.

title: Welding Consumables
text: Welding Consumables Type-approval scheme for welding consumables (electrodes, wire-flux and wire-gas combinations) that Part 3 Chapter 16 requires yards to source from — consumable grading, approval test assemblies, annual inspection/re-test, and upgrading/uprating of an approved grade. Type-approval scheme for welding consumables (electrodes, wire-flux and wire-gas combinations) that Part 3 Chapter 16 requires yards to source from — consumable grading, approval test assemblies, annual inspection/re-test, and upgrading/uprating of an approved grade.

title: General
text: General Sets the general grading and approval procedure a welding consumable manufacturer must follow to have an electrode, wire, or wire-flux/wire-gas combination type-approved by IRS. Sets the general grading and approval procedure a welding consumable manufacturer must follow to have an electrode, wire, or wire-flux/wire-gas combination type-approved by IRS.

title: Electrodes for Normal Penetration Manual Welding
text: Electrodes for Normal Penetration Manual Welding Specifies the approval test assemblies (mechanical test coupons, chemical composition checks) an electrode grade must pass for normal-penetration manual metal arc welding approval. Specifies the approval test assemblies (mechanical test coupons, chemical composition checks) an electrode grade must pass for normal-penetration manual metal arc welding approval.

title: General Hull Structural Requirements
text: General Hull Structural Requirements Part 3 is the main structural strength part of the rule book, published across two volumes running to 17 chapters. Volume I (Chapters 1-9) carries the design-basis chapters — general definitions/documentation, materials and corrosion additions, structural design principles, stability, design loads, hull girder strength, hull local scantlings, finite element analysis and buckling — built on a net-scantling, direct-calculation approach. Volume II (Chapters 10-17) continues with fatigue assessment, special hull requirements (bow flare/bottom slamming, sternframes, rudder horns), openings and closing appliances, rudders, anchoring and mooring equipment, masts and rigging, hull welding, and hull inspection/workmanship/testing. Together these form the baseline hull scantling rules that ship-type-specific Part 5 requirements then build on. title: General, Definitions, Documentation
text: General, Definitions, Documentation Sets Part 3's scope of application, equivalence provision, relationship to national/international regulations, and overall design basis (design principles, design load scenarios, structural capacity assessment, rule design methods, acceptance criteria); defines the structural/dimensional terms and reference coordinate system used throughout Part 3; and lists the plans a yard must submit for information, for approval, and to be kept on board, plus loading guidance information (loading manual/instrument) requirements. Sets Part 3's scope of application, equivalence provision, relationship to national/international regulations, and overall design basis (design principles, design load scenarios, structural capacity assessment, rule design methods, acceptance criteria); defines the structural/dimensional terms and reference coordinate system used throughout Part 3; and lists the plans a yard must submit for information, for approval, and to be kept on board, plus loading guidance information (loading manual/instrument) requirements.

title: Materials of Construction and Corrosion Additions
text: Materials of Construction and Corrosion Additions Sets which steel grades (normal/higher-strength, per Part 2 Chapter 3) may be used for which hull structural members depending on thickness and location, the corrosion-protection assumptions built into the Rules, the net-scantling calculation approach (gross scantling minus corrosion addition equals the net scantling used in strength checks), and the corrosion-addition values themselves by structural member and space type. Sets which steel grades (normal/higher-strength, per Part 2 Chapter 3) may be used for which hull structural members depending on thickness and location, the corrosion-protection assumptions built into the Rules, the net-scantling calculation approach (gross scantling minus corrosion addition equals the net scantling used in strength checks), and the corrosion-addition values themselves by structural member and space type.

title: General Arrangement and Structural Design Principles
text: General Arrangement and Structural Design Principles Covers subdivision arrangement, compartment arrangement, access arrangements (including access to shaft tunnels and steering-gear compartments), and the structural-design principles used throughout Part 3: structural continuity, bottom/side/deck/bulkhead structure, cantilevers, pillars, fore-and-aft peak and engine-room arrangement, local reinforcements, stiffener/primary-supporting-member/corrugated-bulkhead detail design, and the structural idealization (effective breadth, geometrical properties) used in the direct-calculation methods of later chapters. Covers subdivision arrangement, compartment arrangement, access arrangements (including access to shaft tunnels and steering-gear compartments), and the structural-design principles used throughout Part 3: structural continuity, bottom/side/deck/bulkhead structure, cantilevers, pillars, fore-and-aft peak and engine-room arrangement, local reinforcements, stiffener/primary-supporting-member/corrugated-bulkhead detail design, and the structural idealization (effective breadth, geometrical properties) used in the direct-calculation methods of later chapters.

title: Stability
text: Stability Sets the documentation requirements for intact and damage stability assessment and for the damage control plan/booklet each ship must carry — the classification-rule counterpart to (and cross-referencing) SOLAS Chapter II-1's own subdivision and damage-stability regulations. Sets the documentation requirements for intact and damage stability assessment and for the damage control plan/booklet each ship must carry — the classification-rule counterpart to (and cross-referencing) SOLAS Chapter II-1's own subdivision and damage-stability regulations.

title: Design Loads
text: Design Loads Defines the load-definition criteria and probability levels used for strength and fatigue assessment throughout Part 3: ship motions and accelerations, hull girder loads (still-water and dynamic vertical bending moment/shear force, with sign convention), external loads (sea pressure, deck loads, superstructure pressures), internal loads (liquid/dry-bulk-cargo pressures), the design load scenarios combining these for strength and fatigue checks, loading conditions, and dedicated guidelines for ballast loading conditions of cargo vessels using partially-filled ballast tanks. Defines the load-definition criteria and probability levels used for strength and fatigue assessment throughout Part 3: ship motions and accelerations, hull girder loads (still-water and dynamic vertical bending moment/shear force, with sign convention), external loads (sea pressure, deck loads, superstructure pressures), internal loads (liquid/dry-bulk-cargo pressures), the design load scenarios combining these for strength and fatigue checks, loading conditions, and dedicated guidelines for ballast loading conditions of cargo vessels using partially-filled ballast tanks.

title: Hull Girder Strength
text: Hull Girder Strength Sets the direct-calculation checks on the ship as a single hull girder: strength characteristics of hull-girder transverse sections, vertical hull-girder bending and shear strength, the hull-girder yield check (including ships with large deck openings, via an equivalent-stress approach), and the hull-girder ultimate-strength check (ultimate bending loads versus ultimate bending capacity) — with an appendix on direct calculation of shear flow. Sets the direct-calculation checks on the ship as a single hull girder: strength characteristics of hull-girder transverse sections, vertical hull-girder bending and shear strength, the hull-girder yield check (including ships with large deck openings, via an equivalent-stress approach), and the hull-girder ultimate-strength check (ultimate bending loads versus ultimate bending capacity) — with an appendix on direct calculation of shear flow.

title: Hull Local Scantlings
text: Hull Local Scantlings Sets the local (as opposed to hull-girder) scantling requirements for plating, stiffeners, and primary supporting members subjected to lateral pressure: load application/combination, minimum thickness rules, plating/stiffener/PSM scantling formulae, advanced calculation methods, pillars, intersections between stiffeners and primary supporting members, superstructure/deckhouse/companionway scantlings (including aluminium deckhouses), bulwarks and guard rails, and means of embarkation/disembarkation (gangways, accommodation ladders). Sets the local (as opposed to hull-girder) scantling requirements for plating, stiffeners, and primary supporting members subjected to lateral pressure: load application/combination, minimum thickness rules, plating/stiffener/PSM scantling formulae, advanced calculation methods, pillars, intersections between stiffeners and primary supporting members, superstructure/deckhouse/companionway scantlings (including aluminium deckhouses), bulwarks and guard rails, and means of embarkation/disembarkation (gangways, accommodation ladders).

title: Finite Element Analysis
text: Finite Element Analysis Sets when and how finite element analysis must supplement the direct-calculation methods of Chapters 6-7: scope and types of FE analysis (full-ship, cargo-hold, local structural strength), net-scantling modelling approach, material properties, element types, and the analysis-report submission requirements. Sets when and how finite element analysis must supplement the direct-calculation methods of Chapters 6-7: scope and types of FE analysis (full-ship, cargo-hold, local structural strength), net-scantling modelling approach, material properties, element types, and the analysis-report submission requirements.

title: Buckling
text: Buckling Sets the buckling-strength checks for plates and stiffened panels under the loads defined in Chapter 5: slenderness requirements, buckling requirements for plates and for stiffeners, and the buckling-capacity calculation methods used to confirm a panel will not buckle under design loading. Sets the buckling-strength checks for plates and stiffened panels under the loads defined in Chapter 5: slenderness requirements, buckling requirements for plates and for stiffeners, and the buckling-capacity calculation methods used to confirm a panel will not buckle under design loading.

title: Fatigue
text: Fatigue Sets the fatigue-assessment methodology for structural details prone to cyclic loading: the corrosion model and fatigue failure modes assumed, simplified stress analysis (longitudinal end connections, global/local bending stress, stress concentration factors), finite-element stress analysis for hot-spot stress at welded connections, S-N curves and cumulative damage calculation, weld-improvement methods, and a Detail Design Standard appendix. Sets the fatigue-assessment methodology for structural details prone to cyclic loading: the corrosion model and fatigue failure modes assumed, simplified stress analysis (longitudinal end connections, global/local bending stress, stress concentration factors), finite-element stress analysis for hot-spot stress at welded connections, S-N curves and cumulative damage calculation, weld-improvement methods, and a Detail Design Standard appendix.

title: Special Hull Requirements
text: Special Hull Requirements Sets structural requirements for specific hull locations and load cases beyond the general scantling rules: bow flare impact, bottom slamming, stern slamming, wheel loading (ro-ro decks), and special hull structures (stems, keels, breasthooks, sternframes and appendages, rudder posts/horns, propeller shaft brackets/bossings, sea chests, thruster tunnels, machinery foundations, bilge keels), plus tanks subject to sloshing loads. Sets structural requirements for specific hull locations and load cases beyond the general scantling rules: bow flare impact, bottom slamming, stern slamming, wheel loading (ro-ro decks), and special hull structures (stems, keels, breasthooks, sternframes and appendages, rudder posts/horns, propeller shaft brackets/bossings, sea chests, thruster tunnels, machinery foundations, bilge keels), plus tanks subject to sloshing loads.

title: Opening and Closing Appliances
text: Opening and Closing Appliances Sets requirements for hull openings and their closing appliances: access openings and weathertight doors on freeboard/exposed decks, machinery-space openings, windows/side scuttles/skylights, hatch covers and hatch coamings (types, materials, structural/net-scantling requirements, load model, strength criteria, weathertightness, securing devices), hatchways closed by portable covers with tarpaulins/battening devices, side-shell and stern doors, bow doors and inner doors, and ventilators/air pipes/discharges. Sets requirements for hull openings and their closing appliances: access openings and weathertight doors on freeboard/exposed decks, machinery-space openings, windows/side scuttles/skylights, hatch covers and hatch coamings (types, materials, structural/net-scantling requirements, load model, strength criteria, weathertightness, securing devices), hatchways closed by portable covers with tarpaulins/battening devices, side-shell and stern doors, bow doors and inner doors, and ventilators/air pipes/discharges.

title: Rudders
text: Rudders Sets structural design requirements for rudders: scope/material/testing, arrangement, design loads (rudder force and torque), rudder blade construction (double- and single-plated), rudder stock/pintle design and bearings, rudder couplings (flange, cone couplings with/without hydraulic mounting), sole pieces and rudder horns, and guidelines for evaluating bending-moment/shear-force distribution across different rudder support configurations (spade, semi-spade with one or two elastic supports). Sets structural design requirements for rudders: scope/material/testing, arrangement, design loads (rudder force and torque), rudder blade construction (double- and single-plated), rudder stock/pintle design and bearings, rudder couplings (flange, cone couplings with/without hydraulic mounting), sole pieces and rudder horns, and guidelines for evaluating bending-moment/shear-force distribution across different rudder support configurations (spade, semi-spade with one or two elastic supports).

title: Anchoring and Mooring Equipment
text: Anchoring and Mooring Equipment Sets structural and equipment requirements for anchoring and mooring gear: structural arrangement for anchoring equipment, equipment-number-based specification of anchor/chain-cable/rope sizes, anchors (including High Holding Power and Super High Holding Power types), anchor chain cables, towlines/mooring lines and shipboard fittings (design loads, safe working/towing load, direct mooring analyses, emergency towing procedure), windlass and chain-stopper design/testing, and additional requirements for deep-water anchoring. Sets structural and equipment requirements for anchoring and mooring gear: structural arrangement for anchoring equipment, equipment-number-based specification of anchor/chain-cable/rope sizes, anchors (including High Holding Power and Super High Holding Power types), anchor chain cables, towlines/mooring lines and shipboard fittings (design loads, safe working/towing load, direct mooring analyses, emergency towing procedure), windlass and chain-stopper design/testing, and additional requirements for deep-water anchoring.

title: Masts and Rigging
text: Masts and Rigging Sets scantling and construction requirements for masts (scantlings, construction details) and standing/running rigging (stay construction). Sets scantling and construction requirements for masts (scantlings, construction details) and standing/running rigging (stay construction).

title: Welding
text: Welding Governs how a shipyard gets its hull-structural welding procedures accepted by IRS: a welding procedure specification is submitted and procedure-qualification welding/testing is witnessed by the surveyor before that procedure may be used in production; also sets welder proficiency/record-keeping duties and the weld-factor tables used to size fillet welds throughout the hull. Governs how a shipyard gets its hull-structural welding procedures accepted by IRS: a welding procedure specification is submitted and procedure-qualification welding/testing is witnessed by the surveyor before that procedure may be used in production; also sets welder proficiency/record-keeping duties and the weld-factor tables used to size fillet welds throughout the hull.

title: Welders and Supervision
text: Welders and Supervision Sets the proficiency-testing and record-keeping obligations a yard must meet for the individual welders and welding supervisors performing hull structural work. Sets the proficiency-testing and record-keeping obligations a yard must meet for the individual welders and welding supervisors performing hull structural work.

title: Welding Procedure and Approval of Procedures
text: Welding Procedure and Approval of Procedures Describes the welding procedure specification (base material, thickness range, joint design, consumable, position, pre/post-heat treatment) and the procedure-qualification test the surveyor witnesses before a procedure is released for production welding. Describes the welding procedure specification (base material, thickness range, joint design, consumable, position, pre/post-heat treatment) and the procedure-qualification test the surveyor witnesses before a procedure is released for production welding.

title: Hull Inspection, Workmanship and Testing
text: Hull Inspection, Workmanship and Testing Sets the workmanship, inspection, and testing requirements applied to completed hull structure before and during construction survey — the Part 3 counterpart to Part 2's materials-testing regime, verifying that the as-built structure meets the scantling and welding requirements set out in the preceding chapters. Sets the workmanship, inspection, and testing requirements applied to completed hull structure before and during construction survey — the Part 3 counterpart to Part 2's materials-testing regime, verifying that the as-built structure meets the scantling and welding requirements set out in the preceding chapters.

title: Main & Auxiliary Machinery Requirements
text: Main & Auxiliary Machinery Requirements Part 4 covers the class requirements for propulsion machinery, auxiliary machinery, piping systems, boilers/pressure vessels, shafting and electrical installations — design approval, workshop testing, and the onboard trials needed before machinery is accepted into class. It sets the technical basis surveyors use for continuous machinery survey (CMS) item selection and for assessing machinery damage or renewal during service. title: General Requirements for the Design and Construction of Machinery
text: General Requirements for the Design and Construction of Machinery Chapter 1 is the entry point to Part 4: it fixes which machinery items must be built under survey at the manufacturer's works, the extent of Surveyor examination from first work to full-power trials, how IRS handles proposed departures from the Rules or novel machinery designs, the plans/particulars a builder must submit, the environmental design conditions (ambient temperature, humidity, list/trim inclinations, shipboard accelerations) every machinery item is designed against, and the alternative quality-assurance-based certification route for series-produced machinery. title: General
text: General Sets scope, the list of machinery items requiring works survey, extent-of-survey principles, the procedure for Rule departures or novel designs, plan-submission duties, and the standard environmental design envelope (temperature, humidity, list/trim/inclination, shipboard accelerations) machinery must tolerate. title: Trials
text: Trials Covers the general principles and sea-trial requirements used to demonstrate that installed propulsion and auxiliary machinery performs as designed before IRS accepts it into class. title: Pumping and Piping
text: Pumping and Piping Chapter 3 sets the shipboard piping-system design requirements built on the general pipe classes of Chapter 2 — bilge and ballast piping, vent/sounding/overflow/scupper and discharge piping, fuel oil systems, steam and boiler-feed piping, engine cooling water systems, and lubricating oil piping — covering plans, materials, valve/cock arrangements, and system-specific safety features such as remote pump stops and oil-fuel heating/temperature controls. title: Bilge and Ballast Piping Systems
text: Bilge and Ballast Piping Systems Covers drainage and bilge/ballast pumping arrangements for cargo holds, refrigerated spaces, peaks, tanks, cofferdams and machinery spaces, minimum bilge suction sizes, bilge pump/ejector capacity, and additional drainage provisions for passenger ships and vessels without propelling machinery. Covers drainage and bilge/ballast pumping arrangements for cargo holds, refrigerated spaces, peaks, tanks, cofferdams and machinery spaces, minimum bilge suction sizes, bilge pump/ejector capacity, and additional drainage provisions for passenger ships and vessels without propelling machinery.

title: Fuel Oil Systems
text: Fuel Oil Systems Sets design requirements for oil fuel tanks and piping, valve/cock/pump arrangements, heating and temperature-indication provisions, filling arrangements, alternate carriage of fuel oil and water ballast, oil-fuel burning arrangements, remote stop of fuel pumps and fans, and fuel oil treatment systems. Sets design requirements for oil fuel tanks and piping, valve/cock/pump arrangements, heating and temperature-indication provisions, filling arrangements, alternate carriage of fuel oil and water ballast, oil-fuel burning arrangements, remote stop of fuel pumps and fans, and fuel oil treatment systems.

title: Prime Movers and Propulsion Shafting Systems
text: Prime Movers and Propulsion Shafting Systems Chapter 4 covers the main propulsion train end to end — steam turbines, gas turbines, internal combustion engines, reduction gearing, main propulsion shafting, propellers, vibration/alignment, and thrusters — setting materials, design/construction, type-testing, factory acceptance and shipboard trial requirements for each machinery type, plus a general section on turning gear, power ratings and overload capacity common to all prime movers. Chapter 4 covers the main propulsion train end to end — steam turbines, gas turbines, internal combustion engines, reduction gearing, main propulsion shafting, propellers, vibration/alignment, and thrusters — setting materials, design/construction, type-testing, factory acceptance and shipboard trial requirements for each machinery type, plus a general section on turning gear, power ratings and overload capacity common to all prime movers.

title: Internal Combustion Engines
text: Internal Combustion Engines Sets crankshaft design, materials/material testing, crankcase ventilation and safety-device requirements, governing, and starting-arrangement requirements for propulsion and auxiliary diesel engines, together with the type-testing, factory acceptance and shipboard trial programme an engine must pass, plus additional provisions for gas-fuelled engines and handling of exhaust gas cleaning system reductants. Sets crankshaft design, materials/material testing, crankcase ventilation and safety-device requirements, governing, and starting-arrangement requirements for propulsion and auxiliary diesel engines, together with the type-testing, factory acceptance and shipboard trial programme an engine must pass, plus additional provisions for gas-fuelled engines and handling of exhaust gas cleaning system reductants.

title: Main Propulsion Shafting
text: Main Propulsion Shafting Covers material and design requirements for intermediate and thrust shafts, tailshafts and stern tube shafts, couplings (integral, demountable, tooth, flexible), interference-fit assemblies, tailshaft liners, and stern tube bearings, together with the special approval process for alloy steel used as intermediate shaft material — the shafting-design basis behind the propeller-shaft survey requirements in Part 1, Chapter 2. Covers material and design requirements for intermediate and thrust shafts, tailshafts and stern tube shafts, couplings (integral, demountable, tooth, flexible), interference-fit assemblies, tailshaft liners, and stern tube bearings, together with the special approval process for alloy steel used as intermediate shaft material — the shafting-design basis behind the propeller-shaft survey requirements in Part 1, Chapter 2.

title: Steering Gear
text: Steering Gear Chapter 6 sets requirements for the main and auxiliary steering gear that must be capable of moving the rudder within the Rule-specified time and angle envelope: general installation, compartment and material requirements; performance criteria for traditional and non-traditional (azimuthing, waterjet) steering systems; construction/component and steering-control-system requirements; emergency power provision; testing and trials; and additional requirements for large tankers, chemical tankers and gas carriers. Chapter 6 sets requirements for the main and auxiliary steering gear that must be capable of moving the rudder within the Rule-specified time and angle envelope: general installation, compartment and material requirements; performance criteria for traditional and non-traditional (azimuthing, waterjet) steering systems; construction/component and steering-control-system requirements; emergency power provision; testing and trials; and additional requirements for large tankers, chemical tankers and gas carriers.

title: General
text: General Sets scope, definitions, steering-gear-compartment arrangement, plan submission, materials, and the basic rudder/rudder-stock/tiller/quadrant and mechanical-steering-gear requirements common to the chapter. Sets scope, definitions, steering-gear-compartment arrangement, plan submission, materials, and the basic rudder/rudder-stock/tiller/quadrant and mechanical-steering-gear requirements common to the chapter.

title: Performance
text: Performance Sets the rudder-angle, response-time and torque performance criteria a main and auxiliary steering gear must meet, distinguishing traditional rudder-and-stock arrangements from non-traditional steering systems such as azimuthing propulsors and waterjets. Sets the rudder-angle, response-time and torque performance criteria a main and auxiliary steering gear must meet, distinguishing traditional rudder-and-stock arrangements from non-traditional steering systems such as azimuthing propulsors and waterjets.

title: Electrical Installations
text: Electrical Installations Chapter 8 is the electrical rule set for the whole ship: general design/construction and environmental requirements, system design (generator/transformer capacity, emergency source of power, essential-services diversity), cables and busbar trunking, switchgear and control gear, rotating machine construction and testing, converting equipment, miscellaneous equipment (batteries, luminaires, lightning conductors), electric propulsion systems, emergency/safety systems, hazardous-area equipment, high-voltage systems, and the final insulation-resistance/earth-continuity trials before a ship's electrical installation is accepted. Chapter 8 is the electrical rule set for the whole ship: general design/construction and environmental requirements, system design (generator/transformer capacity, emergency source of power, essential-services diversity), cables and busbar trunking, switchgear and control gear, rotating machine construction and testing, converting equipment, miscellaneous equipment (batteries, luminaires, lightning conductors), electric propulsion systems, emergency/safety systems, hazardous-area equipment, high-voltage systems, and the final insulation-resistance/earth-continuity trials before a ship's electrical installation is accepted.

title: System Design
text: System Design Sets requirements for supply and distribution system design, the number/arrangement/capacity of generators and their prime movers, transformer/converter capacity, the emergency source of power, essential-services classification and diversity factor, and circuit-level requirements for lighting, motors, fire systems, lifts and shore/external power connections. title: Rotating Machines - Construction and Testing
text: Rotating Machines - Construction and Testing Sets rating, temperature-rise, generator-control, overload, brushgear and inspection/testing requirements for the ship's rotating electrical machines (generators and motors). Sets rating, temperature-rise, generator-control, overload, brushgear and inspection/testing requirements for the ship's rotating electrical machines (generators and motors).

title: Requirements for Fusion Welding
text: Requirements for Fusion Welding Chapter 10 governs the fusion welding of pressure-retaining machinery items outside the hull-structural scope of Part 3, Chapter 16 — fusion-welded pressure vessels (boilers, receivers) and welded pressure pipes — setting manufacturing classes, preliminary and routine test requirements, construction/workmanship standards, non-destructive examination, weld-seam repair, and post-weld heat treatment. Chapter 10 governs the fusion welding of pressure-retaining machinery items outside the hull-structural scope of Part 3, Chapter 16 — fusion-welded pressure vessels (boilers, receivers) and welded pressure pipes — setting manufacturing classes, preliminary and routine test requirements, construction/workmanship standards, non-destructive examination, weld-seam repair, and post-weld heat treatment.

title: Fusion Welded Pressure Vessels
text: Fusion Welded Pressure Vessels Differentiates the manufacturing, preliminary-test and routine-test requirements for Class 1/2 versus Class 3 fusion-welded pressure vessels, and sets construction/workmanship, non-destructive examination, weld-seam repair and post-weld heat treatment requirements common to both. title: Welded Pressure Pipes
text: Welded Pressure Pipes Sets non-destructive examination, post-weld heat treatment, and heat-treatment-after-forming requirements for welded pressure pipes used in machinery piping systems. Sets non-destructive examination, post-weld heat treatment, and heat-treatment-after-forming requirements for welded pressure pipes used in machinery piping systems.

title: Additional Requirements for Special Ship Types
text: Additional Requirements for Special Ship Types Part 5 layers ship-type-specific requirements on top of the general Part 3/4 hull and machinery rules — additional structural, stability, piping and equipment provisions for tankers, bulk carriers, container ships, gas carriers and other specialised types, published in two sub-volumes. It is where notation-specific requirements (e.g. additional corrosion margins for bulk carriers, cargo containment requirements for tankers) actually live. title: Dry Bulk Cargo Carriers
text: Dry Bulk Cargo Carriers Chapter 1 layers additional structural requirements onto Part 3's general hull rules for ships that primarily carry dry cargo in bulk: Section 1 sets definitions (single- vs double-side-skin construction), class notations, design-load scenarios, access/inspection provisions and double-side-skin construction requirements; Section 2 gives bulk-carrier-specific hull arrangement, bottom/side/deck/bulkhead scantlings, protective coating and dewatering requirements; Section 3 covers ore carriers; and Section 4 sets direct strength (finite element) calculation criteria. Bulk carriers falling under the IACS Common Structural Rules are explicitly excluded from this chapter and instead follow IRS's separate CSR-based rule set. title: Bulk Carriers

title: Ore Carriers

title: Oil Tankers
text: Oil Tankers Chapter 2 sets the additional structural, arrangement, piping and cargo-system requirements for oil tankers on top of Part 3's general hull rules — ship arrangement and tank access (Section 2), longitudinal strength and hull structure (Sections 3-5), pumping/piping and cargo-handling systems (Sections 6-7), gas-freeing/venting, tank-level measurement, cargo heating and inert gas systems (Sections 8-11), combination oil/dry-cargo carriers (Section 12), and special requirements for tankers burning crude oil/slops as fuel and for asphalt carriers (Sections 13-14). title: Pumping and Piping Systems

title: Gas Freeing and Venting of Cargo Tank
text: Gas Freeing and Venting of Cargo Tank Sets requirements for cargo tank venting systems, the purging and/or gas-freeing procedures used before tank entry or hot work, and inerting/ventilation/gas-measurement provisions for the double hull and double bottom spaces around cargo tanks. title: Chemical Carriers
text: Chemical Carriers Chapter 3 applies the IBC Code framework to ships carrying dangerous chemicals in bulk — ship survival capability and cargo tank location based on cargo hazard category, ship arrangement and segregation, cargo containment, cargo transfer piping, materials/linings, temperature control, venting/gas-freeing, environmental control, electrical installations, fire protection, ventilation, instrumentation, personnel protection, and a long list of cargo-specific special requirements (from ammonium nitrate solution to vinyl chloride) plus the summary-of-minimum-requirements index used to look up carriage conditions for a named product. title: General
text: General Sets purpose, scope and definitions. The Guidelines consolidate existing SOLAS/MSC-circular fire-prevention measures into one harmonized reference for designers, owners, masters, surveyors and inspectors, developed without prejudice to existing SOLAS regulations; they explicitly exclude gas-fuel arrangements, which are covered by the IGF Code and related instruments instead. title: Definitions
text: Definitions Defines the temperature thresholds that drive the whole document: high temperature surfaces (above 220 degrees C) versus hot surfaces (below 220 degrees C, including steam systems under 2.3 N/mm2, thermal oil systems, exhaust gas piping and oil-fired/exhaust gas boilers); also flashpoint, auto-ignition point, potential ignition sources, flammable oils and lower flammable limit (LFL). title: Installation Practice
text: Installation Practice General installation-practice chapters applicable across engine-rooms and cargo pump-rooms: the fire-triangle basis for SOLAS's fuel/heat/oxygen control measures, and the detailed piping-system design/construction/installation/inspection rules (flexible hoses, bellows expansion joints, filters/strainers, insulation materials, gauges, pipe fittings) that every flammable-oil pipework component in the vessel is judged against. title: Fire triangle and SOLAS fuel/heat/oxygen control
text: Fire triangle and SOLAS fuel/heat/oxygen control Frames fire prevention as breaking one side of the fire triangle (heat/fuel/oxygen). Fuel control: spray shields, jacketed high-pressure fuel lines, piping location, tank sounding/venting arrangements. Heat control: insulation of high-temperature surfaces, temperature sensing for cargo/ballast/stripping pumps, oil-impervious insulation surfaces, spray protection of electrical equipment. Oxygen control: since air can't practically be excluded from machinery/pump-rooms, cargo pump-rooms must instead be mechanically ventilated at 20 air changes per hour using non-sparking suction-type fans. title: Flashpoint specification of oil fuels
text: Flashpoint specification of oil fuels Oil fuels with a flashpoint below 60 degrees C (closed cup) are not permitted except for restricted-service ships in guaranteed-cold climates, IACS UR M24 crude-oil-as-fuel installations, and emergency generators (minimum 43 degrees C). Storage tanks must not be heated to within 10 degrees C of flashpoint, with limited exceptions for service/settling tanks meeting vent-length, temperature-sensor, flame-screen and no-machinery-space-opening conditions. title: Piping system design, construction and maintenance
text: Piping system design, construction and maintenance Classifies flammable-oil piping as high-pressure (10.0 N/mm2 and above) or low-pressure (0.18-10.0 N/mm2), and sets design/inspection rules for flexible hoses (max 1.5 m length, 5-year pressure-test interval), bellows expansion joints, filters/strainers (steel bodies with melting point above 930 degrees C), insulation materials, pressure/temperature/level gauges (round gauge glasses prohibited; below-top-of-tank level gauges banned on passenger ships), and pipe fittings (steel/spheroidal-graphite valves under static tank pressure). title: Engine-Rooms
text: Engine-Rooms The engine-room-specific chapters: control of flammable oils (pressurized fuel systems, spray shields, jacketed high-pressure fuel lines), control of ignition sources (insulation, electrical equipment protection, ignition-source identification), control of ventilation, useful fire-safety arrangements (tank/pipe spillage prevention, multi-engine fuel isolation valves), and equipment installation (boilers, thermal oil, purifiers, oil heaters, hydraulic power packs). title: Control of flammable oils
text: Control of flammable oils Covers the classic high-pressure fuel injection failure mechanism (pressure pulses of 6-8 N/mm2 at 40-60% engine load, roughly eight times nominal system pressure, driving fatigue failures) and the countermeasures: steel fuel lines (not copper/aluminium-brass, which work-harden), flanged rather than compression connections in the injection/spill lines, multi-engine isolation valves operable from the control position, spray shields around flanged/threaded connections on lines above 0.18 N/mm2, and jacketed piping (rigid or flexible sheathed) for all external high-pressure fuel delivery lines between pumps and injectors — the classic exam topic. title: Control of ignition source
text: Control of ignition source Insulation practice for exhaust gas piping/manifolds/turbochargers (dry-type turbochargers fully insulated where practicable) and superheated steam pipes, using continuous finishing material to avoid insulation gaps at discontinuities; electrical equipment sited in well-ventilated spaces away from flammable oil pipes with metallic/impervious cable sheathing; and identification of ignition sources specific to engine-rooms — cylinder head indicator cocks, burner connections on boilers/incinerators/inert gas generators, repetitively-switched electrical panels (purifier/compressor controls), and exhaust-gas drain cocks. title: Control of ventilation
text: Control of ventilation Machinery-space ventilation must be sufficient to prevent oil-vapour accumulation under normal conditions; smoke-control means and, for Category A machinery spaces, smoke-release arrangements (reversible ventilation may suffice) are required in a fire, and fire-detector positions must account for the space's ventilation pattern. title: Useful arrangements for fire safety
text: Useful arrangements for fire safety Tanks/fittings must prevent overpressure/spillage, with overflow pipes at least 1.25 times the filling pipe's area; sounding-pipe termination is restricted (not in passenger/crew spaces, generally not machinery spaces, with self-closing blanking devices where classification societies permit machinery-space termination); and fuel-oil isolation valves for multi-engine installations (per SOLAS Reg. II-2/4.2.2.5.5) should sit at least 5 m from any engine or be protected by an obstruction so a fire on one engine can't block access to isolate the others. title: Equipment installation
text: Equipment installation Boilers need non-combustible insulation sheathed in oil-impervious material, automatic burner fuel cutoff on flame failure with alarm, and coamings around 'tween-deck boiler spaces; thermal oil heaters need remote-controllable inlet/outlet valves or gravity-drainage, secondary heating circuits for low-flashpoint cargo (or defined single-circuit safeguards), and annual/biennial tube inspection with fixed fire-extinguishing/cooling; purifier rooms need independent ventilation and fire detection/extinguishing, or equivalent scupper/spray-shield protection if not separately roomed; electric oil heaters need a 220 degrees C safety cutout independent of the normal control; hydraulic power packs above 50 kW/100 bar need a dedicated, separately-ventilated space. title: Cargo Pump-Rooms

title: Control of flammable materials
text: Control of flammable materials Aluminium pipes are prohibited in cargo piping except in ballast/inerted cargo tanks; loading pipes should run to the lowest practicable area of the tank to limit static-electricity generation; spray shields/covers are required on detachable connections and cargo pump glands. title: Control of ignition source, incl. temperature monitoring system
text: Control of ignition source, incl. temperature monitoring system Steam/heating media in the cargo area must not exceed 220 degrees C; lighting other than emergency lighting must be interlocked with ventilation. Temperature monitoring is required for cargo, ballast, stripping and tank-cleaning pumps driven by shafts through pump-room bulkheads (small pumps under 1 m3/h and bilge pumps may be exempted), with sensors at bulkhead shaft glands, bearings and pump casings, typically set to shut the pump down automatically at 60-80 degrees C within a 0-250 degrees C sensor range. title: Control of ventilation, incl. gas detection systems
text: Control of ventilation, incl. gas detection systems Cargo pump-rooms need mechanical ventilation at 20 air changes per hour, vent outlets at least 3 m from ignition sources/accommodation openings, and an emergency air intake about 2 m above the lower grating for use if the normal intake floods. title: Application
text: Application States that these Guidelines are advisory: they tell shipbuilders and Administrations how to prepare a damage control plan and set a minimum content standard for damage stability information, for passenger and cargo ships covered by SOLAS regulation II-1/19 as amended by resolution MSC.216(82). title: General purpose and presentation of the plan and booklet
text: General purpose and presentation of the plan and booklet Explains why the damage control plan/booklet exists: to give officers clear information on the ship's watertight subdivision and related closing equipment so that, if flooding occurs, they can act quickly to stop progressive flooding and recover lost stability. Also requires the material to be uncluttered, in the ship's working language, with a translation into an official SOLAS language if needed. title: Damage control plans
text: Damage control plans Sets drawing standards for the plan itself: an adequate scale, with isometric views where useful, covering inboard profile, each deck and transverse sections so as to show every watertight boundary, cross-flooding arrangement, internal/external/weathertight closing appliance and bilge/ballast pump location relevant to fighting flooding. title: Items the plan must show

title: Damage control booklets
text: Damage control booklets Requires the booklet to repeat everything on the plan, then add practical crisis-response instructions: shutting all watertight/weathertight closures immediately, sounding tanks and compartments to gauge flooding rate, and cautions about list/trim correction and the free-surface effect of any liquid transfer. label: Preamble
title: Purpose, scope and status of the list
text: Purpose, scope and status of the list Introduces this as a joint FAL/MEPC/MSC/Legal Committee circular consolidating which certificates and documents an IMO instrument requires a ship to carry, so authorities know what to expect on board and companies know what to have ready. It covers only IMO-instrument certificates (not class, flag-state-only or other governmental paperwork), confirms electronic certificates/record books are acceptable per the Organization's own guidelines, states the list is not to be used as the authority for port State control inspections (the underlying convention text governs that), and records that this 2022 edition supersedes the prior 2017 edition. title: Certificates and documents required of all ships to which the referenced convention applies
text: Certificates and documents required of all ships to which the referenced convention applies The largest section of the annex: every certificate, record book or manual an IMO instrument requires irrespective of ship type, spanning tonnage and load line documents, SOLAS construction/fire/life-saving/navigation records, ISM and ISPS certification, MARPOL pollution-prevention certificates and record books, STCW competency certificates, and the AFS and Ballast Water Management certificates. label: 1a

title: Guidelines for the Fitting and Use of Fall Preventer Devices (FPDs) (MSC.1/Circ.1327)

title: Background
text: Background Traces the requirement for on-load release hooks to the March 1980 capsize of the Alexander Kielland platform, then explains that subsequent lifeboat drill and servicing accidents were traced to poorly maintained, poorly designed or poorly understood hooks that can spring open under the lifeboat's own weight even with their built-in safety interlocks. An FPD is introduced as a secondary load path for when the hook or its release gear fails or fires accidentally — explicitly not a substitute for a safe release mechanism. An FPD is introduced as a secondary load path for when the hook or its release gear fails or fires accidentally — explicitly not a substitute for a safe release mechanism.

title: Design and operation of FPDs
text: Design and operation of FPDs Sets out the two accepted FPD designs and the safeguards each needs, since an FPD that is itself mishandled recreates the very risk it is meant to remove. Sets out the two accepted FPD designs and the safeguards each needs, since an FPD that is itself mishandled recreates the very risk it is meant to remove.

title: Locking pins
text: Locking pins Locking pins must never be added to a hook by drilling without Administration approval since that can weaken it; they must be colour-coded, impossible to insert wrongly, confirmed in place before the lifeboat turns out and during descent, and removed only under a strict warning procedure immediately before the release handle is used — with removal achievable quickly from inside the craft once waterborne, and re-insertion required before the boat is hoisted clear of the water. title: Strops or slings
text: Strops or slings Wires or chains are barred because they cannot absorb shock loading; only synthetic strops/slings are acceptable, function-tested, certified to a safety factor of at least six on the fully loaded lifeboat's weight, inspected every six months, resistant to rot/corrosion/oil/UV, and marked with their in-service date — with the same removal-before-release and re-attachment-before-hoisting discipline as locking pins, plus mandatory replacement and Administration notification if a strop is ever shock-loaded. title: Drills, testing, inspections and maintenance
text: Drills, testing, inspections and maintenance Makes the master or officer in charge responsible for confirming any fitted FPD is properly in place before a drill, test, inspection or maintenance activity with people in the lifeboat, and requires crew familiarity with the specific FPD fitted, documented in the ISM Code procedures and training manual. It flags that on some tankers the FPD release point may not be reachable from inside the boat during an actual abandon-ship, so drill procedure and real-emergency procedure may legitimately differ provided both are clearly written up. title: Modification of existing hooks to fit FPDs
text: Modification of existing hooks to fit FPDs Requires the shipowner or original equipment manufacturer to obtain Administration approval before modifying an existing hook, lifeboat or davit to accommodate an FPD (for example altering tanker lifeboats so the FPD can be released from inside), with any retesting witnessed by the Administration or a recognized organization and recorded in the approval file. label: II
title: Eligibility for the Electro-Technical Rating (ETR) Certificate of Proficiency
text: Eligibility for the Electro-Technical Rating (ETR) Certificate of Proficiency Establishes four alternative entry routes into the ETR CoP, each pairing an educational qualification (10th-standard-plus-ITI trade certificate, a three-year diploma, a full electrical/electronics degree, or a General Purpose Rating course plus a mandatory bridging course) with a matching minimum period of sea-going electrical duty — from six to twelve months — on a ship of at least 750 kW propulsion power, and requires that qualifying service be logged and verified before the CoP is issued. label: TAR Book
title: Mandatory Verification of the ETR Training and Assessment Record Book
text: Mandatory Verification of the ETR Training and Assessment Record Book The sea-going service supporting any of the four eligibility routes must be documented in a DGS-approved ETR Training and Assessment Record (TAR) Book, which a Mercantile Marine Department assessing officer must verify before the ETR CoP can be issued — a mandatory checkpoint, not an optional formality. label: III
title: Progression from ETR to Electro-Technical Officer (ETO)
text: Progression from ETR to Electro-Technical Officer (ETO) Removes the earlier age ceiling for enrolling in the ETO pre-sea course once an ETR CoP holder has completed the necessary sea service, and splits the progression route into two categories keyed to whether the candidate already holds a diploma/degree in an electrical or electronics stream, each requiring a different minimum period of further sea service before the same 4-month pre-sea course and DG Shipping CoC examination. label: Category A
title: Progression Without a Relevant Diploma/Degree
text: Progression Without a Relevant Diploma/Degree An ETR CoP holder without a diploma or degree in an electrical/electronics stream needs a minimum of 24 months' further sea-going electrical-support-level service on a 750 kW+ vessel, of which at least 12 months must be logged under an approved ETO TAR Book, before attending the pre-sea ETO course and sitting the ETO CoC examinations. An ETR CoP holder without a diploma or degree in an electrical/electronics stream needs a minimum of 24 months' further sea-going electrical-support-level service on a 750 kW+ vessel, of which at least 12 months must be logged under an approved ETO TAR Book, before attending the pre-sea ETO course and sitting the ETO CoC examinations.

label: Category B
title: Progression With a Relevant Diploma/Degree
text: Progression With a Relevant Diploma/Degree An ETR CoP holder who already holds a recognized diploma or degree in an electrical/electronics stream needs a shorter minimum of 12 months' further sea-going electrical-support-level service, of which at least 6 months must be logged under an approved ETO TAR Book, before the same pre-sea ETO course and CoC examination. text: Construction — Structure, subdivision and stability, machinery and electrical installations (amendments) Adds four new defined terms to Regulation 2 (lifting appliance, anchor handling winch, loose gear, and the "installed on or after 1 January 2026" test) and inserts an entirely new Regulation 3-13 governing lifting appliances and anchor handling winches aboard ship. title: Definitions (new paragraphs 30-33)
text: Definitions (new paragraphs 30-33) Adds: (30) lifting appliance — load-handling equipment used for cargo, hatch covers/movable bulkheads, as an engine-room/stores/hose-handling/personnel-handling crane, or for launch and recovery of tender boats; (31) anchor handling winch — a winch for deploying, recovering and repositioning anchors and mooring lines in subsea operations; (32) loose gear — an article by which a load is attached to a lifting appliance or anchor handling winch without forming an integral part of it; (33) a defined test for what counts as "installed on or after 1 January 2026" for the purposes of the new Regulation 3-13, tied to keel-laying date or contractual/actual delivery date of the equipment. title: Lifting appliances and anchor handling winches (new regulation)
text: Lifting appliances and anchor handling winches (new regulation) A wholly new regulation, inserted in Part A-1 after Reg. 3-12: applies to lifting appliances, anchor handling winches, and their loose gear (with express carve-outs for MODU-certified lifting appliances, offshore construction ship equipment meeting acceptable standards, integrated hatch-cover-opening machinery, and LSA-Code launching appliances). Requires equipment installed on/after 1 January 2026 to be designed/constructed/installed to a recognized classification society's requirements or an equivalent Administration-accepted standard, load tested and thoroughly examined before first use and after major repairs, permanently marked with safe working load, and — for anchor handling winches — designed/tested to Organization-developed Guidelines. Equipment installed before that date must be brought up to the testing/examination/marking requirements by the first renewal survey on or after 1 January 2026. All such equipment, regardless of installation date, must be operationally tested, examined, inspected, operated and maintained per the Guidelines; a malfunction does not by itself render the ship unseaworthy provided the master has planned the voyage around it. label: V
title: Safety of navigation (amendments)
text: Safety of navigation (amendments) Adds two new ship-type definitions (bulk carrier, containership) and a new carriage requirement for an electronic inclinometer on larger containerships and bulk carriers built on/after 1 January 2026. title: Definitions (new paragraphs 8-9)
text: Definitions (new paragraphs 8-9) Adds: (8) bulk carrier, defined by cross-reference to the existing Chapter XII/1.1 definition; (9) containership — a ship intended primarily to carry containers. title: Carriage requirements for shipborne navigational systems and equipment (new paragraph 2.12)
text: Carriage requirements for shipborne navigational systems and equipment (new paragraph 2.12) Adds paragraph 2.12: containerships and bulk carriers of 3,000 gross tonnage and upwards, constructed on or after 1 January 2026, must be fitted with an electronic inclinometer (or other means) to determine, display and record the ship's roll motion. label: XIV
title: Safety measures for ships operating in polar waters (amendments)
text: Safety measures for ships operating in polar waters (amendments) Replaces Regulation 2 (Application) and Regulation 3 (Requirements for ships certified in accordance with chapter I) in full, and inserts a wholly new Regulation 3-1 extending Polar Code chapters 9-1 (machinery installations) and 11-1 (voyage planning) to fishing vessels, non-trading pleasure yachts, and smaller cargo ships not previously certified under SOLAS Chapter I. Replaces Regulation 2 (Application) and Regulation 3 (Requirements for ships certified in accordance with chapter I) in full, and inserts a wholly new Regulation 3-1 extending Polar Code chapters 9-1 (machinery installations) and 11-1 (voyage planning) to fishing vessels, non-trading pleasure yachts, and smaller cargo ships not previously certified under SOLAS Chapter I.

title: Application (replaced in full)
text: Application (replaced in full) Widens the chapter's application beyond SOLAS Chapter I-certified ships to also cover, unless expressly provided otherwise: fishing vessels of 24 metres in length overall and above; pleasure yachts of 300 GT and upwards not engaged in trade; and cargo ships of 300 GT and upwards but below 500 GT. Retains the existing compliance timelines for Chapter-I-certified ships (first intermediate/renewal survey after 1 January 2018) and sets a new 1 January 2027 compliance date (for Polar Code Part I-A chapters 9-1 and 11-1) for the newly-covered ship categories. Retains the government non-commercial service carve-out and the customary savings clause for States' rights/obligations under international law. title: Requirements for ships certified in accordance with chapter I (replaced in full)
text: Requirements for ships certified in accordance with chapter I (replaced in full) Restates the existing requirement — ships within Reg. 2.1.1 must comply with the Polar Code's safety-related introduction and Part I-A, and be surveyed/certified accordingly in addition to SOLAS I/7-I/10 — and adds that certificates issued under this provision are subject to the port State control regime of Regulations I/19 and XI-1/4, treated as certificates issued under Regulation I/12 or I/13 for that purpose. Restates the existing requirement — ships within Reg. 2.1.1 must comply with the Polar Code's safety-related introduction and Part I-A, and be surveyed/certified accordingly in addition to SOLAS I/7-I/10 — and adds that certificates issued under this provision are subject to the port State control regime of Regulations I/19 and XI-1/4, treated as certificates issued under Regulation I/12 or I/13 for that purpose.

title: Requirements for fishing vessels, non-trading pleasure yachts, and smaller cargo ships (new regulation)
text: Requirements for fishing vessels, non-trading pleasure yachts, and smaller cargo ships (new regulation) A wholly new regulation: ships newly brought within the chapter's scope by Reg. 2.1.2-2.1.4 (fishing vessels ≥24m LOA, non-trading pleasure yachts ≥300GT, cargo ships 300-500GT) must, on Antarctic-area voyages and on Arctic voyages beyond the flag State's territorial sea, comply with Polar Code Part I-A chapters 9-1 (machinery installations) and 11-1 (voyage planning), having regard to the Part I-A introduction and safety-related provisions. The Administration determines the extent to which chapter 9-1's paragraphs 3.1 and 3.2 apply to fishing vessels and to sub-500GT non-internationally-trading cargo ships. title: Equivalents
text: Equivalents An Administration may allow an alternative fitting/material/appliance/procedure/fuel/compliance method if it is at least as effective in emissions reduction as this Annex's own requirements, subject to reporting the particulars to the Organization for circulation and not impairing the environment/health/property of other States. title: Survey, certification and means of control
text: Survey, certification and means of control Sets survey requirements (initial/renewal/intermediate/annual/additional, plus separate EEDI-related surveys for Chapter 4), the International Air Pollution Prevention (IAPP) Certificate and International Energy Efficiency Certificate regimes, the newer Statement of Compliance related to fuel oil consumption reporting and operational carbon intensity rating, certificate duration/validity rules, port State control on operational requirements, and detection/enforcement of violations. title: Surveys
text: Surveys Ships of 400 GT and above (and fixed/floating drilling rigs/platforms) undergo initial, renewal (max. 5-year interval), intermediate, annual, and additional surveys to confirm compliance with Chapter 3; ships subject to Chapter 4 also undergo an initial EEDI-verification survey, a post-major-conversion survey, an EEXI-verification survey (first survey on/after 1 January 2023), and SEEMP-on-board verification at specified survey milestones. title: Issue or endorsement of Certificates and Statements of Compliance
text: Issue or endorsement of Certificates and Statements of Compliance An IAPP Certificate is issued after initial/renewal survey to ships of 400 GT+ on international voyages; an International Energy Efficiency Certificate is issued after the Reg. 5.4 survey to the same ship population; a Statement of Compliance related to fuel oil consumption reporting and operational carbon intensity rating is issued after the Administration verifies reported CII data and determines the ship's A-to-E rating — withheld from a ship rated D for three consecutive years or E until a corrective-action plan is in place. title: Issue of a Certificate by another Party
text: Issue of a Certificate by another Party A Party may, at the requesting Administration's request, survey a ship and issue/endorse an IAPP or International Energy Efficiency Certificate with the same force as one issued under Regulation 6; no certificate may be issued to a ship flying a non-Party's flag. title: Form of Certificates and Statements of Compliance
text: Form of Certificates and Statements of Compliance Prescribes the model forms (in English, French, or Spanish) for the IAPP Certificate (appendix I), International Energy Efficiency Certificate (appendix VIII), the fuel-oil/CII Statement of Compliance (appendix X), and — the resolution's narrower UNSP-barge clause — the International Air Pollution Prevention Exemption Certificate for Unmanned Non-self-propelled Barges (appendix XI), issued under Regulation 3.4. title: Duration and validity of Certificates and Statements of Compliance
text: Duration and validity of Certificates and Statements of Compliance IAPP Certificates run up to 5 years with detailed renewal/extension/grace-period rules; the International Energy Efficiency Certificate is valid for the ship's life (voided by withdrawal from service, major conversion, flag transfer without re-verification, or unapproved equipment changes); fuel-oil/CII Statements of Compliance are valid for the issuing calendar year plus a defined carry-over period into the next, and must be retained on board for at least 5 years. title: Port State control on operational requirements
text: Port State control on operational requirements A ship in another Party's port/offshore terminal is subject to inspection on operational requirements where there are clear grounds the master/crew are unfamiliar with essential air-pollution-prevention procedures; for Chapter 4, inspection may verify a valid Statement of Compliance, International Energy Efficiency Certificate, and SEEMP are on board, and whether the SEEMP is duly implemented. title: Detection of violations and enforcement
text: Detection of violations and enforcement Parties cooperate in detecting violations and enforcing this Annex; a ship may be inspected in any Party's port/terminal to verify compliance, with evidence of a violation forwarded to the Administration, which must investigate and pursue proceedings where sufficient evidence exists. title: Requirements for control of emissions from ships
text: Requirements for control of emissions from ships Sets the Annex's original air-pollution-control regime: ozone-depleting substances, NOx Tier I/II/III engine emission limits and Emission Control Areas, SOx/fuel-sulphur limits (0.50% m/m globally, 0.10% m/m in Emission Control Areas), volatile organic compounds from tankers, shipboard incineration, reception facilities, and fuel oil availability/quality (including bunker delivery notes and sampling). title: Ozone-depleting substances
text: Ozone-depleting substances Prohibits deliberate emissions of ozone-depleting substances (minimal recapture/recycling releases excepted); bans new installations containing such substances (other than HCFCs) on ships built on/after 19 May 2005, and HCFC-containing installations on ships built on/after 1 January 2020; requires an equipment list and, for rechargeable systems, an ozone-depleting-substances record book logging recharges, repairs, discharges, and supply.
