title: Nitrogen oxides (NOx)
text: Nitrogen oxides (NOx) Applies to marine diesel engines over 130 kW; sets Tier I (ships built 2000-2010), Tier II (built 2011+), and Tier III (built on/after Tier-III-ECA-specific dates, operating within a designated NOx Tier III Emission Control Area — North American, US Caribbean Sea, Baltic Sea, North Sea) g/kWh limits scaled by rated engine speed; certification/testing follows the revised NOx Technical Code 2008; defeat devices and irrational emission control strategies are barred. title: Sulphur oxides (SOx) and particulate matter
text: Sulphur oxides (SOx) and particulate matter Caps fuel oil sulphur content at 0.50% m/m globally (0.10% m/m within designated Emission Control Areas: Baltic Sea, North Sea, North American ECA, US Caribbean Sea ECA), with a 12-month grace period for ships in a newly designated ECA, documented fuel-changeover procedures, and in-use/onboard sampling and bunker-delivery-note requirements enforced by the fuel supplier's flag Party. title: Volatile organic compounds
text: Volatile organic compounds Where a Party regulates VOC emissions from tankers in its ports/terminals, it must notify the Organization at least 6 months ahead and ensure approved vapour emission control systems are provided; regulated tankers need an approved vapour collection system, and crude-oil tankers need a ship-specific VOC management plan covering loading/sea-passage/discharge procedures and crude-oil-washing VOC generation. title: Shipboard incineration
text: Shipboard incineration Permits incineration only in a shipboard incinerator (with a narrow boiler/power-plant exception for sewage sludge/sludge oil outside ports/harbours/estuaries); bans incinerating Annex I/II/III cargo residues, PCBs, heavy-metal-contaminated garbage, halogenated refined petroleum products, and non-ship-generated sewage sludge/sludge oil/exhaust-gas-cleaning residues; PVC incineration is barred except in IMO-type-approved incinerators; sets combustion-chamber gas-outlet temperature monitoring requirements (850-1,200°C). title: Reception facilities
text: Reception facilities Each Party must provide adequate port/terminal/repair-port/ship-breaking reception facilities for ozone-depleting substances, related equipment, and exhaust-gas-cleaning-system residues, without undue delay to ships; small island developing States may satisfy this via regional arrangements; a Party must notify the Organization of any port/terminal unable to accept these substances, or of inadequate/unavailable facilities. title: Fuel oil availability and quality
text: Fuel oil availability and quality Parties must promote compliant fuel-oil availability; a non-compliant ship may present evidence of a genuine, documented attempt to obtain compliant fuel without being required to deviate/delay its voyage. title: Regulations on the carbon intensity of international shipping
text: Regulations on the carbon intensity of international shipping The heart of the 2021 revision: applies to ships of 400 GT and above (with defined exclusions for domestic-only voyages, non-mechanically-propelled craft, platforms, and Polar Code category A ships); sets the goal of reducing shipping's carbon intensity toward the Initial IMO GHG Strategy's ambition via technical (EEDI/EEXI, Reg. 22-25) and operational (SEEMP/data collection/CII, Reg. 26-28) requirements, plus technical cooperation provisions (Reg. 29). title: Goal
text: Goal The goal of Chapter 4 is to reduce the carbon intensity of international shipping, working toward the levels of ambition set out in the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships. title: Functional requirements
text: Functional requirements To meet Chapter 4's goal, an applicable ship must comply with the technical carbon-intensity requirements (Reg. 22-25: EEDI/EEXI) and the operational carbon-intensity requirements (Reg. 26-28: SEEMP, data collection, CII). title: Attained Energy Efficiency Design Index (attained EEDI)
text: Attained Energy Efficiency Design Index (attained EEDI) Requires each new ship, and certain converted ships, falling within the Reg. 2 ship-type categories to calculate a ship-specific attained EEDI (indicating estimated energy-efficiency performance) backed by an EEDI technical file, verified by the Administration or an authorized organization, and reported to the Organization within 7 months of the relevant survey. title: Attained Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (attained EEXI)
text: Attained Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (attained EEXI) Requires every ship (new or existing) within the Reg. 2 ship-type categories to calculate a one-off attained EEXI, backed by an EEXI technical file, verified by the Administration or an authorized organization; a ship's already-verified attained EEDI may be used as its attained EEXI if it already meets the required EEXI standard. title: Required EEDI
text: Required EEDI Sets Attained EEDI <= Required EEDI = (1 - X/100) x reference line value, where X is a phase- and ship-type/size-scaled reduction factor (Table 1, phases 0-3 spanning 2013 to 2025+) and the reference line value is calculated per ship type using the a/b/c parameters in Table 2; the most stringent applicable required EEDI governs where a ship fits multiple type definitions; installed propulsion power must remain sufficient for manoeuvrability in adverse conditions. title: Required EEXI
text: Required EEXI Sets Attained EEXI <= Required EEXI = (1 - Y/100) x EEDI reference line value, where Y is a ship-type/size-scaled reduction factor (Table 3) relative to the EEDI reference line (e.g. 15-50% depending on ship type/size); a review of this regulation's effectiveness was due by 1 January 2026. title: Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP)
text: Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) Every ship keeps a ship-specific SEEMP (may form part of the SMS); ships of 5,000 GT+ include a fuel-consumption-data-collection methodology; ships of 5,000 GT+ within the Reg. 2 ship-type categories additionally include (from 1 January 2023) a CII-calculation methodology, a 3-year forward required-annual-operational-CII schedule, an implementation plan, and a self-evaluation procedure — with mandatory revision for ships rated D (3 consecutive years) or E, subject to verification/company audits. title: Collection and reporting of ship fuel oil consumption data
text: Collection and reporting of ship fuel oil consumption data From calendar year 2019, ships of 5,000 GT+ collect fuel-consumption data per Appendix IX, aggregate it annually, and report it to their Administration within 3 months of year-end via standardized electronic format (with special handling for mid-year flag/company transfers); the Administration transfers this data to the IMO Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Database within 1 month of issuing the ship's Statement of Compliance, which underpins an anonymized dataset and an annual Secretary-General report to MEPC. title: Operational carbon intensity
text: Operational carbon intensity From end-2023, ships of 5,000 GT+ within the Reg. 2 ship-type categories calculate an attained annual operational CII (12-month calendar-year basis) from Reg. 27 data, report it within 3 months, and receive an A-to-E rating against a required annual operational CII = (1 - Z/100) x CIIR (Z = annual reduction factor, CIIR = reference value) — C-rating's midpoint equals the required value; a ship rated D for 3 consecutive years or E must develop and implement SEEMP corrective actions; incentives are encouraged for A/B-rated ships; a Reg. 28 effectiveness review was due by 1 January 2026. title: Introduction
text: Introduction States that these 2023 Guidelines revoke the 2021 edition and take account of the harmonized survey/certification scheme across SOLAS 74/88, the Load Line Convention 66/88, MARPOL, the BWM Convention, the IBC/IGC/BCH Codes and the Polar Code. It summarises the harmonized system's core mechanics: a one-year standard survey interval (except MARPOL Annex IV, which uses only initial and renewal surveys), a renewal survey completed up to three months early with no loss of validity, a six-month time window for annual/intermediate/periodical surveys, a maximum five-year certificate validity for cargo ships (twelve months for the Passenger Ship Safety Certificate), a bounded extension system for ships unable to reach a survey port, the flexible two-inspections-per-five-years scheme for the outside of a cargo ship's bottom, and the option of a single combined Cargo Ship Safety Certificate in place of separate Equipment/Construction/Radio certificates. title: Underwater Inspection in Lieu of Dry-Docking
text: Underwater Inspection in Lieu of Dry-Docking Covers the situation where a ship cannot get to a dry dock in time for a required survey: the Administration may instead accept an additional survey at least equivalent in scope to an annual survey, a renewal survey carried out as far as practicable, and — where dry-docking specifically cannot be done — an underwater inspection of the ship's bottom standing in for it until dry-docking becomes possible. title: Remote Survey Conditions and Case-by-Case Assessment

title: Certification Thresholds by Vessel Category
text: Certification Thresholds by Vessel Category Splits Indian ships into two certification tracks: 400 GT and above (not already covered by the SPS Code) must hold an International Sewage Pollution Prevention Certificate, while smaller vessels certified to carry more than 15 persons (including private non-commercial yachts) fitted with one of the notice's approved sewage systems get an Indian Sewage Pollution Prevention Certificate instead, either following a satisfactory initial/renewal survey. River-sea and coastal-vessel categories are certified under their own separate notifications rather than this one. title: Sewage System Equipment Options
text: Sewage System Equipment Options Requires propelled ships in the certified categories to be fitted with one of three sewage-handling arrangements — a treatment plant, a comminuting-and-disinfecting system, or a holding tank of adequate capacity — and allows a holding tank to substitute for a treatment plant where a ship's offshore voyages are only occasional and the tank capacity is matched to voyage duration and persons carried. Smaller vessels below the certification threshold that lack any installed system must instead rely on shore/portable toilet facilities or pump out an onboard holding tank ashore. title: Exceptional Storage of Treated Wastewater or Grey Water in Ballast Tanks

title: Administration
text: Administration Flag State Flag Administration The government of the State whose flag the ship is entitled to fly. The government of the State whose flag the ship is entitled to fly — identical wording to SOLAS's own definition, which the FSS Code cross-references directly rather than restating independently in substance.

title: Bunkering
text: Bunkering Fuel bunkering LNG bunkering The transfer of liquid or gaseous fuel from land-based or floating facilities into a ship's permanent tanks, or the connection of portable tanks to the ship's fuel supply system.

title: Hazardous area
text: Hazardous area Hazardous zone Area classification An area in which an explosive gas atmosphere is or may be expected to be present, in quantities requiring special precautions for the construction, installation, and use of equipment. Classified into Zone 0, Zone 1, and Zone 2 based on frequency and duration of explosive atmosphere presence.

title: Major Conversion
text: Major Conversion Major Character Modification A conversion of an existing ship is treated as a 'major conversion' if it substantially alters the ship's dimensions or carrying capacity, changes the ship's type, is intended (in the Administration's view) to substantially prolong the ship's life, or otherwise alters the ship so much that — had it been built new in that form — provisions of MARPOL not applicable to it as an existing ship would now apply. The practical effect is that a major-conversion ship is generally held to new-ship construction/equipment standards rather than the lighter existing-ship standards. SOLAS does not use the identical defined term, but Chapter II-1 Regulation 1 (Application) reaches the same practical result through different wording: repairs, alterations and modifications 'of a major character' (and outfitting related to them) must meet the requirements for a new ship, so far as the Administration considers reasonable and practicable. Related concept, not an identically-worded definition — flagged here deliberately rather than presented as a matching quote. Annex VI defines 'major conversion' using the same four general limbs as Annex I (substantially altering dimensions/carrying capacity/engine power; changing ship type; substantially prolonging the ship's life in the Administration's opinion; or otherwise making the ship subject to new-ship provisions it would not otherwise meet) plus a fifth limb unique to this Annex: a conversion that substantially alters the ship's energy efficiency and includes any modification that could cause the ship to exceed its applicable required EEDI (Reg. 24) or required EEXI (Reg. 25). This fifth limb is the genuinely distinct addition the 2021 revision made to the term.

title: Lifeboat

title: Company
text: Company Shipowner Ship Manager ISM Company The owner of the ship or any other organization or person such as the manager or bareboat charterer who has assumed responsibility for operation from the owner and agreed to take over all ISM Code duties.

text: Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) GMDSS Maritime Radio Communications The worldwide integrated radio communications network established under SOLAS Chapter IV, incorporating terrestrial and satellite systems for distress alerting and maritime safety information.

title: Verification of Compliance

title: Masthead Light
text: Masthead Light Navigation Lights A white light placed over the fore and aft centerline of the vessel showing an unbroken light over an arc of the horizon of 225 degrees and so fixed as to show the light from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.

title: Gross Tonnage (GT)
text: Gross Tonnage (GT) Gross Tonnage GT The measure of the overall size of a ship determined in accordance with the provisions of Regulation 3 of Annex I of the 1969 Tonnage Convention.

title: Pollution Damage
text: Pollution Damage CLC Liability Damage Loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of oil from the ship, wherever such escape or discharge may occur. Any discharge into the sea of oil or oily mixture from ships of 400 GT and above is prohibited except when en route, processed through 15 ppm oil filtering equipment, and not originating from cargo pump-room bilges on oil tankers.

title: Fixed Foam Fire-Extinguishing System
text: Fixed Foam Fire-Extinguishing System High-Expansion Foam System Deck Foam System A fixed fire-extinguishing installation capable of producing and distributing foam to protect machinery spaces or deck cargo areas.

title: Hot Surface
text: Hot Surface Engine Room Hot Surface Any uninsulated surface in an engine room or boiler space having a temperature exceeding 220°C, capable of igniting fuel or oil spray. Surfaces with temperatures exceeding 220°C which may be impinged as a result of a fuel system failure shall be properly insulated.

text: Anti-Exposure Suit AES Rescue Boat Suit A protective suit designed for use by rescue boat crews and marine evacuation system parties which reduces thermal shock upon immersion and provides adequate insulation during rescue operations.

title: Periodically Unattended Machinery Spaces
text: Periodically Unattended Machinery Spaces UMS Unattended Machinery Space Machinery spaces provided with automated control, alarm, and fire protection systems approved by the Administration to permit safe operation without continuous engine-room watchkeeping.

text: Gas Fuel / Low-Flashpoint Fuel Low-Flashpoint Fuel Gaseous Fuel LNG Fuel Natural gas or other hydrocarbon fuel having a flashpoint below 60°C, carried or used on board ships for propulsion or auxiliary energy generation.

text: Fuel Preparation Room Fuel Prep Room Gas Compressor Room A space containing pumps, compressors and/or vaporizers for fuel preparation and conditioning, provided with dedicated mechanical extraction ventilation maintaining negative pressure.

text: ESD-Protected Machinery Space ESD Machinery Space ESD-Protected Space A machinery space designed to serve as non-hazardous under normal operating conditions, but provided with emergency shutdown arrangements that automatically isolate non-certified electrical equipment and gas supply upon gas detection.

text: Non-combustible material Non-Combustible Material Non-Combustible Material Test A material which neither burns nor gives off flammable vapours in sufficient quantity for self-ignition when heated to approximately 750°C, as determined by the non-combustibility test specified in Part 1 of Annex 1 to the 2010 FTP Code.

title: "A" Class division
text: "A" Class division A-Class Division A-60 Division A-30 Bulkhead A-15 Division A-0 Division Divisions formed by bulkheads and decks constructed of steel or equivalent material, stiffened, and insulated with approved non-combustible materials such that the average unexposed face temperature rise does not exceed 140°C above original temperature, nor single point 180°C, within the specified time (A-60: 60 min, A-30: 30 min, A-15: 15 min, A-0: 0 min), and capable of preventing passage of smoke and flame for 60 minutes.

title: "B" Class division
text: "B" Class division B-Class Division B-15 Division B-0 Division B-Class Bulkhead Divisions formed by bulkheads, decks, ceilings or linings constructed of approved non-combustible materials capable of preventing the passage of flame for 30 minutes, with insulation value such that the average unexposed face temperature rise does not exceed 140°C above original temperature, nor single point 180°C, within the specified time (B-15: 15 min, B-0: 0 min).

title: Surface flammability
text: Surface flammability Low Flame-Spread Surface Spread of Flame The characteristic of a material surface describing its resistance to the propagation of flame under radiant heat exposure, evaluated by measuring Critical Flux at Extinguishment (CFE ≥ 20 kW/m²), Heat for Sustained Burning (Qsb ≥ 1.5 MJ/m²), and Peak Heat Release Rate (qp ≤ 4.0 kW) per Part 5 of Annex 1 to the 2010 FTP Code.

title: Boiler (Exhaust Gas / Composite / Auxiliary)
text: Boiler (Exhaust Gas / Composite / Auxiliary) A pressure-vessel steam or hot-water generator fired by fuel oil, exhaust gas, or both (composite). Regulated from several angles at once: as a machinery-space fire risk (SOLAS II-2), as pressure-containing equipment built under class rules (IRS Pt.4), and, on ships fitted with fixed fire-fighting arrangements protecting the space it sits in, cross-referenced by the FSS Code and by MSC guidance on engine-room fire prevention. Exhaust Gas Boiler Composite Boiler Auxiliary Boiler Waste Heat Recovery Boiler

title: Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System (ODME)
text: Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System (ODME) An automated monitoring and control system mandatory for oil tankers of 150 GT and above under MARPOL Annex I Regulation 14.3. Continuously measures oil concentration (in ppm), discharge flow rate, and ship speed to calculate and record the instantaneous rate of oil discharge (in litres per nautical mile) and total oil discharged, automatically stopping discharge if limits are exceeded. ODME Oil Content Monitor Cargo Oil Discharge Monitor

title: Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP)
text: Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP) A statutory emergency response plan mandatory for all oil tankers of 150 GT and above and all non-tankers of 400 GT and above under MARPOL Annex I Regulation 37. Contains approved operational procedures, initial response steps for oil spills, coastal state contact lists, and reporting guidelines. SOPEP Oil Spill Contingency Plan MARPOL Emergency Plan

title: Lifeboat Davit System (Gravity / Hydraulic / Free-Fall Ramp)
text: Lifeboat Davit System (Gravity / Hydraulic / Free-Fall Ramp) A mechanical launching appliance designed to safely lower or launch a lifeboat from its stowed position into the water under adverse conditions of up to 10 degrees trim and 20 degrees list either way. Regulated under SOLAS Chapter III Regulation 16 and LSA Code Chapter VI Section 6.1. Davit structural members must maintain a factor of safety of at least 4.5 on ultimate tensile strength. Davit System Lifeboat Launching Davit Gravity Davit Free-Fall Ramp

title: Lifeboat On-Load / Off-Load Release Hook Mechanism
text: Lifeboat On-Load / Off-Load Release Hook Mechanism A safety-critical release system connecting a lifeboat to its falls, capable of off-load release when floating and on-load release under emergency tension. Regulated under LSA Code Section 4.4.7.6 and MSC.1/Circ.1392. Requires a mechanical hydrostatic interlock, dual color-coded reset indicators, and a minimum factor of safety of 6 on structural components and painters. On-Load Release Hook Lifeboat Release Mechanism Off-Load Hook Release Mechanism

title: Rescue Boat (Inflatable / Rigid / Fast Rescue Boat)
text: Rescue Boat (Inflatable / Rigid / Fast Rescue Boat) A specialized boat designed to rescue persons in distress at sea and marshal survival craft. Regulated under SOLAS Chapter III Regulation 17 and LSA Code Chapter V Section 5.1. Must be capable of rapid embarkation and launching, towing loaded liferafts at 5 knots, and being recovered in not more than 5 minutes in calm water. Rescue Boat Fast Rescue Boat FRB Workboat

title: Life-Saving Launching Appliance and Evacuation System
text: Life-Saving Launching Appliance and Evacuation System A general statutory term encompassing all mechanical appliances, davits, ramps, falls, winches, and marine evacuation systems (MES) used to transfer survival craft or persons safely from an embarkation deck into the sea under SOLAS Chapter III Regulation 16 and LSA Code Chapter VI. Launching Appliance Evacuation System Marine Evacuation System MES

title: Exhaust Gas Cleaning System (EGCS / SOx Scrubber)
text: Exhaust Gas Cleaning System (EGCS / SOx Scrubber) An approved exhaust gas cleaning arrangement designed to remove sulphur oxides (SOx) and particulate matter from main engine, auxiliary engine, and boiler exhaust gases. Serves as an approved equivalent compliance mechanism under MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 14.8 to allow combustion of high-sulfur fuel oil while ensuring exhaust emissions do not exceed equivalent fuel sulfur limits (0.50% m/m globally or 0.10% m/m inside designated ECAs) per Resolution MEPC.259(68) and MEPC.340(77). SOx Scrubber Scrubber System EGCS Wet Scrubber Dry Scrubber

title: Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) & Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) System
text: Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) & Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) System An exhaust gas secondary treatment system (SCR) using urea injection over a catalyst, or an engine internal recirculation system (EGR), designed to reduce nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from marine diesel engines above 130 kW output. Required to meet MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 13.5 Tier III emission limits (3.4 g/kWh) while operating inside designated Emission Control Areas (ECAs), verified per the NOx Technical Code 2008. SCR System EGR System NOx Reduction System Urea Injection System

title: Ship Energy Efficiency & Carbon Intensity Management System
text: Ship Energy Efficiency & Carbon Intensity Management System An integrated technical and operational framework governing ship energy efficiency and carbon intensity under MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 4. Encompasses technical index compliance (EEDI and EEXI per Regulation 23), operational management plans (SEEMP Parts I, II, and III per Regulation 26), Engine Power Limitation (EPL/Shaft Power Limitation), and annual operational Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII ratings A-E per Regulation 28). EEXI/CII System SEEMP System EEDI System Energy Efficiency System Engine Power Limitation EPL System

title: Main Propulsion Machinery Safeguard & Protection System
text: Main Propulsion Machinery Safeguard & Protection System A comprehensive safety and protective arrangement for marine internal combustion engines under SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 27. Includes mandatory crankcase explosion relief valves for engines >=200 mm cylinder bore or >=0.6 m³ crankcase volume, oil mist detection, automatic safety shutdowns upon critical lube-oil pressure loss, and manual override controls. Engine Safeguard System Crankcase Relief Valve Engine Safety System Lube Oil Low Pressure Trip

title: Machinery Automation, Alarm & Remote Control System
text: Machinery Automation, Alarm & Remote Control System An integrated centralized automation, alarm, and remote control architecture governing periodically unattended machinery spaces (UMS) under SOLAS Chapter II-1 Part E and Regulation 49. Encompasses single-lever bridge propulsion control, independent emergency stop, centralized control station alarm annunciation, generator load shedding, and automatic standby pump changeover. UMS System Bridge Propulsion Control Engine Order Telegraph Machinery Control System Auto-Changeover System

title: Gas & Low-Flashpoint Fuel Bunkering System
text: Gas & Low-Flashpoint Fuel Bunkering System An integrated fuel transfer and safety system under IGF Code Chapter 8 governing the safe receipt of LNG, methanol, and low-flashpoint fuels from shore or floating facilities. Encompasses bunkering station arrangements, remote-operated manifold isolation valves, dry-break self-sealing couplings, Emergency Release Couplers (ERC), nitrogen purging connections, spill drip trays, and automated ESD interlocks. LNG Bunkering System Gas Bunkering Manifold Dry-Break Bunkering Coupling Emergency Release Coupler Bunkering ESD Link Bunkering Manifold ERC Valve Ship-to-Shore ESD Link LNG Transfer System

text: Gas & Low-Flashpoint Fuel Containment System The primary cryogenic and low-flashpoint liquid fuel storage architecture under IGF Code Chapters 5 and 6. Encompasses Type C pressure vessels (MARVS >2 bar), membrane tanks, vacuum insulation, secondary barriers, protective hull distance location (B/5 or 11.5 m inboard, B/15 or 2.0 m bottom), tank filling limits (95%), pressure relief valves, and boil-off gas (BOG) re-liquefaction or combustion control. LNG Fuel Containment System LNG Fuel Tank Type C Independent Tank Membrane Fuel Tank BOG Management System LNG Fuel Storage Type C Tank Cryogenic Tank Secondary Barrier Tank Filling Limit

title: Gas Fuel Conditioning & Preparation System
text: Gas Fuel Conditioning & Preparation System An integrated mechanical and thermodynamic process system under IGF Code Chapters 5, 9, and 13. Encompasses gas compressors, cryogenic LNG vaporizers, glycol/water gas heaters, pressure reduction stations, fuel preparation rooms with negative pressure extraction ventilation (30 air changes/hour), gastight airlocks, and certified safe electrical installations. Fuel Preparation Room Gas Fuel Prep System Gas Compressor System LNG Vaporizer System Gas Heating System LNG Vaporizer Gas Fuel Heater Gas Compressor Room Fuel Prep Room Ventilation

title: Double-Walled Gas Fuel Piping & Ducting System
text: Double-Walled Gas Fuel Piping & Ducting System A safety-critical fuel transmission arrangement required under IGF Code Chapters 5, 9, and 13. Encompasses concentric double-walled pipes routing gas fuel through machinery spaces, continuous mechanical ventilation of the outer duct at 30 air changes/hour (or nitrogen inerting under pressure), gas leak detection within the annular space, and secondary containment protection. Double-Wall Gas Pipe Ventilated Fuel Duct Inerted Gas Piping Concentric Gas Pipe Double Wall Gas Pipe Annular Duct Ventilation Gas Pipe Jacketing

title: Gas Detection & Emergency Shutdown (ESD) System
text: Gas Detection & Emergency Shutdown (ESD) System An integrated safety shutdown and monitoring arrangement under IGF Code Chapters 5, 9, and 15. Encompasses infrared/catalytic gas detectors in ducts, fuel prep rooms, and airlocks; 20% LEL audible and visual alarms; 40% LEL automatic Master Gas Fuel Valve trips; double block and bleed venting sequence within 3 seconds; and automated ESD isolation of ESD-protected machinery spaces. Gas Detection System Master Gas Fuel Valve Double Block and Bleed Valve Gas ESD System Gas Safety Shutdown 20% LEL Alarm 40% LEL Trip Master Gas Valve Double Block and Bleed Valve ESD Protected Space

title: Marine Steering Gear & Hydraulic Actuation System
text: Marine Steering Gear & Hydraulic Actuation System An integrated mechanical, hydraulic and electrical system providing directional control of the ship under SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 29. Encompasses main steering gear (35° to 30° stroke timing in 28 seconds), auxiliary steering gear (15° to 15° in 60 seconds), mandatory power operation for rudder stocks >230 mm, hydraulic single-failure isolation, and dead-ship steering restoration. Main Steering Gear Auxiliary Steering Gear Electro-Hydraulic Steering System Rudder Actuator

title: Emergency Diesel Generator & Power Distribution System
text: Emergency Diesel Generator & Power Distribution System An independent emergency power generation and distribution plant required under SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulations 42 and 43. Serves essential safety consumers (emergency lighting, navigation lights, GMDSS radio, fire pumps, steering gear, internal communications) for 36 hours on passenger ships and 18 hours on cargo ships, with automatic starting and connection within 45 seconds of main power loss, operational under 22.5° list and 10° trim. Emergency Generator Emergency Switchboard EDG System Emergency Power System

title: Lifeboat (Totally Enclosed / Partially Enclosed / Free-Fall)
text: Lifeboat (Totally Enclosed / Partially Enclosed / Free-Fall) A rigid, self-righting survival craft designed to sustain ship complement in emergency abandon-ship scenarios. Regulated under SOLAS Chapter III and LSA Code Chapter IV Section 4.4. Must maintain structural integrity during 3-metre drop tests, achieve at least 6 knots speed in calm water, carry 24 hours of engine fuel, start reliably down to -15°C, and feature an approved on-load/off-load release mechanism with dual reset indicators. Survival Craft Lifeboat Free-Fall Lifeboat Motor Lifeboat TEMPSC

title: Oily Water Separator (15 ppm Oil Filtering Equipment)
text: Oily Water Separator (15 ppm Oil Filtering Equipment) A machinery space pollution-prevention system designed to process oily bilge water and separate oil residues so that discharged effluent contains no more than 15 parts per million (ppm) of oil. Mandatory for ships of 400 GT and above under MARPOL Annex I Regulation 14. Systems on ships of 10,000 GT and above must include an automatic 15 ppm bilge alarm and automatic 3-way stopping valve that redirects discharge back to the bilge tank if effluent oil content exceeds 15 ppm. OWS 15 ppm Bilge Separator Oil Filtering Equipment Bilge Separator

title: Fire Main and Fire Pump System
text: Fire Main and Fire Pump System The ship's permanent, pressurized water-fighting backbone: a piping main run to hydrants throughout the vessel, supplied by two or more independently driven fire pumps sized and numbered by ship type and tonnage, plus a segregated emergency fire pump whose entire purpose is to keep water available at the hydrants even if a fire in the main machinery space takes out every other pump on board. The system's defining engineering problem is not the pump or the pipe individually, but the segregation logic connecting them: isolating valves split the fire main so the machinery-space section can be shut down without losing the rest of the ship, and the emergency pump's space, suction, and power source must sit outside the machinery space specifically so the one fire most likely to disable the main pumps cannot disable this one too. title: ce-relevance
text: ce-relevance Examiners at Kochi MMD like to pair this regulation with a boiler/engine-room fire scenario: expect a follow-up on why the emergency fire pump's space can't be contiguous to a Category A machinery space, and on the isolating-valve logic that keeps the rest of the fire main live if the machinery-space section is shut down. Cross-reference against MSC.1/Circ.1321 for the soot-fire/fuel-leak angle examiners sometimes fold into the same question.

title: engineering-context
text: engineering-context Regulation 10 reads as a flat list of requirements, but it is really a layered defense, and the layers matter for understanding why any one paragraph exists. The fixed water-based system (2: fire main, pumps, hydrants, hoses) is the baseline every ship carries regardless of type. Portable extinguishers (3) exist for first response, before the fixed system is even needed. The additional fixed systems layered on top -- gas flooding (4), water-spray/mist (5), sprinkler/detection/alarm (7), deck foam (8) -- are not redundant with the fire main; they target specific high-consequence spaces (Category A machinery spaces, cargo holds, tanker decks) where a fire main and hose alone would be too slow or too dangerous to approach with. The regulation's real engineering center of gravity is paragraph 2.2's fire pump and emergency fire pump requirement, because it is the one paragraph explicitly designed around a failure scenario rather than a steady-state specification: the emergency pump, its space, its suction, and its power source all have to sit outside the machinery space specifically so that the fire most likely to take out the main pumps -- a machinery-space fire -- cannot also take out the ship's ability to fight it. Every other detailed requirement in 2.1 (isolating valves splitting the fire main so the machinery-space section can be shut down without losing the rest of the ship) exists to serve that same single idea: the system must survive the exact scenario it exists to fight.

title: practical-guidance
text: practical-guidance Working points a Chief Engineer actually needs, not just the regulation number. Pump siting: the pump and its suction must work at the lightest service draft the ship will realistically see, accounting for list, trim, roll, pitch, and the slow internal corrosion buildup in the suction pipe over the ship's life -- a pump that primes fine on commissioning can lose that margin years later purely from pipe fouling. A 'throw-over' sea suction is only acceptable for the second fire pump on older vessels (built before 16 December 1998 under the old MCA LY1 Code) -- not something to expect or specify on a modern build. If the pump sits more than 2 m above the lightest service draft, air-extraction priming should normally be fitted; where a positive-displacement pump is used instead, the recommended suction head limit is 4.5 m. IACS Unified Interpretation SC164 recommends the emergency fire pump specifically be self-priming where priming would otherwise be marginal. Hose/nozzle sizing is a paired decision, not two independent ones: nozzle size is picked from the pressure/discharge table against the smallest fire pump the regulations allow, and standard hose bore is 64 mm unlined, though 45 mm lined hose has been shown to match a 64 mm unlined hose's throughput while being easier to handle -- a real, evidenced tradeoff worth knowing when a smaller-diameter hose shows up in machinery spaces. One detail worth remembering precisely because it is easy to get backwards: the ballast condition of a ship entering or leaving dry dock is explicitly NOT to be treated as a service condition when assessing whether the fire pump will prime and deliver at the lightest draft the ship will see (MSC/Circ.847) -- dry-docking is not the scenario this requirement is protecting against.

title: inspection-guidance
text: inspection-guidance What a surveyor actually checks at initial survey, organized by system component -- useful as a pre-survey self-check before the surveyor arrives. Fire main: correct materials and approved-type joints fitted; hydrostatic pressure test completed (2.0x max working pressure where that pressure exceeds 7 bar at the pump discharge, 1.5x where it is below 7 bar); non-return valves fitted and accessible; isolation valves fitted, labelled, and demonstrated working; any insulated fire-main sections routed through the machinery space confirmed satisfactory. Hydrants and hoses: correct lengths and diameters supplied for each space; couplings correctly bound to hose ends; nozzle size and type correct; the required number of jets, of the required length, actually deliverable to the spaces they are meant to cover; hoses demonstrably controllable by one person at the working pressure. Fire pumps: remote and automatic start functions tested; pumps run efficiently and prime correctly; correct hydrant pressure delivered at the highest hydrant on the ship (the worst case, since pressure is lowest there); any additional non-designated pumps connected to the fire main operate satisfactorily. Emergency fire pump specifically: separation from the main fire pumps' space confirmed satisfactory; remote power sources confirmed separated from the machinery spaces; heating arrangements for a diesel-driven unit in an unheated space confirmed adequate; starting system tested to the actual standard (at least six starts in thirty minutes, at least two of those in the first ten minutes); fuel supply confirmed adequate, both the immediate onboard supply and any required reserve; pump confirmed to run efficiently, prime correctly, and deliver the correct hydrant pressure.

title: maintenance-guidance
text: maintenance-guidance What changes between initial survey and re-survey, and what actually degrades in service rather than just needing a one-time check. Re-survey re-confirms most of the initial-survey items (isolation valve accessibility, insulated machinery-space sections, hose condition, coupling security, nozzle condition, hydrant accessibility, pump start/prime/pressure performance) but adds a leak test of the fire main at maximum service pressure -- a check that only makes sense once the system has had time in service to develop leaks. Two specific, evidenced degradation mechanisms are worth tracking on their own maintenance schedule rather than folding into a generic 'inspect fire system' task: internal corrosion progressively reduces the bore of hydrant standpipes and valves below their as-built minimum (64 mm for galvanised steel, 50 mm for copper alloy), which quietly degrades delivered flow long before the pipe would fail outright -- this is a slow, cumulative loss of margin, not a sudden fault, and is exactly the kind of thing an inspection checklist alone will miss unless bore is actually measured periodically rather than just checked for gross damage. Second, where the emergency fire pump is battery-started, the batteries need active maintenance, not passive storage: they must be kept on trickle charge (with monitored visual/audible fault alarming if only one set is fitted) and stowed away from low temperatures that would reduce their output -- a battery bank that looks fine sitting in a cold space can fail the required six-starts-in-thirty-minutes test precisely when it is needed. Freezing-prone piping runs need periodic confirmation that drainage arrangements still work, not just that they were fitted correctly at build.

title: failure-modes
text: failure-modes Concrete ways this system fails, each traceable to a specific evidenced cause rather than a generic 'pump breaks' statement. (1) Both main fire pumps disabled by a single fire: if the two main pumps, their sea suctions, and their fuel/power sources are not separated by at least A0 divisions, a fire in one compartment can take out both -- this is precisely the condition that makes an emergency fire pump mandatory rather than optional (IACS UI SC162), and the same logic applies if one main pump's compartment has more than one bulkhead or deck boundary adjacent to the other's. (2) Emergency pump fails to prime or deliver when actually needed despite passing its periodic start test: priming margin degrades gradually from internal corrosion in the suction pipe and from the pump sitting too high above the lightest realistic service draft; a start test that only checks 'does it start' without also checking delivered pressure at the highest hydrant can miss this. (3) Emergency pump starting system fails cold: diesel-driven units without electric heating of cooling water/lubricating oil in an unheated space, or battery banks not kept on trickle charge or exposed to low stowage temperatures, can fail to achieve the required six-starts-in-thirty-minutes even though the pump itself is mechanically sound. (4) Hose failure under pressure: incorrect diameter/lining selection can cause a hose to 'nip' or collapse when led around the ship, most likely to surface exactly when the hose is actually run out during a fire rather than during a static inspection. (5) Ship-wide loss of fire-main pressure from a single machinery-space fire: if isolating valves are not correctly positioned outside the machinery space per 2.1, shutting down the machinery-space section to fight a fire there also cuts off hydrants elsewhere on the ship -- the isolating-valve requirement exists specifically to prevent this, and a valve installed inside the space it is meant to isolate defeats the purpose while still technically being 'a valve'.

title: regulatory-lineage
text: regulatory-lineage Regulation 10's current numbering and structure do not descend directly from the 1974 original. SOLAS Chapter II-2 was completely revised by IMO in December 2000, applicable from 1 July 2002 -- the current Regulation 10 is a product of that rewrite, not a lightly-amended version of the 1974 text. Earlier, the 1996 amendments (entered into force 1998) had already revised Chapter II-2's general introduction and Parts B/C/D. Most recently and specifically to Regulation 10: IMO Resolution MSC.409(97) amended SOLAS II-2/1 and II-2/10 to waive the approved foam-type extinguisher requirement (minimum 135 L capacity) for boilers already protected by a fixed water-based local-application fire-extinguishing system, applicable to all ships on or after 1 January 2020. Beyond textual amendments, a substantial body of IMO and IACS Unified Interpretations refines how specific sub-paragraphs are to be applied without changing Regulation 10's numbered text itself -- these are interpretive guidance, not amendments, and should not be confused with one another when tracking what actually changed the regulation versus what merely clarified it: MSC/Circ.847 (dry-docking ballast condition), MSC/Circ.1120 (multiple starting-arrangement and isolating-valve interpretations), MSC.1/Circ.1314 (FSS Code Ch.12 emergency pump capacity interpretation), MSC.1/Circ.1388 (emergency pump suction-head interpretation for cargo ships built on/after 1 January 2012), and IACS Unified Interpretations SC114, SC121, SC146, SC162, SC164, SC165. No amendment to Regulation 10 beyond MSC.409(97) (2020) was found in this research pass; this absence is a checked finding as of 2026-07-25, not an unchecked assumption -- it should be re-verified before being relied on much further past this date.

title: ai-knowledge
text: ai-knowledge Structured decision rule for reasoning about emergency fire pump compliance, distilled specifically for downstream reasoning rather than as free-text explanation. To assess whether an emergency fire pump arrangement satisfies Reg. 10.2.2 as currently understood from evidence gathered in this pass, check in order: (1) CAPACITY -- is it at least 40% of the total required fire pump capacity, and in any case at least 25 m3/h? Below either threshold, non-compliant regardless of other factors. (2) LOCATION -- is the pump space non-contiguous with the boundaries of any Category A machinery space, with no direct access between them? If access is unavoidable, is it via a self-closing airlock with the machinery-space-side door at A-60 standard? (3) STARTING -- can the arrangement achieve at least six starts in thirty minutes, with at least two of those in the first ten minutes, using a starting source independent of the machinery spaces? (4) FUEL/POWER INDEPENDENCE -- do the pump's sea suction, power source, and (where diesel-driven) fuel supply avoid routing through or depending on the machinery space containing the main fire pumps? A single 'no' on any of these four checks is sufficient to flag the arrangement for engineering review -- they are independent requirements, not a weighted score, because each one maps to a distinct failure scenario documented in this node's failure-modes record. This rule reflects only what was verified in this authoring pass (2026-07-25) and should be re-validated against the current regulation text before being relied on for an actual compliance determination.

title: components
text: components The system SOLAS II-1/29 regulates is not one machine but a chain, and each link is separately regulated. Main steering gear: the power unit(s) and actuator that move the rudder stock in normal operation -- typically a rotary vane or ram-type hydraulic actuator on modern tonnage. Auxiliary steering gear: an independent second means of moving the rudder, required specifically so a single failure cannot remove steering capability entirely -- this is the regulation's central engineering idea, not an afterthought. Rudder stock and tiller/quadrant: the mechanical link between actuator and rudder, sized against the 230 mm power-operation threshold. Hydraulic power units and piping: pumps, reservoirs, and the isolating valves Reg. 29.14 requires on large tankers specifically so a single hydraulic-line failure doesn't disable the whole system. Control system: telemotor or electric order-transmission from bridge to steering gear, including the local/emergency control position required in the steering gear compartment itself. Rudder angle indicator: independent of the control system, so the actual rudder position remains known even if control is lost. Steering gear compartment: the physical space housing all of this, itself subject to fire-protection and access requirements shared with other machinery-space regulation.

title: engineering-context
text: engineering-context Steering gear is the one system on a ship where SOLAS regulates around a single design idea rather than a list of specifications: no single failure may remove the ability to steer. Everything else in Regulation 29 -- the auxiliary gear requirement, the hydraulic isolation valves on large tankers, the independent rudder angle indicator, the separate control position in the steering gear compartment -- exists to serve that one idea, not as a checklist of unrelated features. This matters for how the regulation should actually be read: a requirement that looks like an isolated technical detail (why does the auxiliary gear need its own 60-second performance standard, distinct from the main gear's 28 seconds?) usually traces back to the same single-failure logic once you ask what specific failure it's defending against. The 230 mm power-operation threshold exists because below that stock diameter, manual steering genuinely remains a viable auxiliary means -- above it, physical human force cannot reliably move the rudder in the time SOLAS requires, so power becomes mandatory rather than merely convenient.

title: practical-guidance
text: practical-guidance Working points beyond the bare regulation numbers. The changeover to emergency/local steering is a drill, not a document -- SOLAS V/26 requires it demonstrated, and the practical sequence matters: confirm the bridge team is aware control is transferring before disconnecting remote control (Reg. 29.8.2 requires this be operable by a single person without tools, which is a deliberate design choice -- whoever is in the steering gear compartment during an actual casualty will not have time to search for a spanner), then verify rudder response to helm orders relayed by the required bridge-to-steering-gear communication link before declaring the changeover complete. The block diagram showing system configuration and changeover steps must be posted both on the bridge and in the steering gear compartment -- not filed in a manual -- because the whole point is that whoever is physically present at either end during a casualty can follow it without having read it in advance. Recording date and time of every test, check, and drill is not paperwork for its own sake: it is the evidence a PSC officer or auditor uses to confirm the 3-monthly drill interval and 12-hour pre-departure check are actually happening, not just documented as a policy.

title: inspection-guidance
text: inspection-guidance SOLAS V/26's own testing regime, which is also what a surveyor or auditor actually checks. Within 12 hours before departure: main steering gear operation; auxiliary steering gear operation; remote steering gear control systems; steering position indicator on the navigating bridge relative to actual rudder position; emergency power supply to the steering gear; the rudder angle indicator itself, confirmed against actual rudder position, not just that it moves; power failure alarms for the remote control system; power unit failure alarms; and the automatic isolating arrangements required by Reg. 29.14 on qualifying tankers. Full rudder movement is verified against each system's own required performance, not a generic sweep. Beyond the pre-departure check: emergency steering drills at intervals not exceeding three months (SOLAS V/26.4) -- a surveyor checking compliance will ask for the dated drill log, not just confirm a procedure exists. All ship's officers concerned with steering gear operation or maintenance are expected to be familiar with changeover procedures specifically -- an officer who can describe the regulation but not perform the changeover has not actually met the intent of this requirement.

title: maintenance-guidance
text: maintenance-guidance The most evidenced, and most counter-intuitive, maintenance point: hydraulic steering gear failures that present as mechanical faults are frequently actually hydraulic fluid contamination -- water ingress, metal particles from internal wear, or simply degraded oil -- and this can prevent proper operation even when every mechanical component is sound. A maintenance regime that only inspects pumps, valves, and linkages while treating fluid condition as a secondary, infrequent check is addressing the less likely cause first. Seal integrity is the specific, evidenced highest-risk item: oil leaking through seals to the surroundings has been identified as the single most dangerous failure event in steering gear risk analysis, both because it is a genuine single point of failure and because a slow leak is easy to under-prioritise against more visible defects until capacity is already compromised. For tankers of 10,000 GT and above specifically, Reg. 29.14's isolation valves are only as good as their own maintenance -- an isolation valve that has seized in the open position provides none of the single-failure protection the regulation exists to guarantee, and this is not something a routine visual check reliably catches without actually exercising the valve.

title: failure-modes
text: failure-modes Three documented failure categories, not a single generic 'steering gear failure': hydraulic power failure (the actuator loses the pressure needed to move the rudder -- pump failure, contaminated fluid, or a leaking seal, per this system's own maintenance-guidance record), rudder failure (a mechanical failure downstream of the actuator -- stock, tiller, or the rudder itself), and control failure (the order-transmission chain from bridge to actuator fails even though the actuator itself remains capable -- exactly the scenario the independent auxiliary control position in the steering gear compartment exists to route around). These three categories point to different corrective actions, which is why distinguishing them during an actual casualty matters more than recognising 'steering has failed' -- a control failure is resolved by changing over to local control per SOLAS V/26's drilled procedure; a hydraulic power failure is not. A documented illustrative case (MIW Written Answers, WA3-LIEN1.html -- see MIW Resources) traces exactly this chain: a catastrophic hydraulic lock in a rotary vane steering gear stuck the rudder hard-a-port during a port approach, with no time available to complete an emergency changeover before the vessel struck a pier -- illustrating why the drilled changeover time itself, not just its existence, is operationally significant.

title: regulatory-lineage
text: regulatory-lineage IMO Resolution MSC.365(93), adopted 22 May 2014, entered into force 1 January 2016, amended SOLAS II-1/29 to add an alternative compliance-demonstration method: a new paragraph 3.5 permitting main steering gear/rudder stock performance to be demonstrated in ways other than a sea trial at deepest seagoing draught and maximum ahead service speed, for cases where such a trial is impracticable. This is a compliance-methodology amendment, not a change to the underlying 28-second/230 mm/single-failure performance standards this repository's existing nodes already describe -- those numbers are unchanged by MSC.365(93). Beyond MSC.365(93), several Unified Interpretations refine specific sub-paragraphs without amending the regulation's text: MSC.1/Circ.1398, MSC.1/Circ.1416/Rev.1 (SOLAS II-1/28 and 29 jointly), and MSC.1/Circ.1536 (specifically Reg. 29.3 and 29.4). No amendment beyond MSC.365(93) was found in this research pass (2026-07-25) -- stated as a checked finding, not an unchecked assumption, and worth re-verifying before being relied on much further past this date, per the same discipline already applied to SOLAS II-2/10's regulatory lineage in Package 2.

title: ai-knowledge
text: ai-knowledge Structured decision rule for reasoning about steering gear compliance, distilled from this node's other records rather than independently authored. To assess whether a steering gear arrangement satisfies the regime as currently understood from evidence gathered in this pass, check in order: (1) DUAL CAPABILITY -- does the ship have both main and auxiliary steering gear, arranged so a failure of one cannot render the other inoperative? A single-gear arrangement fails regardless of any other factor. (2) PERFORMANCE -- does main gear achieve 35 degrees to 30 degrees opposite side within 28 seconds at max service speed/deepest draught, and auxiliary gear 15 degrees to 15 degrees within 60 seconds at half speed or 7 knots? (3) POWER OPERATION THRESHOLD -- if rudder stock diameter exceeds 230 mm, is power operation actually fitted, not just planned? (4) TANKER ISOLATION -- for tankers of 10,000 GT and above, are hydraulic isolation valves fitted and demonstrably functional, not merely present? (5) TESTING DISCIPLINE -- is the full SOLAS V/26 nine-point pre-departure check actually logged within the 12-hour window, and are 3-monthly emergency drills dated and recorded? A single 'no' on any of these five is sufficient to flag the arrangement for engineering review -- they map to independent failure scenarios documented in this node's failure-modes and maintenance-guidance records, not a weighted score. This rule reflects only what was verified in this authoring pass (2026-07-25) and should be re-validated against the current regulation text before being relied on for an actual compliance determination.
